title: Autovacuum log flood takes workflow database offline, stalling pipelines
trigger: Anti-wraparound autovacuum runs on the orchestration database's biggest tables produced transaction logs faster than archiving could keep up, nearly filling the dedicated log volume; relocating the logs to the main volume meant taking the database down.
impact: Pipelines, workflows and jobs were delayed on October 6, 2026 (15:30-20:30 UTC), after intermittent slowdowns from 13:30; nothing started between 15:48 and 16:38, pipelines triggered after 16:02 failed, and about 3,500 jobs never started. UI data, notifications and commit statuses lagged as well.
detection: Short-lived orchestration alerts from 10:02 were handled as routine; renewed alerts at 13:35 and again near 14:30 led to an incident being declared at 14:54, and CircleCI says the alert combination should have been recognized earlier.
fix: Engineers moved the logs onto the main storage volume (50 minutes offline), then at 18:19 UTC tuned a database parameter that restored throughput and added capacity to drain the backlog. Planned follow-ups: alerts on log-volume fill and archive lag, autovacuum tuning, removing the single transaction log bottleneck via multiple instances or a distributed database, and making clients wait rather than give up.
summary: On 6 October 2026 the CircleCI service that orchestrates all pipelines, workflows and jobs slowed and then stopped. Autovacuum on very large tables generated more transaction log than the database could archive, and the log volume approached full, which would have made the database read-only. Engineers chose to move the logs to the main disk, a step that kept the database offline for 50 minutes. Afterwards it ran at about half speed until a storage-wait setting was changed at 18:19 UTC. No alert existed for log-volume usage or archive lag; CircleCI is adding both.

title: Routing service outruns its schema migration, returning 404 for every Railway domain
trigger: A routing control plane change bundled a schema migration with a new routing service binary; since the control plane was split out of the monolith the two pipelines ran in parallel, and the binary went live first and queried columns that did not exist yet.
impact: For about five minutes on September 30, 2026 (roughly 07:35-07:40 UTC), new connections to all Railway-hosted domains, custom and *.up.railway.app alike, returned HTTP 404 in all regions, and private networking DNS lookups between services failed; existing connections and running workloads were unaffected.
detection: Internal alerting paged the on-call team as soon as route lookups began failing; engineers pinned down the cause at 07:44 UTC.
fix: Routing healed by itself once CI applied the migration and lookups retried, so no rollback was required. Railway says it has unified pipeline ordering with pre-merge checks and makes the service refuse to go live until its matching schema exists; shard-based regional rollouts for the control plane are still to be added.
summary: Railway's new distributed routing control plane tells origin proxies where each domain's traffic should go. A change preparing an authentication feature needed a modified table plus a new service version, but parallel pipelines let the binary deploy ahead of the migration. Every lookup errored, and because a recently modified fallback meant proxies no longer reused the last known route, failures were treated as unknown domains and answered with 404. The outage lasted about five minutes and ended on its own; Railway paused other work on the system to ship guardrails.

title: Stale flag cleanup crashes iOS apps using Firebase Analytics SDK
trigger: A legacy remote configuration flag was deleted (a 2-line change) while the iOS SDK still referenced it, and because the SDK never checked for a nil flag name, fetching the new payload caused a fatal error.
impact: From 17:41 PDT on September 28, 2026 the bad payload went out globally, and many Apple-platform apps (iOS and others) embedding Google Analytics for Firebase crashed once on launch before reverting to the earlier config; the backend served it for 2 hours and 11 minutes, with crash reports trailing in for hours.
detection: Developer crash alerts spiked and GitHub bug reports arrived at 17:59 PDT, paging on-call; status dashboards for both Firebase and Google Ads stayed green because they watch only server-side health.
fix: Responders found the culprit at 19:16 PDT and the rollback was live on all production servers at 19:52 PDT. Planned: an SDK patch that strictly validates payloads and skips malformed flags, an audit of other Firebase SDKs, pipeline checks that block orphaned flag references, slower phased config rollouts and SDK outage coverage on status dashboards.
summary: Google Analytics for Firebase uses remote flags as kill switches, and that mechanism ships globally by design. Cleaning up an unused flag left the iOS SDK pointing at something that no longer existed, so every active user fetching the new config hit a one-time crash. Existing tests passed the change. Status pages showed no problem, since client-side crashes are invisible to server metrics, so the team posted updates on GitHub and a console banner instead. No devices got stuck in a crash loop, but reporting lag made the incident look longer to developers.

title: Bytecode rockspec uploads give attackers code execution on LuaRocks.org
trigger: The upload path evaluated rockspecs with loadstring without restricting it to source text, so any registered user could submit hand-crafted LuaJIT bytecode that escaped the empty-environment sandbox and ran arbitrary code in the web server.
impact: Three attacker-created accounts ran shell commands on the server on July 9 and August 7, 2026, published three malicious packages, and made several hundred automated exploit attempts on August 16 and August 20; LuaRocks assumes everything on the host was read, including bcrypt password hashes, API keys, 2FA secrets and GitHub tokens. No changes to existing packages were found.
detection: A researcher reported the vulnerability, coordinated through CISA, on September 25; the earlier exploitation was only discovered during the follow-up investigation.
fix: On September 26 the loader was switched to text-only mode and files beginning with the bytecode marker byte were rejected, the site went read-only, attacker accounts and packages were removed, and all API keys, sessions, 2FA secrets and server credentials were revoked before moving to a newly provisioned server. Users are asked to upgrade the client to LuaRocks 3.12 or newer.
summary: LuaRocks.org parses uploaded rockspecs by executing them in a sandbox, but loadstring in LuaJIT also accepts precompiled bytecode, which is never verified and can reach arbitrary process memory. Three purpose-made accounts used this to run shell commands on the server between July and August 2026 and to publish three malicious packages. The hole was reported via CISA on September 25 and patched the next day. Comparing storage against an external daily git mirror found no evidence that legitimate modules were altered, though deleted packages and served content could not be fully verified.

title: Unsequenced router upgrade unplugs every fiber path in us-central1 datacenter
trigger: A technician doing a scheduled router capacity upgrade was handed the whole list of transceiver swaps with no instruction to sequence routers individually; the new higher-density transceivers were incompatible with the fabric, and all fiber paths on the affected devices were pulled within 13 minutes.
impact: On 1 September 2026, 07:41-11:52 US/Pacific (4 hours 11 minutes), VMs in part of the us-central1-b and -f zones lost connectivity, with drop rates reaching 100% at peak; GKE control planes, Cloud SQL, Spanner, Cloud Run, App Engine, Cloud VPN and regional Envoy load balancers saw errors or latency.
detection: Automated network loss monitoring and proactive probes caught it immediately and engaged network engineering and incident response.
fix: Engineers diverted traffic at 07:45 and 08:00 while on-site technicians reinserted the original transceivers, with most links back by 08:50. Planned follow-ups: retraining on checking unplugged fibers for light, fully automated sequencing for zonal upgrade workflows, work-stop alerts for live-fiber disconnects, and automatic zone evacuation cutting diversion from approximately 19 minutes to around 5.
summary: A manually orchestrated router upgrade in one Google datacenter skipped both its step-by-step sequencing and its verification checks. The technician swapped transceivers across every redundant router in quick succession, and the replacements could not talk to the existing fabric, isolating compute in parts of two us-central1 zones. A standing rule to stop if light shows on a disconnected fiber was not followed. Multi-zone deployments mostly rode it out. After restoration, Cloud Run and App Engine suffered a thundering herd of instance starts that overwhelmed file-serving tiers until emergency capacity arrived.

title: Over-scoped optical repair cuts West US datacenter off from the WAN
trigger: An automated break-fix repair on one optical device was widened by a bug in the blast radius analysis system to every optical device egressing a datacenter, and the safety check judged each device on its own instead of in aggregate, so routes were withdrawn from all of them at once.
impact: On 23 July 2026, 14:44-19:41 UTC, some customers saw connection failures and latency on traffic entering or leaving West US across services including App Service, AKS, Cosmos DB, ExpressRoute and VPN Gateway, with knock-on Microsoft 365 impact; traffic staying inside the region was fine.
detection: Service alerts fired at 14:45 UTC, but links that still looked healthy steered triage toward a WAN routing anomaly, and engineers only tied it to the break-fix work at 17:19 UTC.
fix: Automated rollback kept failing because it relied on the severed connectivity, so engineers began rolling back by hand at 17:45 UTC, finishing at 18:26 UTC. Done: the scoping defect fixed, validation and safety checks blocking work on all diverse paths, existing requests scanned. Planned by October 2026: change-ledger visibility, faster traffic anomaly detection, tooling guardrails, quicker escalation and a sturdier rollback.
summary: Azure processes single-device break-fix requests automatically because they are assumed harmless. A scoping bug turned one optical repair into a request covering a whole datacenter's egress devices, a case the per-device safety check was never built to evaluate. Physical links and adjacencies stayed up, so the failure resembled third parties being unable to reach Azure, and two investigation tracks chased misleading signals for over two hours. The recovery system also depended on the very connectivity it was trying to repair, so it retried in vain until engineers rolled back manually.

title: UI, logins and pipeline starts fail as API threads exhaust
trigger: A large internal data deletion job ran at the same time as a wave of customer project deletions, slowing a workflows data service; API connections to it had no timeout, so worker threads piled up.
impact: From 15:12 to 16:44 UTC on July 2, 2026 (about 92 minutes), some customers could not load the UI, sign in with GitHub or Bitbucket OAuth, or start pipelines, including via the API.
detection: Monitoring alerted and paged engineers at 15:16 UTC.
fix: Engineers added capacity to the affected services and stopped a long-running maintenance task; afterwards they added timeouts between the API layer and internal data services and are working on resource limits for background tasks plus earlier alerting.
summary: On 2 July 2026 CircleCI users saw errors loading the web app, signing in with GitHub or Bitbucket, and triggering pipelines for roughly an hour and a half. A maintenance deletion job combined with many customer project deletions overloaded a workflows data service. Because API calls to it never timed out, API pods ran out of threads, failed health checks, and the router had no healthy upstreams. Scaling up and cancelling the maintenance task restored service; connection timeouts were added afterwards.

title: Device Trust down after load balancer change hits shared infra
trigger: A security-hardening change to an internal service was applied more widely than intended, recreating the network load balancers behind Device Trust while routing still pointed at the old infrastructure.
impact: All Device Trust services (auth.kolide.com, app.kolide.com, APIs and device server) were unavailable for 100% of Device Trust customers in the US and EU from 19:28 to 20:28 UTC on July 2, 2026.
detection: Automated monitoring alerted at 19:30 UTC, two minutes after the change.
fix: Engineers reverted the change and recreated the load balancer with its original public configuration; planned follow-ups: require approval for destructive infra changes, map shared-component dependencies, validate against all dependent services and evaluate architectural changes for redundancy in traffic routing.
summary: 1Password Device Trust (the Kolide product) was completely unavailable for one hour on 2 July 2026; nobody could authenticate through auth.kolide.com or reach the admin console or API. A network configuration change meant for another service touched a shared infrastructure class, rebuilding Device Trust's Network Load Balancers while traffic routing still referenced the old resources. Unrelated certificate renewal errors slowed diagnosis. Recreating the load balancer correctly restored access. 1Password plans to require approval for changes that destroy and recreate critical network infrastructure.

title: Docker jobs stuck after cluster pulled without routing update
trigger: While retiring an underperforming Nomad cluster that was the only member of its routing group, engineers removed it from the pool but skipped the step that repoints routing, so traffic kept flowing to a group with zero capacity.
impact: Docker jobs queued in a preparing environment state from about 17:25 to 19:20 UTC, with backlog drained by 19:46 UTC (roughly 2 hours 20 minutes total); machine and macOS jobs were unaffected.
detection: A throughput alert fired at 17:26 UTC but was dismissed as an expected side effect of the rotation, so the problem was only recognized after support tickets arrived around 18:19 UTC.
fix: A change returning the cluster to the pool was deployed at 19:20 UTC after delays from CI smoke tests and a botched rollback; follow-ups include tooling that forces routing and availability changes together, cross-group failover, clearer alerts and faster rollbacks.
summary: CircleCI Docker jobs hung in preparing environment for about two hours on 23 June 2026. Engineers took a slow Nomad cluster out of service, but it was the sole cluster in its routing group and the routing config was never updated, leaving jobs with no place to run. An early throughput alert was written off as expected. Recovery was slowed because CI smoke tests assumed healthy clusters and a direct rollback left several active versions. CircleCI is making its rotation tooling refuse out-of-order steps.

title: Expired internal TLS cert halts TeamDynamix email and iPaaS steps
trigger: A TLS certificate for internal service-to-service authentication hit its expiry date before rotation, unnoticed by existing monitoring.
impact: For 19 minutes (3:45-4:04 PM ET) outbound platform email failed, iPaaS workflow steps did not execute and Work Management logging may have gaps, in East US and Canada.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The certificate was renewed and services recovered on their own once trust returned; certificate expiry alerting was expanded and the certificate inventory audited.
summary: TeamDynamix experienced a short backend outage when a certificate used for internal mutual authentication between services expired before it was rotated. Dependent services could no longer authenticate, so emails sent from the platform were not delivered, iPaaS step types inside ticket workflows failed, and application logging may be incomplete for the window. Renewing the certificate restored everything automatically. The company widened expiry monitoring in its observability stack to fire well ahead of deadlines and checked other certificates for near-term risk.

title: Box folder browsing fails in health-check restart cascade
trigger: At peak traffic, a backend API service whose load had crept toward capacity over a period of weeks saturated its runtime, so several instances missed health-check timeouts at once and were restarted.
impact: From 5:22 PM to 7:04 PM PDT on May 6, 2026 (about 1 hour 42 minutes), users saw failures loading folders and collections plus errors in Box AI, Hubs and Classification.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Box broke the restart loop, shifted traffic to alternate paths and added capacity; it also added runtime saturation alerts, retuned autoscaling away from CPU-only signals, is revising health checks and retries, and is load testing and cutting per-request overhead.
summary: Box users struggled to open folders and collections, and Box AI, Hubs and Classification degraded for about 100 minutes on 6 May 2026. A backend API service was saturated at the runtime level while CPU looked normal, so CPU-based autoscaling never kicked in. Slow instances failed health checks and were restarted, pushing load onto survivors, while upstream retries added more traffic, producing a cascade. Earlier small health-check blips had gone unflagged. Stopping restarts, rerouting and scaling up restored service.

title: All CircleCI modals invisible after design system upgrade
trigger: An upgraded internal design system library added Framer Motion fade animations to modals that depend on a React context populated only via DialogTrigger, which CircleCI's app does not use.
impact: Every modal and dialog in the CircleCI web app rendered at opacity 0, blocking approval jobs, SSH key management and project, org, user and billing settings for roughly 40 minutes (20:33 to 21:12 UTC by status updates); builds and data were unaffected.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The design system upgrade was reverted, restoring the old version immediately; a follow-up will reintroduce Framer Motion with all modal components supplied the required context.
summary: On 6 April 2026 CircleCI's web UI stopped showing any modal dialogs, so users could not approve jobs, manage SSH keys or edit various settings pages. A new design system release animated modals from opacity 0 to 1 using Framer Motion, but the animation read open state from a React context set only by DialogTrigger. CircleCI passes open state through props, so every modal stayed in its hidden state. Reverting the library fixed it; builds kept running throughout.

title: CDN config change caches authenticated responses on Railway domains
trigger: A CDN provider configuration update to enable Surrogate Keys for per-domain caching accidentally turned on caching for domains that had CDN disabled.
impact: For 52 minutes (10:42-11:34 UTC) about 0.05% of Railway domains had GET responses cached at the edge, so pages including authenticated data could be served to other or unauthenticated users.
detection: Internal signals combined with user reports surfaced the problem at 11:14 UTC, 32 minutes in.
fix: Railway fully rolled back the change and purged every cached asset globally; it also added caching-behavior tests before production and has sharded CDN rollouts over hours instead of minutes.
summary: A Railway engineer pushed a CDN configuration change meant to introduce Surrogate Keys, but it enabled edge caching on domains whose owners had left CDN off. GET responses lacking explicit Cache-Control headers were stored and replayed, so apps could show one user's pages to someone else; Set-Cookie headers were not cached and origin cache directives were honored. Railway reverted and purged the cache within 52 minutes, said it would email affected customers, and had already added pre-production caching tests and slower, sharded CDN rollouts.

title: Wrong kubectl context scales python.org production to zero replicas
trigger: During local Kubernetes development an engineer's context was switched to a production cluster, so scale-down commands set every deployment there to zero replicas.
impact: python.org, us.pycon.org, PyPI stats, bugs.python.org and related PSF services were unavailable for about 36 minutes (20:04-20:40 UTC); PyPI.org on a separate cluster was unaffected.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Infrastructure was brought back in dependency order using replica counts recovered from Kubernetes event history; actions include separate production kubeconfig files, research into admission controls or policies to prevent bulk scale-to-zero, and a documented recovery runbook.
summary: Several Python Software Foundation websites, including python.org and bugs.python.org, went offline after scaling commands meant for a local test environment ran against a production cluster due to an incorrect kubectl context switch. The script walked through all deployments and set replicas to zero, triggering cascading failures. The PSF Infrastructure Team restored services in dependency order, pulling original replica counts from the Kubernetes event log. Planned fixes include separate kubeconfigs, research into admission controls or policies to prevent bulk scale-to-zero, and a dependency map runbook.

title: Cleanup task bug withdraws about 1,100 BYOIP prefixes via BGP
trigger: A new Addressing API cleanup sub-task sent the pending_delete query flag without a value, which the server treated as a request for every BYOIP prefix, so the task began deleting all of them and their service bindings.
impact: About 1,100 of 4,306 BYOIP prefixes (25%) were withdrawn, leaving Magic Transit, Spectrum, CDN and egress customers on those ranges unreachable, and one.one.one.one served 403 errors, for a total incident length of 6 hours 7 minutes.
detection: Engineers noticed impact on the one.one.one.one website and then found and stopped the faulty sub-task.
fix: The sub-task was killed, customers re-advertised prefixes from the dashboard, and roughly 300 prefixes whose bindings were deleted were restored manually by 23:03 UTC; follow-ups include a stricter API schema, snapshot-based health-mediated config rollout and a circuit breaker on rapid prefix withdrawals.
summary: As part of its Code Orange: Fail Small work, Cloudflare automated removal of BYOIP prefixes with a recurring task. The task queried /v1/prefixes?pending_delete with an empty value, which the Addressing API read as all prefixes, so it began withdrawing BGP announcements and deleting service bindings from 17:56 UTC. Affected users saw BGP path hunting and connection timeouts. About 800 prefixes came back around 20:20 UTC, but bindings stripped from the edge needed a global configuration rollout to restore.

title: Anti-fraud ruleset false positive sends SIGTERM to user workloads
trigger: A new automated abuse-enforcement heuristic matched legitimate processes, including Postgres and MySQL databases, and terminated them during a staged production rollout.
impact: About 3% of services were inaccessible from 14:33 UTC, with dashboards showing wrong deployment states and slow redeploys, until automated recovery finished at 18:31 UTC.
detection: On-call engineers spotted abnormal deployment shutdowns at 14:47 UTC, 14 minutes into the rollout, alongside customer reports.
fix: Railway reverted the ruleset at 14:56 UTC, restored restart ability and automatically recovered affected deployments, and will add broader false-positive testing, longer observation windows, tier-based rollouts and protections for known process types.
summary: Railway rolled out a new anti-fraud rule targeting a freshly found abuse pattern after staging tests and a production dry run looked clean. Once enforcement went live, its matching was too broad: it put legitimate workloads into a forced pause state and sent SIGTERM to apps and databases such as Postgres and MySQL, affecting under 3% of the fleet. Users saw unreachable services, networking errors and stale dashboard status. Engineers reverted the change, ran automated recovery for all impacted deployments, and tightened review of fingerprinting-based enforcement.

title: DNS provider failure makes Clerk APIs unresolvable for some clients
trigger: All four authoritative nameservers at Clerk's external DNS provider failed simultaneously at 17:06 UTC.
impact: Authoritative resolution for Clerk's APIs was down for 2 hours 32 minutes; most traffic still succeeded (above 95% of expected volume), but clients that could not resolve the APIs saw a full outage, the Dashboard was unreachable for some, and auth emails failed DKIM/SPF lookups and bounced or landed in spam.
detection: Detection was slow because alerting never probed the authoritative nameservers directly and uptime checks were masked by long record TTLs.
fix: Caching, fallback resolvers and emergency guidance to customers carried most traffic through; follow-ups include an independent failover DNS provider, moving domains off the provider's registrar, nameserver health alerts and redundant auth email delivery.
summary: Clerk's authentication APIs became unresolvable for a subset of users when its DNS provider lost all four authoritative nameservers across two ASNs. Backend services stayed healthy and caching kept successful request volume above 95% of normal, yet affected apps could not reach Clerk, clerk.com Dashboard access failed, and sign-in emails missed DKIM/SPF checks. Clerk had no secondary DNS provider and could not change nameservers because the same vendor was its registrar. It is adding an independent provider and direct nameserver monitoring.

title: Automated policy change leaks IPv6 routes from Miami router
trigger: An automation change that removed Bogotá prefix lists from Miami export policies left terms matching route-type internal, which in Junos also matches iBGP routes, so peer-learned IPv6 prefixes were exported to transit providers and peers.
impact: For 25 minutes (20:25 to 20:50 UTC) external networks such as Meta had IPv6 traffic pulled through Miami, congesting the Miami-Atlanta backbone, raising loss and latency for some Cloudflare customers and dropping about 12Gbps at peak in firewall filters.
detection: The network team began investigating unexpected route advertisements from Miami at 20:40 UTC, 15 minutes after the change.
fix: An operator manually reverted the router config and paused automation on it at 20:50 UTC, the code change was reverted later; follow-ups include patching the policy automation, earlier detection of bad automated changes and promoting RPKI ASPA.
summary: Cloudflare's network automation pushed a policy update to one Miami edge router to stop announcing Bogotá prefixes. Removing only the prefix-list matches left export terms that accepted any internal route, so IPv6 prefixes learned from peers were re-announced to providers like Lumen and other peers, a Type 3 and Type 4 route leak. Leaked traffic congested backbone links and was discarded by router filters. The incident resembled Cloudflare's 2020 Atlanta backbone outage.

title: 1.1.1.1 resolver reorders CNAME records, breaking some DNS clients
trigger: A memory-saving change to the 1.1.1.1 cache merge code began appending CNAME records after the final A/AAAA answers when filling partially expired chains, and it was rolled out globally starting 2026-01-07 23:48 UTC.
impact: Clients that parse answers sequentially, such as glibc getaddrinfo, saw empty DNS results and some Cisco switches using 1.1.1.1 entered reboot loops; impact lasted until the revert finished at 19:55 UTC on January 8 after the release had reached 90% of servers.
detection: An incident was declared at 18:19 UTC on January 8; the post does not detail what signal prompted it.
fix: The release was reverted starting 18:27 UTC, Cloudflare committed to always placing CNAMEs first, and it submitted an IETF Internet-Draft to clarify answer-section ordering.
summary: A cache optimization in Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 public resolver changed how cached CNAME chains were merged with freshly resolved records, so aliases sometimes appeared after the A/AAAA answers. RFC 1034 is ambiguous on ordering, but stub resolvers like glibc getaddrinfo track the expected name as they iterate, so they discarded the answers and returned nothing; certain Cisco switches rebooted repeatedly. Cloudflare rolled the change back, made CNAME-first ordering a firm guarantee, and proposed an IETF draft on ordered answer sections.

title: WAF killswitch hits latent Lua nil bug, 500s on 28% of traffic
trigger: While mitigating CVE-2025-55182, Cloudflare raised the WAF body buffer to 1MB and used a global killswitch to disable an internal WAF test ruleset that could not handle the larger size.
impact: For about 25 minutes, from 08:47 to 09:12 UTC, roughly 28% of Cloudflare HTTP traffic, sites on the FL1 proxy using the Managed Ruleset, got HTTP 500 errors on nearly every request.
detection: Automated alerts fired and an incident was declared at 08:50 UTC.
fix: The configuration change was reverted at 09:11 UTC, and Cloudflare committed to gradual rollouts for security config, fail-open data plane handling, easier break-glass access and a network change freeze.
summary: Responding to a React Server Components vulnerability, Cloudflare enlarged the WAF request-body buffer and switched off an internal testing ruleset through its killswitch, a change that spreads fleet-wide instantly. In the older FL1 proxy, skipping that rule meant its execute object was never built, and later Lua code indexed it anyway, throwing an attempt to index a nil value error. Affected sites served HTTP 500 for nearly all requests for 25 minutes. The Rust FL2 proxy did not have the bug.

title: Oversized Bot Management feature file crashes Cloudflare's proxy
trigger: A ClickHouse permissions change exposed extra table metadata, so the query building the Bot Management feature file returned duplicate rows and roughly doubled the file.
impact: Core CDN and security traffic returned 5xx errors from about 11:20 UTC, with Access, Turnstile, Workers KV, the dashboard and Email Security also hit; main impact ended at 14:30 and full recovery came at 17:06 UTC.
detection: An automated test flagged the problem at 11:31 UTC and an incident call opened at 11:35, with the team first suspecting a DDoS attack.
fix: Engineers stopped generating new feature files, pushed a known-good file globally and restarted the proxy, then planned to validate internal config like user input, add kill switches and review proxy failure modes.
summary: A database access change at Cloudflare made a ClickHouse query that builds the Bot Management feature file return duplicate columns from a second schema. The bigger file exceeded the 200-feature limit preallocated by the Rust FL2 proxy, causing a panic and HTTP 5xx errors across the network, while legacy FL returned zero bot scores. Because ClickHouse nodes were updated gradually, good and bad files alternated every five minutes, making the outage flap and look like an attack. The independent status page coincidentally went down too.

title: 1Password US sign-in and sync fail on database exhaustion
trigger: A feature refactor magnified an inefficient query, driving runaway resource use on the main database until it rejected connections.
impact: For about an hour (17:03 to 18:05 UTC on November 18, 2025), all US/Global customers using cloud interfaces faced failed or slow sign-in, SSO and MFA, sign-up, device sync, vault access, admin console and CLI/API timeouts.
detection: Automated monitoring detected rising errors at 16:59 UTC.
fix: Engineers halted background services and a suspect cron job, scaled down app servers, then enlarged the database instance; they are refactoring the query, tuning the background service and improving database monitoring.
summary: 1Password's US region was degraded for about an hour on 18 November 2025: users could not sign in, SSO and MFA logins stalled or failed, vault items and the admin console were unreachable, and CLI calls timed out. A code refactor amplified a slow query that had gone unnoticed, exhausting the under-provisioned primary database until it refused connections. Restarts did not help; shedding load and resizing the database instance did. The query is being rewritten and monitoring tightened.

title: Feature flag bug and hosting scaling limit take Bitbucket Cloud down
trigger: A routine deployment shipped a code change that hurt a feature flag evaluation component, and manual scale-up of Git services then hit a regional hosting provider limit.
impact: From 16:25 to 19:13 UTC on November 11, 2025, all Bitbucket Cloud customers were affected: 1 hour 16 minutes of degraded performance followed by 1 hour 32 minutes during which the website, APIs and Git hosting were all down.
detection: Automated monitoring detected the problem within 5 minutes.
fix: The team scaled some services down to relieve the platform, deployed a fix and scaled healthy services back up, then hardened the feature gate component and added safeguards for platform scaling limits during deploys and rollbacks.
summary: A Bitbucket Cloud deployment degraded the component that evaluates feature flags. Engineers manually scaled up Git services to compensate, which ran into an unexpected regional limit at the hosting provider, so new instances failed. Rollback also needed new infrastructure and failed, and the burst of provisioning calls caused retries and a feedback loop that took the website, public APIs and Git over SSH and HTTPS offline. Scaling down freed headroom so a fix could deploy.

title: Removed feature flag crashes metadata service, causing 404s in Oregon
trigger: A cleanup of unreferenced feature flags deleted a flag the metadata service still evaluated, reverting it to a less efficient data transfer path that exhausted memory and crashed it.
impact: Web services and static sites in Oregon returned intermittent 404s in two windows: 10:39 to 11:25 AM PST with about 10% of requests failing in one cluster, then a worse period starting 11:59 AM PST where about 50% of requests in the affected cluster got 404s; new services and recently woken free-tier services were hit.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Render added metadata service memory, temporarily re-enabled the flag, redeployed the metadata service without the flag dependency and added monitoring for this failure, with plans for safer flag hygiene and keeping routing instances out of service until they load state.
summary: Render's HTTP routing layer pulls user-service data from a metadata service. A memory optimization had been gated by a feature flag; the flag was removed from routing code but the metadata service was never redeployed, so a later flag cleanup made it fall back to the old bulk transfer, run out of memory and crash. New routing instances that never loaded initial state still received traffic and answered with 404s, and a traffic spike that triggered routing scale-ups made the errors much worse.

title: Incompatible config metadata crashes Azure Front Door edge globally
trigger: A valid sequence of customer configuration changes made across two control plane builds produced incompatible metadata that hit a latent data plane bug and crashed edge servers asynchronously, after health gates had passed.
impact: From 15:41 UTC on 29 October to 00:05 UTC on 30 October (about 8.4 hours) Azure Front Door and Azure CDN users saw connection timeouts and DNS failures, affecting the Azure Portal, App Service, SQL Database, Microsoft 365, Entra ID components and support case creation.
detection: Monitoring alerts started the investigation at 15:48 UTC, and the configuration protection system had already halted propagation at 15:43.
fix: Engineers manually stripped the bad configs from the last known good snapshot, redeployed it fleet-wide and rebalanced traffic gradually; repairs include fixing both bugs, synchronous config processing, a pre-canary stage, longer bake times and faster data plane recovery.
summary: Customer configuration changes spanning two Azure Front Door control plane versions generated metadata that triggered a crash in the AFD data plane. Because the crash came about five minutes later during asynchronous processing, the change cleared staged health checks, reached most edge sites, and was saved into the Last Known Good snapshot. Edge servers and AFD's internal DNS then failed worldwide, breaking access to the Azure Portal, Microsoft 365 and many other services. Recovery required hand-editing the snapshot and slowly reloading configs at every edge site.

title: Non-concurrent Postgres index build locks Railway's backend API
trigger: A schema change added an indexed column to a roughly 1 billion row table without CONCURRENTLY, taking an exclusive lock on a table used by almost all API calls.
impact: From about 18:34 to 19:15 UTC the dashboard was inaccessible, CLI commands and the Public API failed, and GitHub deploys were delayed, while running deployments stayed up.
detection: Internal monitoring alerted at 18:36 UTC and paged the engineering team.
fix: The lock cleared when the index build finished after about 30 minutes; Railway will enforce CONCURRENTLY in CI, lower PgBouncer pool limits and reserve connections for administrative access.
summary: Railway's dashboard, CLI (such as railway up), Public API and GitHub webhook deploys broke when a routine Postgres migration built an index on a table of about 1 billion records without CONCURRENTLY. Queries piled up behind the table lock, and PgBouncer's pools exceeded Postgres's connection limit, consuming even reserved slots, so engineers got a pg_use_reserved_connections error and could not cancel the index build. The migration completed after about 30 minutes, releasing the lock. Prevention includes CI checks for concurrent index creation and guaranteed admin connections.

title: AWS us-east-1 outage hits incident.io through third-party dependencies
trigger: The AWS us-east-1 outage broke a telecom provider and Docker Hub, which incident.io relied on even though its own platform runs on Google Cloud.
impact: SMS and phone on-call notifications were delayed from 07:20 to 09:26 UTC, SAML login was degraded for about two hours, the Scribe note taker could not join calls for several hours, and about 4% of status page traffic errored for 25 minutes.
detection: An on-call engineer was paged at 07:21 UTC for high SMS and phone error rates, and blackbox exporters in nine regions caught the status page errors.
fix: Once Docker Hub partly recovered the team shipped isolated notification queues and escalation fixes, then removed the Docker Hub dependency and tuned Postgres autovacuum. Adding telecom providers in other clouds and regions was still being worked on.
summary: When AWS us-east-1 failed, incident.io's GCP-hosted platform stayed up but its dependencies did not. A telecom provider outage plus aggressive client retries made notification jobs run up to 60 times longer, and shared queues delayed email, Slack and push alerts too. Fixes could not ship because the build used a Docker Hub base image. Dead tuples in a Postgres escalations index made lock acquisition eat nearly half of worker capacity, and an internal rate limiter only applied to the top 10 organisations.

title: AWS outage and SDK retry flood disrupt LaunchDarkly flag delivery
trigger: The AWS us-east-1 outage degraded EC2, Lambda, DynamoDB and the Route 53 control plane, and a later internal change sent flag delivery onto a legacy path with cold caches.
impact: Service was disrupted for roughly 24 hours; US customers could not log in or manage flags, server-side SDK connection errors reached about 99% globally, and event ingestion lost data until 3:00 PM PT on October 20.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Streaming recovered by 12:05 AM PT on October 21 after load balancers were scaled out and flag delivery was decoupled from the web app; follow-ups include a new delivery architecture, streaming-to-polling SDK failover and moving DR tooling out of us-east-1.
summary: LaunchDarkly's outage had two phases. First, the AWS us-east-1 failure left its web app and API unable to autoscale, so US customers could not manage flags and client-side streaming stalled. Then, at 11:48 AM PT, a change meant to reduce web app load pushed the flag delivery network onto an old routing path with cold caches; SDKs retried heavily, overwhelming the streaming service and its load balancer, while ongoing EC2 capacity problems blocked scale-out until after midnight.

title: DynamoDB DNS automation race empties us-east-1 endpoint
trigger: A latent race condition between two DNS Enactor processes let a stale DNS plan overwrite a newer one, after which a cleanup job deleted it and removed every IP address for dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.
impact: Over about 14.5 hours in US-EAST-1, clients could not connect to DynamoDB for roughly three hours, EC2 launches failed with capacity errors, some Network Load Balancers returned connection errors, and Lambda, ECS, EKS, Amazon Connect, STS, IAM console sign-in and Redshift were degraded.
detection: Engineering teams engaged as soon as errors started and traced the problem to DynamoDB DNS state by 12:38 AM PDT; NLB health check problems were caught by monitoring at 6:52 AM.
fix: Operators manually restored the DNS records, restarted EC2 droplet lease managers and throttled requests to drain backlogs, and temporarily disabled NLB health-check failover; AWS turned off the DNS automation worldwide until the race is fixed and added velocity limits for NLB capacity removal.
summary: A timing bug in DynamoDB's automated DNS management in US-EAST-1 published an empty record set for the regional endpoint, so anything resolving it got no addresses. The outage rippled into EC2, whose droplet lease manager depends on DynamoDB and fell into a congestive backlog that blocked new instance launches. Network propagation delays then made NLB health checks fail healthy targets. Lambda, container services, Amazon Connect and sign-in all suffered, and some Redshift clusters took until the next day to recover.

title: Hacked WordPress site swaps Xubuntu torrents for malware zip
trigger: An attacker brute forced a vulnerable component of the Canonical-maintained WordPress install behind xubuntu.org and injected code that rewrote the download links.
impact: For a short period in October, xubuntu.org/download served a malicious file named Xubuntu-Safe-Download.zip instead of torrents; ISO images, mirrors, packages and build systems were not affected.
detection: Community members reported the compromise on October 15 via Reddit, Matrix, IRC and tickets to Canonical.
fix: Canonical locked down the site, disabled the downloads page, removed injected code, rolled pages back and hardened WordPress by October 19, and the Xubuntu team is moving the site to the Hugo static generator.
summary: In October 2025 the Xubuntu website's download page was altered to hand out a malicious zip archive in place of the expected torrent files. The attacker got in by brute forcing a weak component of the WordPress instance Canonical runs for the project, then injected link-changing code. After users reported it on October 15, Canonical disabled downloads, cleaned and rolled back the site, and confirmed it clean by October 19. Official Ubuntu image hosts and installed systems were unaffected.

title: Dashboard React bug floods Tenant Service, breaking API auth
trigger: A dashboard release with a React useEffect whose dependency array held an object rebuilt on every render kept calling the /organizations endpoint, colliding with a Tenant Service deploy.
impact: From 17:57 to 19:12 UTC the Cloudflare dashboard was heavily degraded and the API failed with 5xx errors in two windows, while CDN and edge security traffic were unaffected.
detection: Automated alerting paged the right engineers, who also saw rising Tenant Service and API traffic.
fix: Engineers applied a global rate limit, added Tenant Service pods, reverted a bad patch and hotfixed the dashboard, then planned Argo Rollouts, jittered retries, more capacity and retry tagging.
summary: A Cloudflare dashboard release included a React useEffect hook that re-ran on every render because an object in its dependency list was recreated each time, firing repeated calls to /organizations plus retries. The extra load overwhelmed the Tenant Service, a Go service on Kubernetes that is part of API authorization, so authorization could not be evaluated and APIs returned 5xx errors. An attempted fix that removed some error handling made things worse, causing a second outage window until it was reverted.

title: One customer's traffic surge congests Cloudflare-AWS links in Ashburn
trigger: One customer in AWS us-east-1 requested so many cached objects that the response traffic saturated Cloudflare's direct peering links with AWS in Ashburn.
impact: Customers whose origins were in AWS us-east-1 saw high latency, packet loss, timeouts and failures reaching origins from 16:27 UTC until about 20:18 UTC, while Cloudflare's other services were unaffected.
detection: Cloudflare's network team was alerted to Ashburn congestion at 16:44 UTC and opened a customer-impact incident at 17:45 UTC, with latency SLO probes also tracking the degradation.
fix: Cloudflare rate-limited the customer and re-engineered traffic while AWS reverted its BGP withdrawals, and follow-ups include per-customer traffic budgets, faster interconnect upgrades and coordinated traffic engineering with AWS.
summary: A surge of requests from one customer in AWS us-east-1 roughly doubled Cloudflare-to-AWS traffic and filled the direct peering links in Ashburn, one of which was already running at half capacity. AWS withdrew some BGP prefixes to relieve the links, pushing traffic onto an offsite interconnect that also saturated, and Ashburn edge routers dropped high-priority packets. Customers with AWS-hosted origins saw timeouts and slow responses for almost four hours until rate limiting and route normalization.

title: Salesloft Drift OAuth theft exposes Cloudflare support cases
trigger: After breaching Salesloft, threat actor GRUB1 used stolen OAuth credentials from the Drift chatbot's Salesforce integration to log into Cloudflare's Salesforce tenant.
impact: The text of Salesforce support case objects, including customer contact details and any secrets customers had pasted into tickets, was bulk-exported, and 104 Cloudflare API tokens were found in the stolen data; Cloudflare's own systems and network were not breached.
detection: Salesforce and Salesloft notified Cloudflare on August 23, 2025, several days after the last attacker activity on August 17.
fix: Cloudflare disabled the Drift integration and revoked its client ID and secrets, removed Salesloft software, disconnected and re-onboarded all Salesforce integrations with new secrets, rotated the 104 exposed API tokens, and told customers to rotate any credentials shared in support cases.
summary: In August 2025 an attacker Cloudflare calls GRUB1, armed with OAuth credentials stolen from the Salesloft Drift integration, accessed Cloudflare's Salesforce tenant on August 12, ran reconnaissance, then used a Bulk API 2.0 job on August 17 to export the text of its support cases. Those cases could include API tokens, passwords and logs customers had pasted in. Cloudflare scanned the data, rotated 104 Cloudflare API tokens, cut off the Drift integration, rotated third-party credentials, and urged customers to rotate anything shared via support.

title: Accidental rebuild breaks Linode Object Storage, LKE and DBaaS
trigger: While troubleshooting an upgrade of Akamai's internal Kubernetes control plane, the team unintentionally triggered an automated process that rebuilt several in-use resources critical to Compute products.
impact: From 19:47 UTC on July 17, 2025, Object Storage E2/E3 endpoints in nine regions went down (the last, Chicago, restored at 15:24 UTC on July 19), while LKE cluster creation, image create/restore and Managed Database operations were unavailable until about 00:20 UTC on July 18; no stored data was lost.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers methodically rebuilt the affected resources with extensive testing and restored regions one by one; changes to the involved Kubernetes systems were frozen while designs and operational processes are reviewed for added safeguards.
summary: Linode (Akamai) Object Storage E2 and E3 endpoints in Chicago, Frankfurt, London, Melbourne, Mumbai, Seattle, Singapore, Tokyo and Washington were down for up to about 44 hours starting 17 July 2025. During an internal Kubernetes control plane upgrade, troubleshooting accidentally fired an automated process that rebuilt live resources. Bucket and key management, LKE cluster creation and restores, image operations and Managed Database provisioning also failed for several hours. Recovery proceeded region by region, and the Kubernetes systems involved were placed under a change freeze.

title: Service topology misconfig withdraws 1.1.1.1 resolver routes globally
trigger: A dormant error from June 6 had tied the 1.1.1.1 Resolver prefixes to a pre-production Data Localization Suite topology, and a July 14 change adding an offline location to it refreshed routing and shrank the resolver's footprint to that single offline site.
impact: For 62 minutes (21:52-22:54 UTC) the 1.1.1.1 public DNS Resolver was unreachable worldwide for most users and Gateway DNS was intermittently degraded, though DoH via cloudflare-dns.com mostly kept working.
detection: Internal health alerts for the 1.1.1.1 Resolver began firing at 22:01 UTC and an incident was declared.
fix: Cloudflare reverted the configuration at 22:20 UTC, restoring about 77% of traffic, then accelerated reconfiguration of the roughly 23% of edge servers that had lost IP bindings; follow-ups deprecate legacy addressing systems in favor of staged, health-gated deployments.
summary: Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 resolver vanished from the Internet when a legacy service-topology system, lacking canary rollout, applied a month-old mistake: resolver prefixes had been bundled with a not-yet-live DLS service. Adding an offline data center to that service triggered a global BGP withdrawal of 1.1.1.0/24, 1.0.0.0/24 and related IPv6 ranges, breaking UDP, TCP and DoT queries for 62 minutes. An unrelated Tata hijack of 1.1.1.0/24 became visible meanwhile. A revert plus expedited re-binding of IPs restored service.

title: Partially deployed renewed certificate breaks Jamf SecureDNS
trigger: An SSL certificate expired at 00:00 UTC because its May renewal had been only partially distributed across Jamf's cloud environment.
impact: All devices configured with the Encrypted DNS Gateway lost internet access or security filtering in Jamf Safe Internet, Jamf Protect and Jamf Trust for 270 minutes.
detection: Customer reports alerted Jamf to the outage, with troubleshooting starting about 25 minutes after expiry.
fix: The new certificate was deployed manually to the affected services; Jamf is reviewing certificate management, expanding expiry alerts and adding synthetic and traffic-anomaly monitoring.
summary: Jamf's SecureDNS service failed when a certificate expired even though a replacement had been issued on May 22, 2025, because the deployment process left it missing from parts of the global cloud. End-user devices using the encrypted DNS gateway lost web threat prevention and content filtering, and many lost internet connectivity outright. Root cause was found at 01:45 UTC and the fix completed at 04:30 UTC. Remediation covers certificate documentation and verification steps, expiry monitoring and synthetic checks.

title: Workers KV storage outage cascades to Access, WARP and more
trigger: The central storage backing Workers KV, part of which runs on a third-party cloud provider, failed when that provider had its own outage.
impact: For about two and a half hours, roughly 90% of Workers KV requests failed and dependent products broke globally, including 100% of Access identity logins, WARP registrations, Gateway proxying, dashboard logins, Workers AI, Stream and Pages builds.
detection: The WARP team saw device registration failures at 17:52 UTC and declared an incident, and Access error-rate alerts and SLO drops followed at 18:05 UTC.
fix: Teams degraded features that depended on KV and prepared an alternate datastore until the storage recovered, then committed to removing single-provider dependence for KV, moving critical namespaces to Cloudflare infrastructure and limiting per-product blast radius.
summary: Workers KV relies on a central source-of-truth store, part of which was hosted by a third-party cloud that suffered an outage. With that store unavailable, KV cold reads and writes failed, and because many Cloudflare products are built on KV, the failure spread: Access identity logins, WARP sign-ups, Gateway, dashboard login, Turnstile, Workers AI, Stream, Images and Pages all saw heavy errors. No data was lost. Service returned when the storage recovered, followed by cache repopulation errors.

title: Blank policy fields crash Google Service Control in every region
trigger: A quota policy record with unintended blank fields was written to Spanner and replicated globally, hitting an unguarded null pointer in a new Service Control quota check added on May 29.
impact: Google Cloud and Workspace external APIs and consoles returned elevated 503 errors worldwide for about three hours across 76 Cloud and 10 Workspace products, with us-central1 and some products such as Vertex AI recovering later.
detection: SRE triage started within two minutes and the root cause was found in about ten, but the status dashboard was itself down so the first public notice took about an hour.
fix: A kill switch disabling the faulty code path was rolled out in about 40 minutes, task creation was throttled in us-central1, and follow-ups include fail-open checks, feature flags on critical binaries and randomized exponential backoff.
summary: Service Control, the binary that enforces API policy and quota across Google Cloud, gained a new quota check in May with no error handling and no feature flag. On June 12 a policy update with blank fields replicated globally through Spanner within seconds, the check dereferenced a null pointer, and Service Control crash-looped in every region. External API calls to Cloud and Workspace failed with 503s. In us-central1, restarting tasks without backoff overloaded the Spanner table they relied on, slowing recovery further.

title: Unplanned automatic OS update breaks dyno outbound networking
trigger: An automated operating system package upgrade that should have been disabled ran on production hosts and restarted their networking service, which did not reapply routing rules.
impact: Starting at 06:00 UTC on June 10, many customers saw up to 24 hours of downtime, with most Private Space dynos unable to make outbound HTTP requests, intermittent logins, and an unreachable status page until resolution at 05:50 UTC on June 11.
detection: Customer reports and monitoring of widespread dyno networking errors at 06:00 UTC, though the root cause took until 13:42 UTC to pinpoint.
fix: Heroku had a vendor revoke the token driving the automatic updates, disabled the upgrade service, recycled all dynos fleetwide, and is adding immutability controls, independent status channels and faster fleet diagnostics.
summary: Heroku dynos lost outbound connectivity after an automated OS package upgrade ran on production hosts and restarted networking. A legacy script only installed the correct routes at first boot, so the restart left dynos, mainly in Private Spaces, without egress. Heroku's own internal tooling and its Status Page ran on the same broken infrastructure, slowing diagnosis and communication; updates went out via X instead. Engineers revoked the updater's token, restored the Dashboard, recycled dynos fleetwide, and plan immutable base images and isolated communication channels.

title: DNS nameserver change cripples MongoDB Atlas control plane
trigger: An operator updated a DNS nameserver record that an inaccurate internal configuration source indicated was unused, breaking communication between Atlas internal metadata servers.
impact: From 17:05 to 22:54 GMT on June 4, 2025 (nearly 6 hours), customers could not manage clusters, users, networking or projects via the UI, Admin API or autoscaling, and App Services, Search, Stream Processing and Backup control operations stalled; cloud.mongodb.com was down for part of it, while data plane workloads ran normally.
detection: The operator noticed the misconfiguration within minutes.
fix: The change was rolled back, but because top-level records carried a 2-day TTL, recovery required the upstream DNS provider to flush the cached records; MongoDB is adding safety checks to tooling for top-level DNS changes and stronger review, testing and gating.
summary: MongoDB Atlas's control plane was disrupted for almost six hours on 4 June 2025. An operator changed a DNS nameserver record thought to be unused, but it was relied on by internal metadata servers that resolve names through public recursive DNS. Customers could not change clusters, users or network settings, and cloud.mongodb.com was unavailable for a stretch, though databases kept serving traffic. Rolling back did not help because of a 2-day TTL; flushes of local caches failed until the upstream provider purged its cache.

title: Feature flag flip strands Spot VMs and slows GCE control plane
trigger: A configuration change to a Compute Engine component wrongly turned off a feature flag governing VM state reporting, and safety checks that should have staged it gradually did not fire.
impact: For 8 hours 42 minutes Spot VM terminations hung globally and VM creation and reservation use in us-central1 and us-east4 slowed from seconds to minutes (tail latency to hours), affecting GKE, Dataflow, Cloud SQL, Dataproc, App Engine and others.
detection: Internal monitoring alerted engineers at 21:08 US/Pacific on 19 May.
fix: Engineers rolled the change back between 03:29 and 03:55 on 20 May; Google paused flag rollouts for the system, is auditing safety checks, and will address GCE scalability and Spot deletion monitoring.
summary: A recently deployed Google Compute Engine config change disabled a feature flag controlling how instance state is reported, and it spread quickly because rollout safety checks were not enforced. Preempted Spot VMs got stuck mid-termination, piling up a backlog that degraded control-plane operations for all VM types in us-central1 and us-east4. Median VM operation latency rose from seconds to minutes, slowing dependent products like GKE, Cloud SQL and Dataflow. Rolling back the change mitigated the 8h42m incident; Google is auditing its phased-rollout safeguards.

title: EKS upgrade strips node IAM permissions, ZenML Pro workspaces offline
trigger: Enabling KMS secrets encryption through Terraform during an EKS module upgrade also removed key IAM permissions from the worker nodes.
impact: Every production ZenML Pro workspace server was unreachable for about 8 hours overnight, blocking workspace UIs and pipelines, while the ZenML Pro dashboard stayed up and no data was lost.
detection: Engineers found the cluster degraded when they resumed the upgrade at 06:00 after leaving it running unattended overnight.
fix: After IAM role edits failed, the node group was deleted and recreated with correct permissions; Terraform modules and EKS were brought current and the upgrade strategy is under review.
summary: ZenML Pro workspaces went dark during a weekend upgrade of an outdated production EKS cluster. Applying KMS-based secret encryption via upgraded Terraform modules hit what ZenML describes as an undocumented bug, which removed IAM permissions from worker nodes, making server pods unreachable from outside the cluster. The change had been left to run overnight after a smoother staging rehearsal at much smaller scale. Recovery required recreating the whole node group; ZenML cites skipped versions and misjudged risk as contributing factors.

title: Papal election traffic record overloads Amsterdam edge load balancers
trigger: The announcement of a newly elected Pope drove Wikipedia readership up to 800k requests per second, more than 6x normal, and the legacy IPVS load balancers in the esams (Amsterdam) site overloaded.
impact: For about 10 minutes (17:19-17:29 UTC) some European users got error pages or very slow loads, editors hit many edit conflicts and some on-wiki search requests failed.
detection: Automated monitoring fired ProbeDown alerts for text-https at esams, while many engineers were already watching the event.
fix: Traffic from Germany and Poland was moved from esams to the drmrs (Marseille) site via GeoIP DNS, and the report emphasizes finishing the rollout of the Liberica load balancer with a Katran data plane.
summary: When the new Pope was announced, Wikimedia's CDN saw a traffic peak above double its previous all-time record, with egress reaching 134 gigabit/sec. The esams Amsterdam edge's IPVS load balancers, processing over a million packets per second and five million connections, became the bottleneck, causing roughly ten minutes of errors and slowness for some European readers. Moving German and Polish traffic to Marseille via GeoDNS ended the outage; the drmrs and magru sites, Kubernetes MediaWiki and multi-DC reads absorbed the rest.

title: Job dispatch stalls after blue/green Postgres upgrade race
trigger: During a blue/green upgrade of the job-dispatch database using logical replication, a restarted pod re-ran a task event against the new database before the old status replicated, triggering a unique constraint error; replication broke and orphaned task records were left behind.
impact: From 22:20 UTC on May 1 to 02:00 UTC on May 2, 2025, most jobs in the Docker large, medium, small and Linux large resource classes were delayed, and some GitHub status checks were late.
detection: An alert at 22:40 UTC flagged a growing Docker job backlog, and a second alert at 00:56 UTC caught the recurrence.
fix: Engineers marked the orphaned task records as completed, disabled logical replication and cleared the queue; the upgrade runbook will now pause writes during cutover, add a second replication check, disable replication after sync and require joint review by database and service owners.
summary: CircleCI jobs in several Docker and Linux resource classes barely started for about 3.5 hours after a Postgres upgrade of the dispatch service. Pods failed to follow the new DNS route at cutover and were restarted; one re-ran a task event on the green database ahead of replication, a constraint error broke logical replication, and stale rows created orphaned tasks that blocked the dispatcher queue. Clearing those records helped briefly until replication restarted and wrote more, so replication was turned off.

title: Agent-driven database growth hits Kubernetes and control plane limits
trigger: Agentic AI platforms drove a sustained 5x rise in database creation and a 50x rise in branch creation, pushing US regions past Kubernetes cluster limits and slowing control plane Postgres queries.
impact: Database start and suspend operations failed repeatedly over May and June, leaving about 3.5% of monthly active databases in May and about 0.7% in June below 99.95% uptime.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem for individual incidents; slow-query alerts existed but missed sudden query plan switches.
fix: Neon shipped its horizontally scaled Cells architecture and routed new projects to new Cells, added branch and workload limits, rewrote fragile queries, and plans to split start/suspend logic into a small dedicated service.
summary: In May and June 2025 Neon suffered more incidents than in the prior year as agentic AI customers created databases 5x faster and branches 50x faster. Each active database is a Kubernetes pod, and US clusters neared EKS etcd memory and networking ceilings of around 12,000 concurrent databases before the Cells project was ready. Branch metadata growth caused Postgres query plan drift and vacuum lag in the control plane, slowing cold starts for scale-to-zero databases. Fixes include Cells, stricter limits and a slimmer hot-path service.

title: PGAudit hang during migration locks incident.io database
trigger: A routine migration adding an empty table and an index ran shortly after a Postgres 17 upgrade, and the re-enabled PGAudit extension froze while holding critical locks.
impact: The dashboard, mobile app, Slack app and API were slow or timing out for about 11 minutes, including a 2-minute full primary database outage, though on-call alerts and escalations were still delivered.
detection: Monitoring alerted the team quickly.
fix: Because the stuck PGAudit processes ignored kill signals, the team restarted the database and then disabled and removed PGAudit, with further root-cause investigation and monitoring improvements planned.
summary: A few days after upgrading to Postgres 17, incident.io ran an ordinary schema migration. The PGAudit logging extension, switched back on after the upgrade, interacted badly with the migration and stopped responding while holding locks, so other queries piled up behind it. Users saw intermittent slowness and timeouts across the web dashboard, mobile and Slack apps, and API. Terminating the stuck backends did not work, so engineers restarted the primary database, causing two minutes of full downtime, and then removed PGAudit.

title: Stale stats after Postgres upgrade delay CircleCI workflows
trigger: A blue/green upgrade of the workflows service database ran ANALYZE before a second major version upgrade in the same rollout, leaving planner statistics stale.
impact: For about 1 hour 37 minutes, starting and cancelling workflows and jobs was slow or failed, some jobs were dropped after 10 minutes of retries, and the workflows UI was hard to use.
detection: Rising latency and job errors were spotted at 22:17 UTC and a public incident was declared at 22:35 UTC.
fix: After restarting pods and upsizing the database did not help, the team re-enabled writes on the old database and made it primary again, and now runs statistics analysis after every major version change with extra tests and checkpoints before cutover.
summary: CircleCI upgraded the Postgres database behind its workflows service using a blue/green deployment that included two major version jumps. Table statistics were rebuilt after the first jump only, so after the second the query planner made poor choices and queries went to disk. Workflow starts and cancellations slowed, some jobs were dropped, and the UI struggled to show workflows. Restoring the previous database as primary ended the incident. The report's date is inconsistent, citing both April 3 and April 4.

title: Manual WAF rule change blocks CircleCI UI and builds
trigger: An operator who thought they were doing read-only security checks edited a WAF rule by hand, possible because an IAM role could bypass the Terraform pipeline, and the rule blocked legitimate traffic.
impact: From 00:16 to 01:49 UTC, about 1 hour 33 minutes, customers could not load the CircleCI UI or start builds, as traffic to the api.circleci.com and circleci.com CloudFront distributions was blocked.
detection: Monitoring flagged degraded services from 00:26, but the cause was only found at 01:35 when automated Terraform drift detection reported the WAF difference, nearly 80 minutes after the change.
fix: The rule was reverted on both CloudFront distributions at 01:41; follow-ups include tighter IAM policies blocking out-of-band changes, faster drift alerts, WAF rule testing and monitoring, and organization-wide Security Control Policies.
summary: On April 4, 2025 CircleCI's UI and build triggering failed for about 93 minutes after an operator, believing they were only reading configuration, manually altered a Web Application Firewall rule that then blocked real traffic to its CloudFront distributions. An IAM misconfiguration let that role skip Terraform. Responders were slowed by an unrelated incident ending at the same time and by assuming WAF changes always went through Terraform; drift detection eventually pinpointed the rule, which was reverted. CircleCI tightened IAM and WAF change controls.

title: R2 credential rotation sent to wrong Worker environment
trigger: During a credential rotation for the R2 Gateway Worker, the new secret was deployed without the --env flag, landing in a non-production Worker before the old credentials were deleted.
impact: For 67 minutes, from 21:38 to 22:45 UTC, all R2 writes and about 35% of reads failed globally, and Images, Stream and Vectorize uploads failed completely, with log delivery delayed up to 70 minutes.
detection: R2 global availability alerts fired at 21:45 UTC and an incident was declared at 21:50, though the gradual decline delayed diagnosis.
fix: Engineers deployed the credentials to the production Worker at 22:45 UTC, and added credential ID logging, a check before deleting old keys, tooling that enforces environment selection and two-person review.
summary: Cloudflare engineers rotating the storage credentials used by the R2 Gateway Worker ran wrangler secret put and wrangler deploy without specifying --env, so the new secret went to the default, non-production Worker. Once the old key was deleted, production R2 could no longer authenticate to storage. Writes failed outright and reads partly failed, cascading to Images, Stream, Vectorize, Cache Reserve, log delivery and billing downloads. A first retry repeated the same mistake; release history review finally exposed the wrong target. No data was lost.

title: PHP 8.1 rollout loses Memcached access, overloading External Storage
trigger: A Scap deploy run with -Dbuild_mw_container_image:False skipped updating helmfile-defaults, so mw-api-int, mw-parsoid and mw-jobrunner stayed on the PHP 7.4 image while envvars.inc was mounted at the 8.1 path, leaving them with no Memcached address.
impact: During 10:44-13:44 UTC on March 12 and 11:15-14:15 UTC on March 13, internal MediaWiki deployments saw high latency and database errors as the External Storage cluster was overloaded, while user-facing traffic had only about a 0.03-0.04% error rate.
detection: Responders were working from a storm of 78 alerts, but the MediaWikiMemcachedHighErrorRate alert never fired because roughly 2 million memcached errors per minute backed up the Logstash-to-Prometheus pipeline.
fix: The rollout patches were reverted and each affected deployment redeployed; follow-ups cover reducing memcached log volume on failure, helm rollback in Scap, letting Scap update helmfile-defaults without image builds, and possibly removing envvars.inc from images.
summary: Over two days, Wikimedia's PHP 8.1 migration of the mw-api-int, mw-parsoid and mw-jobrunner deployments went wrong because a commonly used Scap flag also skipped the image tag update. Pods kept the 7.4 image but looked for environment variables in the 8.1 path, so MediaWiki lost its mcrouter address and fell back to the databases, overloading the External Storage cluster that holds revision text. A flood of memcached errors hid the relevant alert. Reverting the rollout resolved it; user-facing impact stayed minimal.

title: Apache config sends www.wikipedia.org into an infinite redirect loop
trigger: An Apache configuration change deployed on February 27 made www.wikipedia.org issue a 301 redirect to itself, which CDN caches hid until their stored responses expired overnight.
impact: From about 03:30 UTC on February 28, a growing share of users and eventually a majority could not open the www.wikipedia.org portal due to too many redirects until 10:35 UTC, while reading and editing wiki content was unaffected.
detection: No alert fired; a staff member saw users on social media saying Wikipedia was down and pinged on-call responders at 09:29 UTC, after a Phabricator task filed at 08:25 had not reached SREs.
fix: The change was reverted, a conflicting unrelated config error was fixed, and CDN caches were purged; the follow-up is a rewritten patch with explicit infinite-redirect checks.
summary: A Puppet-managed Apache rewrite for the www.wikipedia.org portal created a 301 loop that went unnoticed for hours because Varnish edge caches kept serving old responses for up to a day. As cached copies expired overnight, more users at eqiad and drmrs got Too Many Redirects errors. With an error rate too low to trip monitoring, detection came from social media. Engineers traced it to the previous day's deploy, reverted it, purged caches, and planned stronger httpbb-style tests.

title: DNS cleanup removes record behind Entra Seamless SSO sign-in
trigger: An IPv6-era routing cleanup removed an intermediate DNS record and Traffic Manager for autologon.microsoftazuread-sso.com after a defective drift-detection check and a misjudged risk review let the change through.
impact: From 16:42 UTC on 25 February to 01:15 UTC on 26 February, Entra ID Seamless SSO and Entra Connect Sync users could not sign in silently and some were fully blocked; 94% of affected customers were mitigated by 18:35 UTC.
detection: Internal DNS reachability monitors failed and started the investigation at 17:18 UTC, though misconfigured auto-engagement delayed response and notifications.
fix: A CNAME restored most resolution, and at 01:05 UTC the original A record was reinstated to fix Kerberos clients; follow-ups fix drift detection, review reachability alerting, freeze DNS changes during an audit and plan tenant-level health alerts.
summary: During maintenance to retire interim IPv6 routing, Microsoft deleted a DNS record and Traffic Manager that sat in the resolution chain for autologon.microsoftazuread-sso.com, used by Entra ID Seamless SSO and Entra Connect Sync. A drift-detection bug marked the record as unused. Once the 5-minute TTL expired, users were forced into interactive sign-in or blocked. A quick CNAME fix helped 94% of tenants, but Kerberos clients needing an A record kept getting 403 Forbidden errors until the exact original record was restored over eight hours later.

title: Database provider's expired TLS certificate takes LootLocker offline
trigger: The external database provider let an SSL certificate expire, so LootLocker's services could no longer connect to it starting at 22:29 UTC.
impact: All customers lost access to the LootLocker platform for roughly an hour and a half.
detection: Monitoring raised no alert, which LootLocker says lengthened the response.
fix: Certificate verification was temporarily switched off to restore service and re-enabled after the provider renewed; new database alerting rules and better third-party visibility were added.
summary: The LootLocker game backend platform went down on a Saturday night after its managed database provider's TLS certificate expired in an EU region, causing connection failures throughout LootLocker's systems. No internal alert fired, delaying diagnosis. Once the cause was known, engineers disabled certificate verification as a stopgap and service returned about 90 minutes after the start, then restored verification once the provider renewed. Follow-ups include proactive database monitoring, incident response improvements and audits of third-party dependencies.

title: Phishing takedown mistakenly disables the R2 Gateway service
trigger: While handling an abuse report about a phishing site on R2, an operator applied a product disablement action that shut off the production R2 Gateway service rather than the reported bucket, because internal accounts were not protected from such actions.
impact: All R2 operations failed for 59 minutes (08:14 to 09:13 UTC), breaking dependent services such as Stream, Images, Vectorize and Cache Reserve, with Log Delivery losing up to 13.6% of R2-bound logs and Durable Objects errors rising 0.09% during reconnection until 09:36 UTC.
detection: Critical R2 alerts fired when the Gateway stopped answering health checks, and sales engineering separately escalated customer reports of HTTP 500s.
fix: A team with more limited, lower-level permissions re-enabled and redeployed the Gateway because the usual admin tooling depended on R2; Cloudflare then blocked disablement of internal-account services, paused such actions in the abuse UI and planned two-party approval.
summary: A routine abuse remediation at Cloudflare disabled the R2 Gateway, the front door for R2's S3 and REST APIs, instead of one phishing endpoint. R2 requests failed at a 100% rate for 59 minutes, cascading into Stream, Images, Vectorize, the KT auditor and Log Delivery. Recovery was slowed because internal admin tooling itself relied on R2. No stored objects were lost, and Cloudflare added guardrails so abuse tooling cannot disable products in internal accounts.

title: Box logins fail as load balancer shared memory runs out
trigger: Organic traffic growth and more proxied backends exhausted the shared memory zone on some external load balancer instances, which was not tracked as its own metric.
impact: Between 3:52 PM and 5:10 PM PST on January 15, 2025 (78 minutes), some users had intermittent errors and slowness logging in and using the Box web app, including uploads and downloads.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; no alert fired because shared memory usage was not monitored separately.
fix: Box did a rolling restart across the affected load balancers and added instances for peak traffic; it now alerts on shared memory zone utilization and is automating fleet restarts and improving external tests and SLO baselines.
summary: On 15 January 2025 Box users hit intermittent login failures and slow or failing web app, upload and download requests for about 78 minutes. Starting that morning, some public load balancer instances gradually filled their shared memory zone as traffic and backend counts grew; overall memory looked fine, so no alert fired. At afternoon peak they began failing to pass traffic to backends. A rolling restart plus extra load balancer capacity fixed it, and shared memory utilization is now monitored.

title: Over-tight permission change cuts Pub/Sub off from its metadata DB
trigger: A service configuration change that over-tightened access to Pub/Sub's regional metadata database was pushed to several regions quickly, outside the normal progressive rollout.
impact: Publish and subscribe failed in about ten regions for 1 hour 13 minutes, also hitting Cloud Logging and BigQuery Data Transfer Service, and some ordered subscriptions stayed stuck with backlogs until 23:09 US/Pacific.
detection: Internal telemetry alerted engineers at 07:03 US/Pacific, nine minutes after impact began.
fix: The config change was rolled back by 08:07 and stuck ordered subscriptions were repaired by 23:09; follow-ups enforce pre-prod/prod parity, progressive config rollouts, ordering-inconsistency monitoring and a fix for the ordering metadata bug.
