summary: On 8 January 2025 a bad configuration change restricted Cloud Pub/Sub's permission to read its regional metadata store, which sits on the critical path for publishing and subscribing. A mismatch between pre-production and production hid the problem, and the change reached multiple regions within minutes. Publishes, pulls and backlog metrics failed for 73 minutes. The outage also exposed a latent bug where ordering metadata diverged from message metadata, leaving some ordered subscriptions unable to drain until late that night. Google is tightening rollout process and fixing the bug.

title: SFO3 load balancers, DOKS and App Platform lose connectivity
trigger: A routing change during network maintenance moved traffic to a new datacenter path, but stale routing configuration left on the core switches caused that traffic to be dropped.
impact: Regional External Load Balancers, DOKS control planes and App Platform apps in SFO3 lost connectivity (notably over IPv6) from about 12:10 to 14:30 UTC on January 7, 2025, and Load Balancer provisioning failed.
detection: A Load Balancer alert fired at 12:40 UTC, about half an hour after impact began, followed by a customer report at 13:00 UTC.
fix: Engineers reverted the change and updated the core switch routing configuration; follow-ups close validation gaps, add automated audits, require incremental rollout for every network change and add LB and Kubernetes reachability tests to runbooks.
summary: DigitalOcean's SFO3 region lost traffic to Regional External Load Balancers, Kubernetes (DOKS) control planes and App Platform apps for over two hours on 7 January 2025. Planned network maintenance redirected traffic onto a new path, yet the core switches still carried an outdated routing config, so packets were dropped. Customers saw timeouts and failed load balancer creation. A code revert plus a core switch config update restored service, and DigitalOcean now requires staged rollouts even for changes judged minor.

title: Shard migrations and post-holiday load cause Buildkite outages
trigger: Backfills from a batch of customer shard migrations overloaded a target database, and returning post-holiday traffic then exposed further bottlenecks in that cluster and its connection pooler.
impact: Between 2025-01-05 13:30 UTC and 2025-01-08 19:30 UTC Buildkite Pipelines had four degraded periods, three of them outages, mainly hitting the Agent API so jobs could not complete, including a stretch from 2025-01-06 23:00 to 2025-01-07 07:10 UTC where locked shards were fully down.
detection: Latency alerts fired at 13:45 UTC on January 5 and again at 16:37 UTC on January 6.
fix: Buildkite paused and throttled backfills, doubled the database size and split a busy shard onto its own cluster, added pooler capacity and load shedding, dropped a dangling replication slot, and is adding cluster-level connection limits and shard isolation.
summary: Buildkite was moving customers off its original database onto horizontally sharded clusters. Backfill load on one target shard exhausted connections in the pooling tier and threads in the Agent API, cascading to every shard, and the target database also segfaulted. As customers returned from holidays, the pooler limited connections per shard rather than per cluster, overloading one database at 3-4x peak load; a forgotten replication slot later caused more degradation. Fixes added capacity, load shedding, backpressure and shard bulkheads.

title: Deleted aws-auth ConfigMap takes Dyte's Mumbai Kubernetes region down
trigger: An error during a routine update of auto-scaling groups and Kubernetes add-ons deleted the aws-auth ConfigMap in the Mumbai cluster.
impact: All clients served from the Mumbai region lost service from 10:08 UTC until full recovery at 11:10 UTC, about an hour.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The ConfigMap was recreated so nodes could reauthorize with the control plane, extra capacity was added to speed recovery, and Dyte plans safeguards for critical configs plus stronger validation of infrastructure changes.
summary: Dyte's real-time video platform had a region-wide outage in Mumbai when an infrastructure update to auto-scaling groups and EKS add-ons unexpectedly removed the aws-auth ConfigMap. Without it, worker nodes lost authorization to talk to the Kubernetes control plane, went unhealthy and could not schedule pods, leaving the cluster unreachable for users and internal components. Restoring the ConfigMap and adding capacity brought services back in roughly an hour; follow-ups target config protection, change validation and faster recovery procedures.

title: Expired internal mTLS certificates break Render routing updates
trigger: TLS certificates on the internal metadata service expired because they were only refreshed on restart and that service was being redeployed less often.
impact: From 10:03 to 10:37 PST (34 minutes), many services deployed in that window were fully down with 404 no-server responses, and from 10:08 PST restarting routing instances cut off in-flight HTTP connections across regions.
detection: Engineers were paged at 10:18 PST when routing stopped receiving updates in some clusters, shortly after an internal Render web service failed post-deploy and an internal incident was opened.
fix: Restarting the metadata services refreshed the certificates and routing recovered by 10:37 PST; planned work includes automatic certificate rotation, earlier and reachability alerts, a higher stale-data restart threshold and handling partial connectivity in the cache logic.
summary: Render's routing service keeps an in-memory cache of user services fed by a metadata service over mTLS. When the metadata service's certificates expired, connectivity broke only partially, so updates for newly deployed services were half-applied and the cache could not route them, yielding 404s. Routing instances then deliberately crashed after minutes of stale data, which did not help and severed long-lived connections. Restarting the metadata service renewed the certificates and restored routing in all clusters.

title: Registrar clientHold takes digitaloceanspaces.com off DNS
trigger: Registrar Network Solutions erroneously placed an EPP clientHold status on the digitaloceanspaces.com domain, stopping it from resolving.
impact: From 22:38 UTC on November 28 to 04:03 UTC on November 29, 2024 (about 5.5 hours), Spaces, Spaces CDN, Container Registry, App Platform builds, Functions, Load Balancer creates and Mongo backups failed, and the Cloud Control Panel was down until 01:42 UTC, with the worst errors after 03:00 as DNS caches expired.
detection: Internal monitoring and customer reports of the Control Panel not loading led to an incident at 22:38 UTC, with an internal alert at 22:44 UTC.
fix: DigitalOcean escalated to Network Solutions and Verisign executives until the clientHold was lifted at 04:03 UTC; it is investigating the registrar error, evaluating other registrars and improving detection of registrar and DNS changes.
summary: DigitalOcean's object storage domain digitaloceanspaces.com stopped resolving for about five and a half hours after its registrar, Network Solutions, wrongly set an EPP clientHold on it on 28 November 2024. Spaces buckets, CDN, Container Registry, App Platform builds, Functions, Load Balancer creation and MongoDB backups all failed, and the Cloud Control Panel could not load until engineers routed around the dependency. Failures worsened as DNS TTLs expired. Escalation to Verisign got the hold removed; DigitalOcean is reviewing alternative registrars.

title: Blank Logfwdr config triggers Buftee overload and lost customer logs
trigger: A change adding a Logpush dataset hit a bug that gave Logfwdr a blank configuration, and Logfwdr's fail-open safeguard then forwarded logs for every customer, making Buftee create about 40 times its usual buffer count.
impact: For roughly 3.5 hours most Cloudflare Logs customers were affected and about 55% of the logs normally delivered were lost.
detection: The team noticed the bad configuration quickly and reverted it in under five minutes, but the overload it set off persisted.
fix: The overloaded Buftee systems needed a full reset and restart; follow-ups add alerts for these misconfigurations, fix the bug and its tests, and introduce regular overload tests alongside existing cut tests.
summary: Cloudflare's Logpush pipeline lost about 55% of customer logs over 3.5 hours after a config generator bug briefly handed Logfwdr an empty customer list. An old fail-open failsafe made Logfwdr ship events for all customers instead of none, and Buftee, the buffering layer, tried to create a buffer per customer, ballooning to about 40 million. Buftee's protections against exactly this had never been configured, so it became unresponsive and required a full restart. Cloudflare is adding alerts and overload testing.

title: Decommissioning job deletes Traffic Manager profiles for Azure Storage
trigger: When a legacy storage service was decommissioned, subscriptions holding Traffic Manager profiles for live storage accounts had not been reassigned, so the cleanup deleted those profiles.
impact: From 00:50 to 12:30 UTC (about 11.7 hours) a subset of Blob Storage and Data Lake Storage accounts across dozens of regions became unreachable with DNS resolution failures, also disrupting Container Registry pulls, Databricks cluster launches and Log Analytics data; no stored data was lost.
detection: A customer report at 01:24 UTC prompted the on-call team to investigate.
fix: Engineers rebuilt the deleted Traffic Manager profiles in phases with manual and automated recovery, finishing at 12:30 UTC; follow-ups include an artifact audit, a strict deployment approval process, resource locks, safer cleanup tooling and outside-in endpoint monitoring.
summary: Azure Traffic Manager profiles route requests to Blob and Data Lake storage endpoints. When the Azure Storage service was split in two and one half was retired, ownership of the subscriptions containing those profiles was never moved to the surviving service, so the decommissioning process deleted them. Affected storage accounts stopped resolving in DNS, breaking downstream services such as ACR, Databricks and Log Analytics. Most accounts were restored by 06:24 UTC and all by 12:30 UTC. Microsoft added resource locks, stricter approvals and better monitoring.

title: Edge autoscaling flaw cascades into Sentry US ingestion outages
trigger: An ingestion region built a traffic backlog, and the shifted traffic overloaded other regions whose CPU-based autoscaling reacted too slowly or scaled the wrong way.
impact: US SaaS ingestion was rejected or unavailable in incidents on October 4, 16 and 21, including no data ingested from 9:42 to 10:06 AM PT on October 21, with customer-visible effects lasting past the initial minutes.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Sentry added three smaller edge regions, switched autoscaling to stronger signals than CPU, slowed scale-downs, and is improving edge metrics to tune scaling further.
summary: Three Sentry incidents in October 2024 shared one failure pattern at the ingestion edge. A backlog in one region caused traffic to move to other regions, which then backed up and rejected events too. Autoscaling keyed on CPU load reacted slowly, and when the slowdown showed up as iowait it did not scale or even scaled down, so the problem cascaded across US ingestion. Remediation added more, smaller edge regions and new scaling rules.

title: RunSQL migration without timeouts exhausts Sentry database connections
trigger: A database migration using RunSQL ran without lock and statement timeouts, so long-running queries used up all Postgres connections.
impact: Both the Sentry US site and ingestion were unavailable from 3:42 to 4:04 PM PT (22 minutes).
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: A fix restored the database, and Sentry plans to remove RunSQL from migrations, upgrade its database framework, add recovery runbooks for lock and timeout problems, and improve alerting.
summary: A schema migration at Sentry used a raw RunSQL operation, and the migration tooling had no safeguards enforcing lock and statement timeouts. The migration's queries ran long and held resources until Postgres connections were exhausted, leaving the database unreachable and taking down the Sentry US dashboard, API and event ingestion. Service returned after a fix, and the team intends to replace RunSQL usage with framework-supported operations, write runbooks for migration lock issues and react faster through better alerting.

title: Thousands of maintenance-job network policies overload Calico in codfw
trigger: A batch of requeueTranscodes.php runs launched through mwscript-k8s created a full helm release per invocation, piling up close to 2k Calico network policies (1791 jobs) until Calico components exceeded their resource limits.
impact: From 05:01:36 to 06:10 UTC (about 69 minutes) uncached traffic such as logged-in page views, edits and API calls in the primary datacenter saw elevated latency and errors, with successful responses dipping about 25% (4k to 3k) for roughly 5 minutes.
detection: Automated alerting paged on elevated rest-gateway 5xx errors and fired a growing number of KubernetesCalicoDown alerts.
fix: Engineers raised the resource limits for the calico and typha pods and redeployed them, after which Calico recovered; the follow-up task T376795 targets mwscript-k8s creating too many resources.
summary: On Wikimedia's WikiKube cluster in codfw, a new mwscript-k8s tool used for a long video transcode maintenance run deployed a helm release per script invocation, silently accumulating 1791 jobs and their Calico network policies. Calico controllers and calico-node pods throttled, failed liveness probes and crash-looped, knocking hardware nodes out of rotation one by one and degrading MediaWiki for logged-in users, edits and APIs for about an hour. Bumping Calico and Typha resource limits restored the cluster.

title: Relay disk buffer bottleneck halts Sentry US ingestion
trigger: A code change exposed a Relay capacity limit where the disk buffer could not keep up with high write throughput.
impact: Sentry US could not ingest any event type from 8:16 to 9:00 AM PT (44 minutes).
detection: Monitoring and alerting worked as expected, but the change initially rolled out to a single pod, which made early impact hard to spot.
fix: The change was rolled back after delays caused by uncertainty over the target version and unfamiliar rollback tooling, and Sentry is building a production-like load-testing setup, benchmarking write throughput and adding Relay observability.
summary: A Relay change in Sentry's ingestion pipeline revealed that its disk buffer could not sustain the write rate under real traffic. Pods running mixed versions reacted differently, newer ones breached memory limits, and the failure spread across services until US ingestion stopped for all event types. Recovery was slowed because the team was unsure which version to revert to and was unfamiliar with rollback tools. Sentry plans pre-deploy stress tests against mirrored production traffic.

title: Renumbering bug leaves 1,661 sites on withdrawn IPv4 prefixes
trigger: A release withdrew fifteen IPv4 prefixes thought to be empty, but an earlier change to a legacy SSL-related sync function had skipped renumbering for sites without legacy certificates, leaving 1,661 websites on those addresses.
impact: From 17:51 to 18:50 UTC (about one hour) IPv4 visitors to 1,661 Business plan websites got errors as roughly 10 Gbps of traffic stopped reaching Cloudflare; IPv6 was unaffected.
detection: Alerts about unreachable address space at 17:57 UTC were dismissed as expected for a withdrawal, and an incident was only declared at 18:36 UTC after two customers escalated.
fix: The release was rolled back at 18:50 UTC, re-announcing the prefixes via BGP, and the bug was fixed; follow-ups add checks for leftover site assignments, traffic verification before prefix withdrawal and a review of legacy stored procedures.
summary: Cloudflare's Addressing team withdrew fifteen IPv4 prefixes from BGP after a July renumbering of Business plan sites, assuming all had moved. A months-earlier fix to legacy SSL code had a side effect: sites lacking a legacy certificate reference were never remapped, so 1,661 websites still lived on the retired prefixes. For about an hour their IPv4 traffic never reached Cloudflare. Initial unreachable-space alerts looked routine; customer escalations prompted a rollback, and new tests and traffic checks now gate withdrawals.

title: Rust RwLock deadlock in fly-proxy halts Fly.io request routing
trigger: A customer's virtual services configuration hit a code path in fly-proxy where an if let held a read lock while a nested call tried to take a write lock, and Corrosion gossiped that config to every proxy.
impact: Apps on Fly.io could not receive Internet requests fleetwide, acutely for roughly 40 minutes and recurring for about another hour, also breaking the dashboard and API.
detection: Synthetic alerting opened a formal incident at 19:25 UTC, seven minutes after the poisoned configuration was added.
fix: Engineers ran rolling fly-proxy restarts, disabled the virtual services API endpoint and shipped a proxy fix, then added semgrep checks and plan proxy sharding and a watchdog for hung proxies.
summary: Fly.io's Anycast router fly-proxy deadlocked across the fleet on September 1, 2024 after a virtual services feature deployed days earlier met a specific customer configuration. In Rust, the read guard in an if let lives through the else arm, where init_for eventually requested a write lock. Corrosion spread the configuration to every proxy, so restarts only helped briefly. A tcp_migrate_req sysctl issue muddied diagnosis. Disabling the virtual services endpoint and patching the proxy resolved it; follow-ups include semgrep rules, proxy sharding and watchdogs.

title: Kinesis cell overload degrades CloudWatch Logs, Lambda, S3 events
trigger: A routine deployment in an internal Kinesis Data Streams cell with an unusual mass of very low-throughput shards caused the new cell management system to pile shards onto a few hosts, whose oversized status messages led it to wrongly declare healthy hosts dead.
impact: From 2:45 PM to 9:37 PM PDT CloudWatch Logs, Data Firehose, S3 event delivery, ECS, Lambda, Redshift and Glue in US-EAST-1 saw elevated errors and latency, with CloudWatch log backlogs draining by 5:50 AM July 31 and S3 event backlogs by 2:38 AM August 1.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem beyond engineers engaging once the cell's latency and errors rose at 2:45 PM PDT.
fix: Engineers shed load from less urgent internal streams at 4:25 PM and added capacity to the secure-connection provisioning subsystem; connection limits, load-shedding tooling and capacity changes were applied in all Regions using the new architecture while the cell manager is improved.
summary: One internal-only Kinesis Data Streams cell in US-EAST-1, recently migrated to a new cell management architecture, failed under an unusual workload of very many tiny shards. A routine deploy reshuffled shards unevenly; overloaded hosts sent huge health messages that arrived late, so the manager marked healthy hosts unhealthy and redistributed shards in a storm that overwhelmed the component provisioning secure data-plane connections. AWS services built on that cell, including CloudWatch Logs, Firehose, S3 event notifications and Lambda logging, degraded for about seven hours.

title: Premature capacity reclamation blocks Persistent Disk deletes
trigger: A coordination error started an internal capacity reclamation process before the software it depended on had been rolled out.
impact: For 8 hours 14 minutes, disk deletes, disk updates such as resize, VM deletions and managed instance group scale-downs sat pending, affecting about 85% of scopes globally.
detection: A monitoring alert fired at 9:57 US/Pacific.
fix: Engineers cleaned up blocked operations and sped the software update to remaining scopes so stalled work completed; follow-ups add stricter review of cleanup jobs, better handling of stuck operations and phased reclamation.
summary: On 26 July 2024 Google kicked off an internal Persistent Disk capacity reclamation job too early, before the required software update was deployed everywhere. The job blocked user-initiated disk deletions, so delete and resize requests, VM deletions waiting on their disks, and managed instance group scale-downs stayed in a pending state for more than eight hours across roughly 85% of scopes. Accelerating the software rollout let the queued operations finish on their own. Google will review cleanup operations more rigorously and phase future reclamation work.

title: Faulty Falcon content update crashes Windows hosts worldwide
trigger: A Rapid Response Content update, Channel File 291, supplied 21 input fields to a sensor template expecting 20, causing an out-of-bounds memory read in the Falcon Windows sensor.
impact: Windows hosts running Falcon sensor 7.11 or later that were online between 04:09 and 05:27 UTC crashed with blue screens, and recovery took days, with about 99% of sensors back online by July 29.
detection: Not stated in detail; the hub says the problem was identified quickly and the file was reverted 78 minutes after release.
fix: CrowdStrike reverted the channel file and guided manual and later automated host remediation, then added field-count validation, Content Interpreter bounds checks, staged deployment rings and customer control over content rollout.
summary: CrowdStrike released a Rapid Response Content file for its Falcon Windows sensor that provided one more input field than the sensor's Content Interpreter expected. A bug in the Content Validator let it through, and the mismatch caused an out-of-bounds read that crashed Windows into a blue screen on every affected host that was online during a 78-minute window. Mac and Linux were unaffected. Many machines needed hands-on fixes such as booting to recovery and deleting the channel file.

title: Global config cleanup deletes Azure OpenAI GPU and endpoint resources
trigger: A change to a global automation config file dropped 14 resource groups believed to be unused, but they held GPU VMs and model endpoints, which the automation then deleted.
impact: From 00:00 to 23:35 UTC on 13 July 2024 some customers got 5xx errors from Azure OpenAI in 14 of its 28 regions, and customers could not create new fine-tuned model deployments in four regions until 16:54 UTC on 15 July; RAG and fine-tuning data were not lost.
detection: Service monitoring alerted engineers at 00:05 UTC when failure rates crossed thresholds.
fix: Engineers stopped the automation, added resource locks and rebuilt resources region by region, with manual work for GPT-4o, DALL-E and fine-tuning; repairs make config rollouts regional under safe deployment, fix resource tags and tighten change controls.
summary: Azure OpenAI uses automation driven by a single global configuration file to manage GPU VMs and Azure Machine Learning endpoints that serve models. Over time some resource groups mixed managed and unmanaged resources, and a cleanup change removed 14 groups listed as unused that actually held production compute and endpoints. With no regional gating, the deletion hit 14 regions within about 40 minutes, causing 5xx errors for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o and DALL-E. Rebuilding large models took most of a day; Microsoft now applies config changes region by region.

title: BGP hijack and route leak make 1.1.1.1 unreachable for many networks
trigger: Eletronet (AS267613) originated an unauthorized 1.1.1.1/32 route that a tier 1 provider accepted as a blackhole, while Nova (AS262504) leaked 1.1.1.0/24 upstream to AS1031, which spread it widely.
impact: Starting at 18:51 UTC, users in over 300 networks across 70 countries found 1.1.1.1 unreachable or very slow, though the overall user share was small (under 1% in the UK and Germany), and the leak was not fully resolved until 02:28 UTC the next day.
detection: Cloudflare opened an internal incident at 20:03 UTC, about 72 minutes after the hijack began, for 1.1.1.1 reachability problems from various countries.
fix: Cloudflare shut down peering with AS267613 at multiple locations and contacted the networks involved, and is expanding real-time data for its route leak detection while pushing RPKI origin validation, ASPA and rejection of prefixes longer than /24.
summary: Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver was disrupted by outside networks: Brazilian AS267613 announced 1.1.1.1/32 despite an RPKI ROA allowing only AS13335 up to /24, and one tier 1 transit treated it as a remote-triggered blackhole route. At the same time AS262504 leaked 1.1.1.0/24 to AS1031, which redistributed it at exchanges, steering traffic to Brazil with drops or high latency. Cloudflare disabled affected peerings, engaged the operators, and advocates ROV, ASPA and stricter BGP filtering.

title: New DDoS rule triggers infinite Lua loop, pinning edge CPUs
trigger: A gradually deployed DDoS mitigation rule that rate-limited by cookie value hit a latent bug in the legacy rate-limiting code when clients sent mixed valid and invalid cookies.
impact: For 114 minutes, many data centers served errors to 1.4-2.1% of CDN requests at peak, with total 5xx reaching 3.45% and p99 time to first byte roughly tripling.
detection: An incident was opened automatically at 18:04 UTC when global CPU load stayed high, though engineers first blamed a concurrent backbone congestion event.
fix: Engineers ran mass rolling restarts, fixed a Traffic Manager bug, and disabled the rule, then planned to replace the legacy rate limiter and guard against endless tail-call loops.
summary: A new Cloudflare DDoS rule keyed rate limits on cookies, and its key-generation function ended up calling itself. Two cookie validity checks disagreed when a request had several cookies, so the function recursed forever; Lua proper tail calls kept the stack flat, meaning no overflow error ever surfaced and the process just spun at 100% CPU. One bad request poisoned a worker, and load shifted by Unimog and Traffic Manager spread failures between servers and data centers, raising error rates and latency worldwide.

title: Buggy host migration workflow triggers IO overload and retry storms
trigger: A host migration workflow issued a redeploy per replica instead of per deployment, flooding the high-IO status endpoint at the same time as normal deploys and hourly crons.
impact: About 20% of instances in the US and EU fleet were degraded, some workloads had up to 20 minutes of downtime (sometimes repeatedly), and about 5% of machines lost private networking until 12:29 PM UTC.
detection: On-call engineers were paged for elevated IO pressure on instances, first in Europe and then across US-west, and an incident was called at 8:24 AM UTC.
fix: Railway cancelled migrations, crons and deploys, paused Hobby provisioning and restarted locked machines, then planned cached status responses, region-scoped scheduler calls and tuned reaper priorities.
summary: Railway's scheduler queries every machine's status endpoint, which reads many files and is IO-heavy. On June 11, 2024 a host migration script fired redeploys for every replica while deployment, cron and secondary queues were already busy, quadrupling load on that endpoint. Unanswered status calls made machines unschedulable, causing retries that spread across regions and IO-locked hosts. Engineers cancelled queued work and restarted boxes through 10:45 AM UTC. Fixes include caching status in the V2 runtime's in-memory database and keeping scheduling calls within a region.

title: Maintenance automation shuts down VPC controllers in every zone
trigger: Automation meant to retire one zone's unused VPC controller ignored its zone parameter, after an earlier refactor broke it and disabled a scoping safeguard, and stopped the controller in all zones.
impact: Multiple Google Cloud products lost network control-plane functions (new VMs, autoscaling, config changes, health updates) for most of 2 hours 48 minutes, with some products recovering later; for example about 10% of AlloyDB instances in us-central1 auto-failed over.
detection: Internal monitoring alerts fired at 15:41 US/Pacific.
fix: Engineers paused maintenance work and brought controllers back, with all restored by 18:09 and the dataplane backlog cleared by 18:40; follow-ups add zone-scope validation, tooling that rejects zoneless operations, tighter access controls and negative test cases.
summary: On 16 May 2024 a maintenance job intended to shut down a single idle VPC controller instead took down VPC controllers across every Google Cloud zone, because a refactor had caused the target-zone parameter to be ignored and a test failure flagging this was misread as expected. Thanks to the fail-static design existing data paths kept forwarding, but VM creation, autoscaling, configuration pushes and health-state updates stalled and some zones saw congestion. Controllers were restored after roughly three hours; Google is adding zone-scope safety checks and tests.

title: Blank provisioning field auto-deletes UniSuper's GCVE private cloud
trigger: When Google operators provisioned the customer's Google Cloud VMware Engine private cloud in early 2023 with an internal tool, one parameter was left blank, which silently defaulted to a 1 year term followed by automatic deletion.
impact: UniSuper in Australia lost one of its GCVE Private Clouds across two zones with no deletion notice, and recovery took several days of 24x7 work; no other customers were affected.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Google and the customer rebuilt the private cloud from backups held in Google Cloud Storage and third-party backup software, and Google retired the internal tool, fixed the deletion behavior and audited all GCVE private clouds.
summary: A Google Cloud VMware Engine deployment for UniSuper was created through a legacy internal capacity tool with one input left empty. The system filled in an unknown default fixed term of 1 year, and when it expired the private cloud was deleted without the notification a customer-initiated deletion would trigger. Backups stored in Cloud Storage in the same region survived and, with third-party backup software, let the teams restore networking, applications and data over several days.

title: Domain audit repoints Azure China system domains to dead nameservers
trigger: A compliance-driven domain audit misattributed ownership of chinacloudapp.cn and chinacloudsites.cn, and a decommission workflow whose tooling could not see Azure China zones swapped their nameservers to inactive servers.
impact: From 03:45 to 06:00 CST on 23 April 2024, Azure China customers had trouble reaching Cosmos DB, AKS, Service Bus, Data Factory and other services plus portal.azure.cn and APIs, and Log Analytics and Sentinel in China East 2 and East 3 had latency and query failures.
detection: Internal monitors alerted on service degradation at 04:37 CST.
fix: Engineers reverted to the previous nameservers at 04:59 CST with recovery as caches expired; Microsoft suspended the domain lifecycle process and will add all-cloud signals and direct internet resolution checks to its validation.
summary: An internal audit of domain ownership, done for a Chinese regulatory requirement, wrongly flagged two critical Azure China system domains as candidates for retirement. The DNS zone lookup tool did not cover Azure China, so it reported no zone file, which looked normal for a dead domain, and the workflow moved the domains to inactive nameservers. As resolver caches expired, names under chinacloudapp.cn and chinacloudsites.cn stopped resolving, breaking many Azure China services and the portal. The revert took minutes, but DNS caching stretched recovery to about two hours.

title: Second Portland power loss tests Code Orange failover work
trigger: Four facility circuit switchboards at the Flexential PDX01 site failed together, reportedly because breaker trip settings were too low, taking out both primary and redundant power to all Cloudflare cages.
impact: Control plane APIs and dashboards recovered in about seven minutes, but analytics stayed down until later that day; the edge network serving traffic was unaffected.
detection: Loss of connectivity to PDX01 triggered alerts immediately, and a total facility power loss was confirmed shortly after.
fix: Over 100 databases across more than 20 clusters failed over automatically to other Portland sites, Flexential reset and corrected the switchboards, and the top follow-up is finishing high availability for the analytics platform and eliminating remaining manual steps.
summary: Five months after a similar outage, another full power failure hit a Cloudflare core facility in Portland when four circuit switchboards tripped at once. This time the control plane failed over on its own within minutes, thanks to work done under the Code Orange program: HA database topology, pre-provisioned capacity elsewhere, and Logpush failover to Amsterdam. Analytics, which still depended on the lost facility, was the main gap. Cold-starting the site took around 10 hours versus roughly 72 previously.

title: Faulty control-plane change restarts every workload on Render
trigger: A code change with a feature-flag bug that hid it in staging restarted all customer and system workloads at 16:07 UTC.
impact: Static sites and stateless services recovered within 20 minutes, but PostgreSQL, Redis and disk-backed services stayed down much longer, with paid services restored by 18:45 UTC and free ones by 20:00 UTC.
detection: Automated alerts paged engineers as soon as the restarts began.
fix: Render disabled the faulty code, raised disk detach-attach rate limits with its infrastructure provider and paused free PostgreSQL to prioritize paid users, and is batching disk operations, restricting control plane permissions and aligning test environments.
summary: On March 26, 2024 a Render code change restarted every workload on the platform. A subtle feature-flag bug kept the faulty path from running in non-production environments, so testing missed it. Stateless services bounced back quickly, but hundreds of thousands of disk-backed services, including managed PostgreSQL and Redis, needed disks moved between hosts at once, hitting internal and provider rate limits and leaving logs and metrics gaps. Render lifted limits, prioritized paid customers, and is restricting which control plane components can restart services.

title: Demand spike overwhelms regional metadata store in us-west1
trigger: An unexpected surge of demand on the regional metadata store in us-west1 grew faster than the store could automatically add capacity.
impact: From 09:45 to 12:52 US/Pacific (about 3 hours) many Google Cloud services in us-west1 had control-plane errors and latency, e.g. GCE API errors touching about 33% of projects in the region, Cloud Pub/Sub publish errors peaking near 99%, and Vertex AI errors around 50%.
detection: Internal monitoring alerted engineers.
fix: Engineers throttled the spiking workloads so the store could process its backlog, and plan earlier detection of load spikes plus more aggressive automatic throttling.
summary: Most Google Cloud products in a region rely on a shared regional metadata store for request handling and metadata. On 14 February 2024 a sudden spike in demand on the us-west1 store outran its autoscaling, causing elevated latency and errors across dozens of services: GCE API timeouts, a small number of VM crashes, Pub/Sub and Pub/Sub Lite publish failures, App Engine and Cloud Run deployment failures, and Vertex AI and Dialogflow errors. Throttling the offending workloads restored normal reads and writes after roughly three hours.

title: Migration with TRUNCATE CASCADE wipes production tables at Linear
trigger: A reviewed database migration used TRUNCATE with CASCADE on new tables, which emptied every table with foreign keys pointing to them, including issue descriptions, comments and notifications.
impact: Linear was offline for one hour, data written between 04:47 and 09:56 UTC was temporarily lost for 12% of workspaces (plus automated changes in another 7%), and over 99% was restored within 36 hours.
detection: About 30 minutes after the migration an engineer noticed odd behavior in their notification inbox, user reports followed, and a spike of client warnings on the notificationUpdate GraphQL endpoint pointed to the bad commit.
fix: Linear entered maintenance mode, restored the 04:47 UTC full backup, replayed sync-engine actions per workspace to recover lost changes, and plans to remove TRUNCATE privileges, lint migrations and tool up point-in-time recovery.
summary: A Linear schema migration meant to clear test data in two new tables used TRUNCATE CASCADE, silently deleting production rows for issue and document descriptions, comments, notifications, favorites and reactions. Client and backend caches hid the damage for about 30 minutes. Because point-in-time recovery was untested, the team restored a daily backup from 04:47 UTC, taking the app down for an hour, then reset a Redis sync cursor and replayed logged sync actions to rebuild workspaces. Over 99% of data came back within 36 hours.

title: Log Analytics ramp-up stalls Cloud Logging ingestion in five regions
trigger: Moving another group of projects onto Log Analytics triggered a burst of concurrent dynamic provisioning requests that contended on a configuration database used by the Log Router.
impact: Logs from us-central1, us-east1, europe-west1, europe-north1 and asia-east1 were delayed for between 40 minutes and 4 hours 45 minutes, with Log Router throughput down about 40%; log-based metric queries degraded for about 25 hours and Personalized Service Health alerting was affected.
detection: A support case and internal alerts notified engineers at 09:55 PT.
fix: Engineers rolled back the ramp-up at 11:15, disabled provisioning for the affected logs to drain the backlog by 14:15, and raised a connection quota for Log Analytics; follow-ups include safer ramp-ups, shorter DB timeouts, load fault-injection tests and removing provisioning from the routing path.
summary: Cloud Logging provisions BigQuery-backed storage the first time a Log Analytics bucket receives data, which updates a configuration database the Log Router reads. Ramping a new batch of projects onto Log Analytics flooded that database with provisioning requests, and a latent issue stopped the Log Router from isolating the slow traffic fast enough, cutting throughput by roughly 40%. Recent logs were invisible in the Console and exports lagged for hours. Scaling up to drain the backlog then caused high-cardinality metric timeouts and a Log Analytics quota breach.

title: Latent preview-feature bug crash-loops Azure Resource Manager nodes
trigger: An internal maintenance process changed the configuration of an internal tenant enrolled in the ARM Continuous Access Evaluation preview, triggering a latent defect that made ARM nodes fail on startup.
impact: Between 01:30 and 08:58 UTC (about 7.5 hours) ARM management operations via CLI, PowerShell and the portal failed, chiefly in Central US, East US, South Central US, West Central US and West Europe, and dependent services such as Storage, Key Vault, Event Hubs and Service Bus rejected requests once cached RBAC data expired.
detection: Monitoring detected falling availability at 01:59 UTC.
fix: Microsoft disabled the preview feature via config from 04:51 UTC and throttled a 20x retry storm in West Europe to recover; follow-ups offboard all preview tenants, harden startup logic, use Front Door against retry storms and move RBAC lookups off ARM.
summary: A private-preview integration between Azure Resource Manager and Entra Continuous Access Evaluation contained a bug that crashed ARM nodes at startup whenever authentication to an enrolled tenant failed. A config change on such a tenant meant periodically restarting ARM nodes never came back, draining capacity until the remainder were overwhelmed by timeouts and retries. Management calls failed across several regions and services caching RBAC policies from ARM began denying traffic. Disabling the feature restored most regions by 05:30 UTC; West Europe needed extra throttling of internal retry traffic.

title: Atlas Proxy bug floods control plane with config syncs
trigger: A new Atlas Proxy version released on January 9 had a bug that, when triggered fleet-wide on January 17 at 08:00 UTC, synced Shared and Serverless cluster configurations far too often.
impact: From 08:00 to 23:30 UTC on January 17, 2024, Atlas control plane servers and their databases were overloaded, delaying metrics and cluster changes, and some Shared and Serverless tier customers could not connect to their clusters; Dedicated cluster connectivity was not affected.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers throttled the Atlas Proxies at 13:30 UTC, repaired overloaded internal services, then rolled back and unthrottled the proxy so all delays were gone by 23:30 UTC.
summary: On 17 January 2024 MongoDB Atlas metrics and cluster modifications were delayed for most of a day after a latent bug in a new Atlas Proxy release caused proxies across the fleet to resync Shared and Serverless cluster configuration excessively, overloading control plane app servers and their databases. Throttling the proxies helped Dedicated operations but then a backlog swamped other internal services, and proxies on servers rebooted by OS patching could not initialize, cutting some Shared and Serverless users off from their clusters. A rollback ended it.

title: DDoS and upstream null routes force 170-hour SourceHut outage
trigger: A layer 3 DDoS attack on SourceHut's PHL datacenter led Cogent and the colocation provider to null route its subnet, cutting off the whole network.
impact: SourceHut services were out for about 170 hours, with partial service returning on January 12 and full service, including chat.sr.ht last, restored on January 17.
detection: Monitoring raised alarms around 06:00 UTC on January 10 as the attack began.
fix: SourceHut performed an emergency migration to its Amsterdam installation from backups, fronted it with OVH's DDoS-protected network via NAT, credited paying users, and is retiring the PHL site.
summary: A layer 3 DDoS against SourceHut's Philadelphia site prompted Cogent to null route its /24, and the colocation provider was unreachable because its ticket portal had been retired after acquisitions. After the attack escalated and the subnet was null routed again, SourceHut rebuilt everything in its AMS research installation from a near-current Postgres standby and backups up to 12 hours old, routing traffic through OVH anti-DDoS. git.sr.ht, builds, pages and chat came back over several days, and object storage for pages had not been in off-site backups.

title: Empty backup ID mixes free-tier database data in shared storage
trigger: A buggy migration left some databases with an empty backup identifier, so their backups pointed at one shared storage path, and databases recreated from it after scale-to-zero picked up others' data.
impact: About 0.07% of managed databases were affected: from 1 to 4 December 2023 they could see data from the shared location, and the fix rolled them back to 1 December backups, losing later writes.
detection: An external researcher reported the leak at 8:10 AM UTC on 4 December 2023.
fix: Turso patched the bug about an hour later, reran the migration with correct parameters and restored affected databases under correct IDs, and planned per-database backup isolation, ownership checks and safer migrations.
summary: Turso free-tier databases scale to zero after an hour idle. A configuration change shipped on 20 November contained a migration bug that blanked the backup identifier for some databases, pointing their backups at a common bucket path. When fly.io lacked resources to restart such a database, Turso rebuilt it from that shared location, so customers could read data belonging to other databases. After a researcher reported it, Turso fixed the bug, restored from 1 December backups, and accepted the resulting data loss.

title: Misconfigured metrics agent soft-locks CPUs on Railway US-West hosts
trigger: A newly rolled out metrics collection agent was misconfigured to sample every process on the host at high frequency, triggering CPU core soft locks.
impact: 30% of US-West machines failed between 16:40 and 20:53 UTC, leaving some customer workloads unreachable for 10 minutes to 1 hour, with no data loss.
detection: Internal monitoring alerted that users could not reach their workloads, and deployment scripts reported hosts as unavailable.
fix: Engineers manually restarted soft-locked hosts and failed over suspect ones, and committed to mandatory staged rollouts (10%, 25%, 50%, 100%), faster deployment feedback and better automatic recovery from hypervisor-level faults.
summary: Railway began deploying a new metrics collector across its fleet on December 1, 2023. A configuration error made it sample all host processes at high frequency, causing heavy kernel-to-userspace memory transfers that soft-locked every CPU core on some hosts, apparently interacting with a Google Cloud hypervisor bug. Since 70% of machines ran it fine, the agent was not suspected at first. Locked hosts had to be restarted by hand via serial console checks, taking 10-30 minutes each, until all were back by 20:23 UTC.

title: Trello outage from authorization change causing broadcast DB queries
trigger: A code change to standardize request authorization turned a targeted database query into a broadcast query, which overloaded database servers while Trello was nearing its daily peak.
impact: All Trello customers on web, iOS and Android saw slow responses, HTTP 504 and 429 errors from 14:04 to 16:57 UTC, nearly 3 hours.
detection: Automated monitoring on the database servers flagged the overload immediately.
fix: Atlassian disabled the code change, shed some inbound traffic and added database capacity while over a million websocket connections re-established, and plans to refactor authorization, test for broadcast queries and make load shedding fail fast.
summary: On 30 November 2023 Trello was largely unusable for almost three hours. An authorization refactor, fully rolled out the previous evening, made web requests use a broadcast query against the collection Trello needs for every authorization decision, overloading database nodes at peak traffic. Websocket servers then crashed with OutOfMemoryErrors, and the reconnection of over a million clients generated still more broadcast queries, creating a feedback loop. Load shedding happened after authorization, so it did not relieve the database. Atlassian reverted the change, blocked traffic and scaled the database.

title: Out-of-sync JWT verification keys break Firebase auth in nam5
trigger: During a Cloud IAM cutover to a new configuration management system, a key-distribution bug let signing switch to new keys before matching verification keys reached every region.
impact: Firebase Authentication, Identity Platform and Firebase Security Rules users in the nam5 multi-region got spurious permission-denied errors for 6 hours 41 minutes; about 20% of Firestore access checks failed globally and up to 90% of nam5 Firestore Streaming calls saw invalid-token errors.
detection: Engineers learned of the problem through customer support cases on 15 November.
fix: Google finished rolling the new verification keys out to us-central1 to restore a consistent configuration, and is reviewing config rollout consistency, adding customer-perspective monitoring and slowing the pace of auth-system changes.
summary: A Cloud IAM configuration migration rotated OpenID Connect JWT signing keys before the corresponding verification certificates had propagated to all regions. Tokens signed with the new keys were rejected wherever they landed on an out-of-date region, producing 403 and invalid-token errors in Firestore, Cloud Storage for Firebase and Firebase Auth APIs such as CreateSessionCookie. The nam5 impact lasted 6h41m until Google completed the key rollout to us-central1. Follow-ups target rollout consistency checks, better outside-in monitoring and fewer concurrent auth changes.

title: Database manager deploy triggers unplanned Postgres restarts
trigger: A code deploy to Render's database management system produced an unintended configuration change that forced affected Postgres instances to restart to apply it.
impact: A subset of Point-In-Time Recovery-enabled Postgres databases across all regions was unavailable for 3 to 8 minutes, while in Ohio a separate scale-up bug stretched downtime to as long as 37 minutes and 2 instances needed manual recovery.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Render rolled back an unrelated change that blocked Ohio scale-up and plans guard rails against unintended restarts, a fix so this config change no longer restarts databases, pre-deploy testing for restart-triggering changes and better alerting.
summary: A release of Render's internal database management system altered configuration on specific managed Postgres instances, causing those PITR-enabled databases in every region to restart unexpectedly and go offline for several minutes. In the Ohio region, a concurrent and unrelated bug prevented capacity from scaling up to absorb relocated databases, extending the outage there until a separate rollback, and two databases had to be brought back by hand. Follow-ups target restart guard rails, testing and faster detection.

title: ScyllaDB OS upgrade plus degraded disk takes down Discord auth
trigger: A zonal OS upgrade took zone c of the scylla-authentication cluster offline while a node in zone b had a degraded NVMe disk and cold row cache.
impact: For about 50 minutes starting at 10:52 AM PST users could not log in, connect or send messages, with HTTP success rate falling to roughly 25%.
detection: Engineers were already on an incident call before the first alerts fired at 10:56 AM, about four minutes in.
fix: Discord shed load by disabling typing events and read markers, waited for zone c's RAID rebuild then restarted the b nodes by 11:43 AM, and later doubled the cluster, replaced the bad disk and began automating upgrades with cache-hit checks.
summary: Discord's Rust authentication service depends on a small ScyllaDB cluster spread across three zones. During an OS upgrade, zone c was drained while zone b nodes had cold caches and one, scylla-authentication-b-2, had a degraded NVMe SSD that slowed its RAID rebuild. Losing quorum headroom overloaded the cluster, and client retries created a retry storm, so authentication lookups failed platform-wide. Recovery waited on a roughly 45 minute RAID rebuild. Follow-ups include doubling cluster size, detecting subtle disk degradation, and a Scylla control plane.

title: Data center power loss takes down control plane and analytics
trigger: Utility maintenance and a suspected transformer ground fault cut both grid and generator power at the Flexential PDX-04 facility in Oregon, and its UPS batteries ran out after roughly four minutes.
impact: The Cloudflare dashboard, APIs and analytics were degraded for about 41 hours, raw logs were unavailable for most customers for the whole event and much Logpush data was lost, while edge traffic kept flowing.
detection: Alerts fired when the two routers linking PDX-04 dropped offline at 11:44 UTC; the earlier switch to generator power went unnoticed and the facility operator did not notify Cloudflare until 12:28 UTC.
fix: Cloudflare failed control plane services over to European disaster recovery sites, rate limited a thundering herd of API retries, and rebuilt PDX-04 servers from scratch, then launched a Code Orange program to remove single-facility dependencies and test full data center loss.
summary: A power event at a single Portland-area colocation facility knocked out Cloudflare's control plane and analytics for roughly two days. Services labeled highly available still relied on Kafka and ClickHouse clusters that lived only in PDX-04, and losing an entire facility had never been rehearsed. Customers saw dashboard and API errors, missing analytics and dropped log pushes while proxy traffic stayed up. Recovery required a failover to Europe and a slow, full re-bootstrap of every server in the building.

title: Workers KV rollback points production at a staging build
trigger: While rolling back a KV release, a deployment tool bug that listed staging and production releases together pointed production at a version only deployed to staging.
impact: For 37 minutes, from 19:54 to 20:31 UTC, KV returned HTTP 401 errors, breaking Pages, Access logins, WARP device posture, Workers edits, Turnstile, Images, AI Gateway and the dashboard.
detection: Automated alerting fired right after traffic began being misrouted.
fix: Engineers used break-glass procedures to repoint production to the previous good build, and planned standardized deployments, Access-independent rollbacks, input validation and environment checks.
summary: A progressive rollout of a new Cloudflare Workers KV build hit a routing problem, so the team rolled back. A latent bug in the deployment tool mixed staging and production releases, so the rollback targeted a script that ran nowhere in production, black-holing traffic and making KV answer reads and writes with HTTP 401. Pages sites returned 500, Access logins and posture checks failed, Turnstile failed closed, and internal tooling broke because it depended on KV via Access, slowing the manual fix.

title: Management plane change OOMs virtual router controllers in us-central1
trigger: A slowly rolling management plane change for instance groups and NEGs drove unexpected memory growth in virtual router controllers once it reached the large workloads of us-central1.
impact: For 7 hours 47 minutes new and migrated VMs in us-central1 had delayed or broken networking and there was cross- and intra-region packet loss, affecting GCE, GKE, Dataflow, Cloud SQL, Filestore, Dataproc and other products.
detection: Alerts on control plane slowness arrived at 21:45 US/Pacific on 4 October, and memory-exhaustion alerts at 02:11 on 5 October.
fix: Engineers raised controller memory, then rolled back the management plane change by 09:35 and manually restarted a few stuck routers; follow-ups add memory alerting, faster memory reallocation, cross-team change visibility and router memory optimizations.
summary: A management plane behavior change meant to decouple API updates for Instance Groups and Network Endpoint Groups had rolled out safely elsewhere, but in us-central1 the large workloads made virtual network router controllers run out of memory and crash-loop. Because the change touched a regional API, every zone's controllers were hit at once, and routers stopped receiving fresh state for new VMs, migrations, dynamic routes and backend health. New VMs waited a long time for connectivity and packet loss appeared. Rolling back the change ended the OOMs.

title: Unparseable ZONEMD record leaves 1.1.1.1 on stale, expired root zone
trigger: The DNS root zone began carrying a ZONEMD record on 21 September, which Cloudflare's root zone parser could not handle, so updates silently stopped loading.
impact: From 07:00 to about 10:32 UTC, the 1.1.1.1 resolver returned SERVFAIL for valid lookups, peaking at 15% of queries versus a 3% baseline, affecting WARP, Zero Trust and downstream resolvers.
detection: Users reported unexpected SERVFAIL responses starting 07:57 UTC and an incident was declared at 08:03 UTC.
fix: Engineers stopped 1.1.1.1 from preloading the root zone at 10:30 UTC, and planned stale-zone alerts, ingestion that tolerates new record types, parse-failure tests and a cap on stale zone use per RFC 8806.
summary: Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 resolver serves a local copy of the DNS root zone through a static_zone component that only swaps in a new version after a clean parse. When the root zone added a ZONEMD record, parsing failed and the 21 September copy stayed in use for two weeks. Its DNSSEC signatures expired on 4 October, so validation broke and resolvers returned SERVFAIL, mostly in large sites like Ashburn, Frankfurt and Singapore. An initial override rule failed because a tag was not forwarded between cache nodes.

title: Leader-election change blanks some Cloud Load Balancer configs
trigger: A resiliency rollout altered leader election in the load balancer configuration pipeline, exposing a race in a downstream component that replaced some customer configs with empty ones.
impact: Some Global External Load Balancer customers served HTTP 4xx errors over an incident spanning 1 day and 4 minutes; for the Internet NEG configuration type up to 20% of queries failed and up to 9.3% of such projects were affected at peak.
detection: Dataplane monitoring for HTTP 4xx responses alerted engineers at 04:51 US/Pacific on 22 September.
fix: Engineers froze the pipeline, restored a known-good snapshot, manually repaired configs and then ran a custom rollback of the management component finished at 23:34; follow-ups fix the race, speed up rollbacks, improve 4xx alert triage and move config management to regional scope.
summary: Google changed how a component of the Cloud Load Balancing configuration management pipeline elected its leader. That change triggered a race condition downstream which overwrote certain customer configurations with empty ones, so affected External Application Load Balancers returned 4xx errors and URLs failed to load. Restoring a good snapshot helped briefly, but leader flips kept reintroducing bad state until a custom rollback completed late on 22 September. Customers could work around it by editing their load balancer config. Google plans faster rollback tooling and regional isolation.

title: Connection churn on GKE node causes Postgres and memcached timeouts
trigger: A recent change with an accidental database join made the app fire thousands of duplicate calls to an external third party, flooding a node with short-lived connections.
impact: Postgres connection timeouts spiked and a small share of requests hit memcached i/o timeouts over several days; the post gives no precise duration or user count, and the incident date is not stated beyond the September 2023 publication.
detection: An incident was declared after a spike in Postgres connection timeouts, with new connections being opened at hundreds per second.
fix: The team fixed the accidental join, lengthened connection lifetimes, used static pool sizes and more idle memcached connections, and plans to cap outbound concurrency and use keep-alives.
summary: Soon after moving to Google Kubernetes Engine, incident.io saw Postgres connection timeouts and sporadic memcached i/o timeouts. Connection pools were churning, reopening hundreds of connections per second, and a buggy join was making thousands of duplicate external API calls. The team's leading theory is that this burst of TCP connections drove up CPU in GKE Dataplane V2 anetd pods, dropping packets for other traffic on the same node. Deploying the join fix and stabilizing pools brought new Postgres connections down from about 200 to 1 per second.

title: Edge router RPKI bug knocks AMS3, LON1 and SFO2 offline
trigger: A bug in edge router operating system software made the routing process crash when an RPKI-related routing update arrived, and every redundant edge device ran the vulnerable version.
impact: AMS3, LON1 and SFO2 suffered repeated Internet outages from 09:55 UTC, mostly 10-15 minutes each and affecting up to 100% of traffic in places, with full stability only at 14:23 UTC on August 9, 2023.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: After vendor investigation, DigitalOcean performed an emergency software upgrade of all affected edge routers (which caused some extra disruption while traffic was shifted) and is continuing broader network upgrades for reliability.
summary: On 9 August 2023 DigitalOcean's AMS3, LON1 and SFO2 datacenters lost Internet connectivity in several waves. Edge routers hit a software bug that crashed their routing process on receipt of an RPKI-related update; since all redundant devices shared the buggy version, the whole edge failed, and each restart took minutes to rebuild global routing tables. Droplets, Load Balancers, Kubernetes and Managed Databases were affected. An emergency router upgrade, itself briefly disruptive, ended the instability by 14:23 UTC.

title: Stuck cache writes trigger MySQL deadlock and full Honeycomb outage
trigger: After a routine switch between two Retriever clusters, the query engine stopped writing last-written timestamps the schema cache depended on, and a feature-flag bug kept writes disabled even after the flag was reverted.
impact: All of Honeycomb was down for about 68 minutes (13:40 to 14:48 UTC), with no ingest or querying, and data sent during the window was lost unless customers buffered it.
detection: A Shepherd SLO began burning slowly hours after the cluster switch, and the next morning charts showed the database update calls had stopped.
fix: Engineers tripped circuit breakers to shed Shepherd traffic, failed the locked MySQL primary over to a replica and manually refreshed schema timestamps; the cluster migration was finished and the code able to disable cache writes removed.
summary: Honeycomb moved traffic between Retriever clusters to dodge a bug, but the active cluster stopped updating last-written timestamps, weakening the Shepherd ingest schema cache. Flipping writes back with a feature flag failed because hosts told to stop writing never resumed until restarted, a flaw previously hidden by frequent deploys. As cache misses surged, reads piled onto the main MySQL database on RDS, a rare deadlock locked threads and exhausted connections, and every service failed. A failover to a replica restored the database.

title: Missing slash in redirect URL breaks all crates.io downloads
trigger: A refactor moving S3 access to the object_store crate dropped the slash between the CDN prefix and path, so download redirects pointed to the bogus host static.crates.iocrates.
impact: For about 13 minutes (12:17 to 12:30 UTC), every crate download failed, with roughly 3.7 million failed requests (including cargo's retries) at about 4,700 per second, and cargo users saw could not resolve host errors.
detection: The deploying developer saw elevated request rates in Grafana, and a community member reported the GitHub issue on Zulip about 11 minutes after deployment.
fix: The deploy was rolled back in the Heroku UI within about a minute, a corrected change with realistic tests shipped later, and crate downloads were added to the staging smoke test plan.
summary: A crates.io pull request finished migrating S3 access to the object_store crate and refactored how download endpoints build redirect URLs. Tests used values unlike production's environment variables, so nobody noticed that the slash between the CDN host and path was lost. After deploy, cargo was redirected to static.crates.iocrates/..., failed DNS lookups, and retried, producing millions of failed requests. The change had merged without review and staging smoke tests covered publishing only. A Heroku rollback restored service.

title: Latent Lambda Frontend bug hit at new cell size in us-east-1
trigger: Routine daily scaling of the Lambda Frontend pushed one cell past a size it had never reached, exposing a latent defect in execution environment allocation.
impact: Lambda in US-EAST-1 returned elevated errors and latency for about 3 hours 48 minutes, and STS, AWS Sign-in, EventBridge, EKS, the Management Console, Amazon Connect and Support Center were degraded.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; it says engineering teams engaged immediately and found the defect by 12:26 PM PDT.
fix: Engineers scaled the Frontend fleet back below the triggering size, which restored invocations, then disabled that scaling, fixed and deployed the bug fix to all Regions and planned to bound every cell to a tested size.
summary: As Lambda's Frontend fleet grew to meet normal afternoon traffic, one US-EAST-1 cell crossed a capacity threshold never seen before. A latent bug then caused execution environments to be allocated but never used, so Lambda could not provision environments for new invocations. Synchronous calls failed until about 1:45 PM PDT and async backlogs drained by 3:37 PM. Services built on Lambda, including STS, console sign-in and EventBridge, also saw errors.

title: Foreign key type overflow breaks Heroku logins and deploys
trigger: A foreign key column used a smaller integer type than the primary key it pointed to, and once the primary key outgrew it new authorizations failed.
impact: All customers were unable to log in or deploy for about 1 hour 45 minutes, followed by roughly 2 hours of full outage of the Heroku API, Dashboard and CLI; running apps stayed up.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem beyond a public notice at 15:57 UTC reporting global authentication failures, with users seeing HTTP 500 Application error pages.
fix: Engineers migrated the column to the correct type, which wiped Postgres statistics and slowed queries, so they ran the API read-only until statistics were rebuilt, and plan schema-mismatch monitoring, alerts on columns nearing type limits, and playbook updates to refresh statistics.
summary: Heroku's platform API went down when a primary key grew past the range of a narrower foreign key column referencing it, stopping new OAuth authorizations and therefore logins and deploys. Fixing the column type with a migration reset Postgres table statistics, and the resulting slow query plans escalated a partial failure into a full API, Dashboard and CLI outage. Running dynos were unaffected. Service returned once statistics were refreshed.

title: redis-py connection bug shows ChatGPT users other users' data
trigger: A server change at 1 a.m. Pacific raised Redis request cancellations, exposing a redis-py asyncio bug that left cancelled connections holding stale responses for the next request.
impact: Some users saw other users' chat titles, and payment details such as name, email, address and card last four digits of 1.2% of ChatGPT Plus subscribers active in a nine-hour window may have been exposed; ChatGPT was taken offline and a few hours of history were lost.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: OpenAI took ChatGPT offline, patched redis-py with the Redis maintainers, added checks that cached data matches the requesting user, notified affected users and hardened its Redis Cluster.
summary: ChatGPT caches user data in Redis Cluster via the asyncio redis-py client. If a request was cancelled after being sent but before its reply was read, the pooled connection kept the orphaned reply and handed it to the next unrelated request. A change on March 20 sharply increased cancellations, so some users saw other people's conversation titles, and some subscription emails and account pages exposed other Plus users' names, emails, addresses and partial card details. Full card numbers were never exposed.

title: Kubernetes upgrade corrupts iptables, CircleCI jobs stop starting
trigger: An in-progress Kubernetes upgrade of the main production cluster led to kube-proxy sync failures that left iptables rules corrupted on many nodes.
impact: Docker, Machine, macOS and Windows jobs were delayed and then stopped starting, and the UI and API degraded, from about 18:00 UTC on March 14 until about 01:27 UTC on March 15, with follow-on RabbitMQ and GitHub checks problems later that day.
detection: Engineers noticed rising service-to-service communication errors around 18:00 UTC; the postmortem does not describe a specific alert.
fix: The team restarted services, every node and the rest of the infrastructure, then RabbitMQ nodes to clear corrupted queues, and added kube-proxy sync error alerts while reworking the upgrade process.
summary: During a Kubernetes version upgrade of CircleCI's main cluster, kube-proxy repeatedly failed to sync and left broken iptables rules on multiple nodes, causing widespread internal networking failures. Restarting node-local DNS and CoreDNS made name resolution fail entirely, and full recovery needed restarts of every node and later of RabbitMQ to fix corrupted queues. Jobs across executors stopped starting for about seven hours. The postmortem notes there was no single trigger.

title: Kubernetes 1.24 upgrade drops label, breaking Calico route reflectors
trigger: Upgrading the legacy Kubernetes cluster from 1.23 to 1.24 removed the node-role.kubernetes.io/master label that the Calico route reflector configuration selected on.
impact: Reddit was broken for 314 minutes on the afternoon of March 14 in US hours, with error pages or empty home feeds.
detection: The site halted about two minutes after the upgrade began and an incident was opened immediately; the cluster had lost its metrics, so engineers relied on CDN edge stats.
fix: After failing to fix forward, the team restored the control plane from backup, regenerated TLS certificates for a hostname mismatch, and ramped traffic back in steps; follow-ups target safer, more uniform cluster upgrades.
summary: On Pi Day 2023 an in-place upgrade of Reddit's largest, hand-built Kubernetes cluster to 1.24 knocked out pod networking. Calico route reflectors were configured years earlier to run on nodes carrying the master label, which 1.24 removes, so all routes dropped and in-cluster and Consul DNS stopped resolving. With no supported downgrade, engineers restored etcd from an outdated backup procedure, hit AWS instance capacity limits and certificate errors, then reopened traffic gradually from 1% to 100%.

title: Auto systemd update drops Cilium routes, downing all Datadog regions
trigger: A legacy OS security update channel automatically installed a systemd patch at 06:00 UTC, and restarting systemd-networkd on Ubuntu 22.04 deleted the routes managed by the Cilium CNI plugin, taking nodes offline.
impact: Starting 06:03 UTC on March 8, 2023, the US1, EU1, US3, US4 and US5 regions lost web, API and monitor access across all services as tens of thousands of nodes dropped; all services were operational by 08:58 UTC on March 9 and historical backfill finished at 06:25 UTC on March 10.
detection: Internal monitoring alerted three minutes after the first faulty update, and a public incident was declared at 06:31 UTC.
fix: Datadog rebuilt compute capacity region by region with its cloud providers, restored control planes and then services, prioritizing live data; it disabled the legacy update channel, set systemd-networkd to leave routes alone on restart and audited for similar channels.
summary: Datadog's first global outage hit five regions on three cloud providers at once. The base OS image for its Kubernetes nodes still had an old automatic security-update channel enabled, with a default 06:00-07:00 UTC window, so a systemd update landed everywhere simultaneously. On running nodes, the systemd-networkd restart wiped Cilium-managed container routes, knocking tens of thousands of nodes off the network. Recovery was slowed by providers replacing unhealthy nodes, regional rate limits and quorum-based metadata stores, with live data restored before historical backfill.

title: Expired Squiz Edge certificates cause SSL errors for AU/NZ sites
trigger: Certificates used by Squiz Edge to talk to web servers for some clients.squiz.net subdomains expired.
impact: Some Australia/New Zealand customers saw SSL errors when opening their sites or running searches from about 11:02 to 11:30 AEDT.
detection: Squiz internal monitoring raised SSL alerts at about 11:02 AEDT.
fix: Engineers renewed the expired certificates and restarted the Openresty service; internal certificate renewal procedures will be reviewed and updated.
summary: A subset of Squiz customers in Australia and New Zealand whose sites sit on clients.squiz.net subdomains hit SSL error pages and failing searches when certificates used between the Squiz Edge layer and backend web servers lapsed. Internal monitoring flagged the SSL failures, and the Technical Engineering team renewed the certificates and restarted Openresty, recovering service in under half an hour. Squiz said it would revisit the processes for renewing these internal certificates to avoid a repeat.

title: Incomplete topology snapshot drops traffic across Google's network
trigger: A routine refresh of network-modeling snapshot data handed the bandwidth-routing control plane a partial topology that omitted several sites, so their outbound traffic was discarded.
impact: Heavy packet loss for up to seven minutes from 04:58 US/Pacific, with dependent services such as BigQuery, Bigtable, Apigee, Cloud SQL, Dataflow and the Cloud Console erroring for roughly 13 minutes in total (e.g. up to 20% of Apigee requests timing out in some regions).
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Automation pushed a full topology snapshot on the next programming cycle and the network converged by 05:05; follow-ups include control-plane input validation, a fix for the snapshot bug, sharding the topology input per region and safer site-removal ordering.
summary: On 27 February 2023 a control-plane component that computes bandwidth paths for Google's production backbone consumed an incomplete topology snapshot that left out several sites. Traffic originating from those sites was dropped for up to seven minutes until automation pushed a correct snapshot. The packet loss rippled into Google Cloud and Workspace: BigQuery and Bigtable returned 503s, Dataflow streaming jobs stalled, Persistent Disk I/O hung, and load balancers served 500s. Google is adding input validation, regional sharding of topology inputs and a fix for the snapshot defect.

title: Terraform deploy deletes static.crates.io DNS during cert swap
trigger: A single Terraform apply bundled a new CDN TLS certificate with DNS record changes, deleting the old records first and waiting about 10 minutes for the certificate before recreating them.
impact: For an estimated 10 to 15 minutes from about 09:15 UTC, static.crates.io failed to resolve, so Rust builds that needed to download crates failed, with some users affected longer due to resolver caching.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The outage ended when Terraform recreated the DNS record, and the team committed to documenting deploys, shipping staged changes one at a time, and deploying on merge to avoid drift.
summary: crates.io infrastructure is managed with Terraform, and production lagged behind the main branch. A deploy therefore applied two separately tested changes together: a new TLS certificate for the CDN and updated DNS records. Terraform removed the existing certificate and DNS entries, spent around 10 minutes issuing the certificate, and only then wrote the new records. During that gap static.crates.io had no DNS entry, so cargo builds needing crate downloads failed until propagation finished around 09:40 UTC.

title: Router command during Madrid capacity work destabilizes Microsoft WAN
trigger: While adding WAN capacity in Madrid, an engineer followed a modified, unvalidated procedure that ran an IGP database purge command which on one vendor's routers acts across every IGP-joined router.
impact: From 07:08 to 12:43 UTC customers saw high latency, timeouts and connectivity loss to Azure regions, Microsoft 365, Power Platform and dependent Azure Government services, with most recovered by 09:05 UTC.
detection: Monitoring flagged DNS and WAN problems at 07:11 UTC, within five minutes, but the engineer was not told and repeated the step on a second router 33 minutes later.
fix: Routing reconverged automatically and engineers manually restarted paused WAN health and traffic engineering systems; repairs include blocking similar high-impact commands, real-time visibility of device changes, mandatory SOP training and review of unqualified SOPs.
summary: On 25 January 2023 a network engineer adding routers to Microsoft's global WAN in Madrid ran a revised procedure that had skipped required testing. It included an IGP database purge command, which, on one router vendor's platform, makes every router in the IGP domain recompute topology, and it was missing from the AAA block list. All WAN routers recalculated paths and BGP routers re-advertised internet prefixes, causing two waves of routing instability. Convergence took about 1 hour 40 minutes, with residual packet loss until automation was manually restarted.

title: Access service token change blanks secrets, breaking many products
trigger: A release adding a last seen timestamp to Access service tokens wrote tokens back after reading them with the client secret redacted, saving empty secrets.
impact: For 121 minutes, from 17:50 to 19:51 UTC, WARP, Zero Trust, Gateway, R2, Cache Reserve, Cache Purge, Images and parts of the API failed, with Gateway peaking above 50,000 extra 5XX errors per minute.
detection: An internal alert fired when WARP device posture uploads fell to zero, followed by alerts from Cache Purge, R2, Images and Cache Reserve.
fix: Engineers restored correct token values for the affected internal accounts and then restored them from a database backup, and planned unit tests, auth failure alerts, faster table rollbacks and empty-string checks.
summary: A Cloudflare Access feature to show when service tokens were last used read each token through a path that redacts the client secret, then saved it, leaving an empty secret. A not-null constraint did not catch the empty string. Four internal accounts used by WARP, Gateway, R2, Cache Reserve, Cache Purge and Images lost working credentials as updates propagated, so devices failed posture checks and lost Internet access, R2 requests errored, and purges failed. A later bad update briefly restarted the API impact.

title: Hidden transaction pile-up starves Go DB pools and times out API
trigger: Many short-lived database transactions, including a needless one opened on most Slack modal submissions, held connections in the Go database/sql pools.
impact: Over about two weeks, some API requests timed out intermittently while waiting up to around 20 seconds for a connection, with each episode clearing in about a minute; request counts are not given.
detection: A customer report and a spike of context canceled errors in Sentry, followed by Grafana dashboards and traces showing time spent waiting on the pool.
fix: The team added a one-second lock timeout, moved Slack event handling to async PubSub, built per-operation connection-hold metrics, and finally removed the unnecessary transaction so only code needing atomicity opens one.
summary: In early 2023 incident.io saw sporadic API timeouts with no obvious cause: no deploys, no traffic spike, no slow query. Traces eventually showed requests waiting on the client-side database/sql connection pool, not on Postgres itself. The culprit was transaction overuse, especially a wrapper that opened a transaction for most Slack modal submissions, which kept connections checked out. Early quick wins like indexes and a materialised view did not help; new instrumentation of connection hold time found the real issue. Exact dates are not stated.
