title: Malware steals engineer SSO session, customer secrets exfiltrated
trigger: Malware on an engineer's laptop, undetected by antivirus, stole a valid 2FA-backed SSO session cookie, letting the attacker impersonate the employee and use their ability to mint production access tokens.
impact: On December 22, 2022 the attacker took customers' stored secrets from production databases, including environment variables and credentials for outside services, and pulled encryption keys from a running process; under 5 customers had reported resulting unauthorized access when the report was published.
detection: A customer flagged suspicious GitHub OAuth activity on December 29, 2022, which led to a joint review with GitHub that uncovered the intrusion.
fix: CircleCI cut off the compromised employee, narrowed production access, rebuilt all production hosts, revoked Project and Personal API Tokens, rotated GitHub OAuth and Bitbucket tokens, told every customer to rotate all stored secrets, and added MDM/antivirus detection plus step-up authentication for production access.
summary: A CircleCI engineer's laptop was infected with malware on December 16, 2022, which stole a 2FA-backed SSO session cookie. Using that session, the attacker escalated into production, ran reconnaissance on December 19 and exfiltrated customer environment variables, API keys and OAuth tokens on December 22, along with encryption keys taken from memory. A customer's report of odd GitHub OAuth use started the investigation. CircleCI revoked Project and Personal API Tokens, rotated GitHub and Bitbucket tokens, rebuilt hosts and urged all customers to rotate every secret stored on the platform.

title: Lagging backend index breaks IAP SSH to new Compute Engine VMs
trigger: A problem with a global index on the backend database IAP uses to verify instances made writes fall behind GCE instance updates, so new or changed VMs were unknown to IAP.
impact: For a total of 22 hours 46 minutes, SSH via Identity-Aware Proxy to GCE instances created or updated after 17:30 PT on 1 December failed with error 4047 Failed to lookup instance; running workloads were unaffected.
detection: Engineers were first notified through a support case at 22:44 PT on 1 December.
fix: Engineers sent IAP traffic to a standby database replica, and after a rollout flipped it back at 17:45 PT they redirected again for full resolution at 20:50 PT; follow-ups add backlog alerting, finer-grained rollouts and exclusive locks to avoid deadlocked transactions.
summary: Identity-Aware Proxy checks that a Compute Engine instance exists in a real-time backend database before allowing SSH tunnels. An issue with a global index on that database meant writes could not keep pace with GCE instance changes, so newly created or modified VMs never appeared and gcloud start-iap-tunnel failed with a 4047 lookup error. Failing over to a standby replica mitigated it, but an unrelated rollout reverted the override and the outage recurred for three more hours. Google is adding backlog alerting and decoupling IAP config rollouts.

title: Ruby 3.1.3 extension path change breaks Open Build Service deploy
trigger: An application deploy ran without the pending Ruby 3.1.3 update, whose changed OS detection had moved gem C extensions from x86_64-linux to x86_64-linux-gnu.
impact: The OBS reference server answered every request with a maintenance page for 13 minutes, blocking all API and web UI use.
detection: The deployment itself reported errors, monitoring alerted, and users reported the problem through several channels.
fix: The pending Ruby stack update was deployed and obs-api services restarted; the deploy process will now warn about pending package updates and apply trusted updates together.
summary: After a routine production deploy, the Open Build Service reference server failed to start because bundler could not load gems with native extensions such as mysql2 and nokogiri. A Ruby 3.1.3 patch release had altered Linux OS detection, relocating compiled extension directories, and the app was deployed separately from that update. The same failure had appeared on staging a day earlier but was blamed on a new deploy method. Installing the pending Ruby packages and restarting obs-api-support.target restored service.

title: AWS security group connection tracking limit breaks Atlassian DNS
trigger: Organic traffic growth pushed connections through Atlassian's EC2-based DNS servers in us-east-1 past the AWS security group connection tracking allowance, so DNS packets were dropped.
impact: From 19:39 to 21:28 UTC (1 hour 49 minutes) a subset of Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket customers saw anything from intermittent errors to full outages, slow pages and API 5xx responses, with up to 90% of DNS lookups in us-east-1 failing.
detection: An automated monitoring system detected the incident within nine minutes.
fix: Atlassian scaled up the DNS servers to raise the allowance, then made a configuration change so DNS traffic no longer consumes the security group allowance, and is adding packet-drop monitoring and migrating to the AWS VPC resolver.
summary: Atlassian Cloud services in AWS resolve names through centralized EC2 DNS servers protected by security groups. A new daily traffic peak hit the hidden per-security-group connection tracking limit, causing dropped DNS packets in us-east-1; services retried on SERVFAIL and timeouts, adding even more connections. Apps failed to resolve dependencies, hurting Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket and partner apps globally. Diagnosis was slow because allowance usage and related drops were not observable, and the fix was scaling up followed by a permanent config change.

title: Redis eviction of agent heartbeats strands Buildkite agents
trigger: A backfill grew a large Redis set until the shard ran low on memory and the volatile-lru policy evicted agent heartbeat keys, and a later DEL of that huge set froze the shard.
impact: Some agents disconnected from about 2022-11-19 13:00 UTC and could not reconnect, Agent API errors peaked at 80% from 02:35 to 03:10 UTC on 2022-11-21 so most customers' builds stopped, and older agents stayed offline until 05:54 UTC.
detection: High Redis memory should have paged but a misconfigured monitor stayed silent; the low-memory shard was noticed on Sunday evening UTC.
fix: Buildkite failed over to a new empty Redis cluster and bumped the session cache key version so agents could reconnect; follow-ups include fixing the alert, treating missing heartbeats as unknown, incremental deletes and having agents re-register on 401.
summary: Buildkite tracked a data backfill in a Redis set whose size was underestimated. When the ElastiCache shard filled up, eviction removed agent heartbeat keys, so long-running agents looked lost past the 24-hour limit and got HTTP 401s, which the agent kept retrying instead of re-registering. Deleting the big set with an O(N) DEL hung the shard, forced a failover and pushed Agent API errors to 80%. A rolling switch to a new cluster left a split-brain session cache, fixed by invalidating it.

title: Poison-pill Pub/Sub message repeatedly crashes incident.io Go app
trigger: A Pub/Sub message for a welcome-message subscription caused a panic in a goroutine spawned by the Google Cloud Pub/Sub client, where the existing recover() did not reach.
impact: The app was down for 13 minutes within a 32-minute window (15:40 to 16:12 GMT), with Heroku reporting H10 App crashed errors.
detection: Heroku H10 errors paged the on-call engineer through PagerDuty.
fix: The team purged subscriptions holding unacknowledged messages and disabled non-critical async features, then added recover() to the shared Pub/Sub handler and split web, worker and cron into separate Heroku dyno tiers.
summary: incident.io ran web, worker and cron code in one Go binary on Heroku. A message that crashed its handler kept being redelivered by GCP Pub/Sub, and because the client's Receive runs handlers in fresh goroutines, the panic escaped recovery and killed the whole process, so the app crash-looped. Diagnosis was slow because Heroku dropped the huge goroutine dump, log rate limits hid lines before each crash, and Sentry never got the error. Purging subscriptions stopped the crashes.

title: Tracing wrapper in Tiered Cache strips headers, causing HTTP 530s
trigger: A CDN release that wrapped the Tiered Cache entrypoint with opentracing code cleared internal control headers on every request, so upper-tier data centers lost the hostname needed for origin DNS lookups.
impact: Sites using Tiered Cache, Cloudflare Images or Bandwidth Alliance returned HTTP 530 errors for almost six hours in total, peaking at about 5% of all requests at 17:28 UTC.
detection: Customer reports and a per-customer alert at 10:35 UTC flagged rising errors, and alerts plus more reports fired once the release reached large data centers.
fix: After a rollback in Atlanta confirmed the cause at 17:03 UTC, an accelerated global rollback finished at 18:30 UTC; follow-ups include earlier upper-tier sites in the release plan, broader Tiered Cache test topologies and fail-fast behavior.
summary: Cloudflare added distributed tracing around its Tiered Cache Lua code, but the opentracing module's header extractor wiped control headers that lower tiers pass to upper tiers. Without the hostname, the upper tier's internal DNS lookup for the origin failed and visitors got HTTP 530 errors. The slow rollout starting 08:40 UTC masked the cause, and a concurrent internal DNS release misled responders. Rolling back the CDN release in all upper tiers ended impact at 18:04 UTC.

title: RPC library deadlock jams BigQuery Storage Write API in US
trigger: A surge of inbound and logging traffic, together with a bug in Google's internal streaming RPC library, deadlocked Write API streaming frontend instances.
impact: BigQuery Storage Write API customers in the US multi-region saw elevated connection failures for 5 hours, from 23:30 on October 13 to 04:30 US/Pacific on October 14, 2022, and InsertAll API calls saw a slight increase in failures.
detection: An internal alert raised the issue at 23:47 US/Pacific on October 13.
fix: After automatic memory increases and raising the instance cap from 200 to 1000 did not help, engineers restarted the stuck instances; the RPC library and Write API bugs were fixed and connection-aware load balancing is being added.
summary: BigQuery's Storage Write API, its main high-volume ingestion path, returned elevated errors in the US multi-region overnight. A traffic increase exposed a bug in Google's internal streaming RPC library that, together with a Write API bug, caused a cascading deadlock in frontend tasks. Autoscaling added memory and instances, but the deadlocked tasks stayed in rotation and load balancing kept routing customers to them. Only restarting the stuck instances cleared the problem, about five hours after it began.

title: Envoy Redis filter bug blocks Bitbucket website scale-up
trigger: An Envoy proxy config for a new ElastiCache Redis cluster hit an Envoy bug with hostnames in the Redis cluster command, so newly launched website instances could not start.
impact: From 7:17 to 8:12 AM UTC (about 55 minutes) Bitbucket Cloud users could not reach the website, while the API and Git over SSH and HTTPS kept working.
detection: Automated monitoring detected the issue within 14 minutes and paged on-call engineers.
fix: Engineers reverted the Envoy config, and follow-ups include redeploying and verifying after Envoy config changes, upgrading Envoy to a release with the Redis filter fix, faster control plane rollbacks and better alerting.
summary: Bitbucket Cloud pushed an Envoy sidecar configuration for a Redis cluster that other microservices would use later. Running instances were unaffected, but new instances created during a traffic-driven scale-up loaded the config, tripped an Envoy Redis filter bug with hostnames and never started. Without new capacity, existing website instances hit high CPU, failed health checks and crashed, taking the Bitbucket web UI offline. Reverting the configuration restored service, and Atlassian will upgrade Envoy and verify config changes on fresh instances.

title: Unannounced Azure CosmosDB change makes partition key mandatory
trigger: Azure began requiring a partition key when creating CosmosDB SQL containers, a field Metrist's unchanged monitoring code had never set, without announcing the change.
impact: Metrist's CosmosDB monitor failed about 75 percent of runs on September 14 and around 90 percent of 140 daily East US tests through September 20, spreading to Central US and reaching 100 percent failure by September 21.
detection: Metrist's own scripted functional tests started erroring in East US at 18:42 UTC on September 14, and the service was marked partially down at 19:12 UTC.
fix: After error logs showed One of the specified inputs is invalid on CreateContainer and the Azure portal revealed a required partition key, the team added an explicit WithPartitionKey call to the container, insert and delete checks.
summary: Metrist runs synthetic tests against cloud services, including creating containers in Azure CosmosDB. Starting September 14 its East US CreateContainer step began failing intermittently with an invalid-input error, then the failures rose and spread to Central US, suggesting a gradual Azure rollout. Nothing appeared on Azure's status page and the monitor code had not changed in months. Filling out the portal form showed the partition key had become mandatory; setting it explicitly in the SDK calls resolved the partial outage.

title: Internal service exhausts global Filestore API quota for all customers
trigger: A malfunctioning internal Google service that manages many GCP projects flooded the Cloud Filestore API with requests and used up a global request limit.
impact: Customers in every region got HTTP 429 errors on read-only Filestore calls such as List and GetOperation via Console, gcloud and the API for about three hours (07:30 to 10:42 US/Pacific), with no workaround.
detection: Automated alerts paged Google engineers at 07:47 US/Pacific, about nine minutes after the incident began.
fix: Engineers manually paused the misbehaving internal service, and follow-ups aim to remove the global quotas and improve alerting on internal limits.
summary: Cloud Filestore protects itself with a single global cap on API requests. When an internal Google backend that manages a large fleet of projects went haywire and hammered the API, it consumed that shared cap, so Filestore throttled everyone. For roughly three hours, customers worldwide saw 429 errors on read operations like ListInstances in the Console and gcloud, although create and update calls still worked. Recovery came only after engineers shut the internal service down by hand.

title: Schema cache lock contention crash-loops Honeycomb ingest for hours
trigger: The original trigger was never identified; Shepherd ingest hosts entered a persistent loop of running out of memory and restarting.
impact: Ingest was disrupted for more than eight and a half hours in total, and the team estimates that most customers ingesting during that window saw at least partial impact.
detection: Engineers recognized a familiar shark fin pattern in latency graphs, but unlike past episodes it did not clear within about 15 minutes.
fix: Engineers reduced lock contention in the schema cache and pre-filled it before Shepherd hosts took traffic, then added Refinery capacity; longer-term work targets cache contention and ingest re-architecture.
summary: Honeycomb's Shepherd edge hosts validate incoming events against an in-memory schema cache whose updates took a table-wide lock, so backfilling a missing entry stalled unrelated requests. On September 8 Shepherds fell into a metastable cycle of memory exhaustion and restarts, which also crashed the Refinery cluster sampling their traces. Scaling, slower deploys and aggressive sampling did not help, the autoscaler added hosts in response to crash-loop CPU, and an unpinned chart change redeployed mid-incident. Pre-warming the cache at boot finally stabilized ingest.

title: Ubuntu 18.04 systemd update breaks DNS on Azure VMs and AKS
trigger: A Canonical security update delivered systemd 237-3ubuntu10.54 via unattended-upgrades, whose race-condition bug wiped DNS settings on Ubuntu 18.04 VMs that identify their NIC by driver name.
impact: From 06:00 UTC on 30 August to 16:00 UTC on 31 August 2022 (about 34 hours) Ubuntu 18.04 VMs in all Azure regions lost DNS resolution, causing AKS ImagePullBackoff errors and missing or delayed data and alerts in Azure Monitor, Application Insights, Log Analytics and Sentinel.
detection: Production alerts in several Azure teams, including AKS and Azure Container Apps, fired shortly after the packages were published.
fix: Customers were told to reboot or run a fix script and AKS rolled out automatic detection and remediation; follow-ups include better AKS monitoring, an escalation path to Canonical and AKS taking control of security patch rollout and testing.
summary: A Canonical security update for Ubuntu 18.04 shipped a systemd build with a race condition that, combined with an earlier update, erased DNS configuration on systems that match network interfaces by driver name, as Azure VMs do. VMs with unattended-upgrades installed it automatically and lost name resolution, so AKS nodes could not pull container images and Azure Monitor, Log Analytics and Sentinel lost or delayed data. Because security patches skipped Azure's safe deployment process, impact was global. Microsoft provided reboot and script workarounds and auto-remediated AKS nodes.

title: Broken x2 MainStash replication surfaces edit-time errors
trigger: Cross-datacenter x2 replication broke because the databases used ROW-based replication while the application needed STATEMENT-based, and attempts to skip events with sql_slave_skip_counter then broke the local eqiad replicas, which ChronologyProtector treated as a reason to block MainStash writes.
impact: For 36 minutes (04:07:58-04:43:22 UTC) some editors got Explicit transaction still active exceptions during edit-related actions, though edit saving itself kept working, and about an hour of volatile MainStash data was lost.
detection: Two pages fired as soon as replication broke on the x2 primaries, followed later by pages about the replicas and user reports once the user-facing errors began.
fix: DBAs switched the write hosts to STATEMENT replication, disabled GTID and repositioned the eqiad replicas to resume replicating; follow-ups include fixing the uncaught exception in LoadBalancer::approvePrimaryChanges(), removing ChronologyProtector checks for x2 and reviewing x2 runbooks.
summary: While Wikimedia was enabling multi-DC writes, replication between eqiad and codfw x2 (MainStash) databases split because server binlog format did not match what MediaWiki expected. Manual skip-counter fixes then broke replication inside eqiad, and because ChronologyProtector was still enabled for x2, lagging replicas made MediaWiki refuse MainStash writes. A latent bug let those failures escape as user-visible exceptions on edit actions for 36 minutes. Replication was restored by moving to STATEMENT format without GTID, at the cost of about an hour of cache data.

title: Dependency upgrade stalls workers, routers deleted, US apps fail
trigger: A change to the Common Runtime infrastructure manager brought in a dependency upgrade with a locking problem that slashed task worker throughput, letting its work queue back up.
impact: Between 21:54 and 22:42 UTC (48 minutes) apps in the US Common Runtime region saw elevated latency and request errors because too few routers were left to carry traffic.
detection: Routing availability fell below acceptable levels and engineering was notified, but misconfigured alerts meant nobody was told earlier that new router instances were booting incorrectly.
fix: Engineers reverted the change and manually added public routers, then tightened deployment testing, raised default scaling headroom and added more alertable metrics.
summary: On Heroku's US Common Runtime, a release of the core infrastructure-management application included a dependency bump that introduced a timing lock and throttled its task workers. The resulting queue backlog, combined with insufficient scale-up, left new router instances in an apparent bad boot state even though they were already serving live traffic. Readiness checks then deleted them, shrinking the router pool until incoming requests outpaced capacity, producing 48 minutes of latency and errors. Rolling back the change and hand-scaling routers restored service.

title: Endless SLO backfill drains Lambda capacity, delays triggers
trigger: A single customer SLO whose SLI never produced a valid result had no cache line, so the Basset SLO evaluator relaunched a cold-storage backfill of up to 60 days of data every minute.
impact: Query performance and alerting through triggers and SLOs degraded, with the worst effects lasting about 4 hours out of roughly 9 hours of incident and investigation.
detection: Honeycomb's own SLO measuring trigger runs began firing, and BubbleUp showed trigger runs spacing out, slowing or failing.
fix: The team corrected the broken SLO on the customer's behalf, then fixed how SLO failures are handled, clamped down harder on future-dated timestamps and limited how much triggers can depend on Lambda.
summary: Honeycomb stores recent telemetry on query hosts and older data in S3 queried through AWS Lambda. Future-stamped events from one customer had already pushed short trigger queries into cold storage. Responders assumed those triggers were exhausting Lambda, but most usage came from Basset repeatedly backfilling one SLO whose SLI never returned true, false or null, so no cache entry was ever written and the backfill restarted every minute. Triggers and SLO alerts lagged for hours until a fresh engineer found it.

title: Node replacement knocks out Consul and Vault, PyPI briefly down
trigger: The cloud provider automatically replaced several Kubernetes node instances from 17:24 UTC, reshuffling pods and restarting the Consul and Vault clusters.
impact: PyPI's backends were unresponsive for 7 minutes, from 18:46 to 18:53 UTC.
detection: An alert at 18:23 UTC told PSF Infrastructure that a Vault container was down and needed unsealing.
fix: The responder force-deleted a Consul pod stuck in Terminating so leader election could complete, then unsealed the new Vault containers, letting application pods start again.
summary: An unexplained provider-side failure caused automatic replacement of multiple nodes in the Kubernetes cluster hosting PyPI. Pod rescheduling restarted Consul and Vault; all Vault containers came up sealed and Consul could not elect a leader because a pod hung in Terminating left discovery waiting on an extra server. Without these backing services, rescheduled PyPI app containers failed to launch until the site stopped responding. Forcibly removing the stuck pod and unsealing Vault restored service within minutes of the outage.

title: Missing planner statistics after DB upgrade overload Sentry
trigger: After a database cluster upgrade finished at 9:30 UTC, incomplete query planner statistics led queries to use poor plans and drove database CPU very high.
impact: Queries slowed and API and web requests failed for a total of 49 minutes, affecting the dashboard, API and US ingestion while an event backlog built up.
detection: An alert on database CPU usage fired at 09:50 UTC.
fix: Engineers killed queries to stop the backlog growing and rebuilt database statistics by 10:13 UTC, and plan to ensure statistics are fully computed after upgrades and to manage table attributes as code.
summary: Shortly after Sentry upgraded its database cluster, CPU on the database servers spiked because the upgraded cluster lacked complete planner statistics, causing inefficient query plans. Slow queries piled up and API and web requests began failing while ingested events backed up. Engineers manually terminated queries, recalculated statistics so queries ran quickly again, and cleared the event backlog by 10:31 UTC. The remediation focuses on the upgrade runbook: always fully analyze tables afterward and keep table attributes in code.

title: London heatwave cooling failure powers down part of europe-west2-a
trigger: Several redundant cooling systems, including two chillers, failed simultaneously during record outside temperatures at a data center hosting zone europe-west2-a.
impact: Over roughly a day and a half, about 35% of Compute Engine VMs in the zone were terminated, 38% of zonal Persistent Disk volumes went unavailable, 57% of GKE nodes in the zone dropped out, and dozens of other services including Cloud SQL, Bigtable, BigQuery and Cloud Storage reported errors.
detection: Automated temperature monitoring flagged rising heat in the data center and engineers were paged soon after.
fix: Engineers deliberately powered down part of the zone to protect hardware, shifted load away, then restarted services in sequence after cooling was repaired, with follow-ups to fix zonal failover automation, shed thermal load gradually, and audit cooling equipment globally.
summary: During the July 2022 UK heatwave, chillers at a Google Cloud data center in London failed and temperatures climbed until engineers shut down a portion of zone europe-west2-a. VMs were terminated, disks and GKE nodes became unreachable, and caches in Memorystore were flushed. A legacy Cloud Storage placement scheme put three storage clusters in the same failure domain, and a mistaken routing change briefly blocked replicas in other zones too. Restoring the long tail of instances took many extra hours after cooling returned.

title: Backbone control plane rollout cuts low-priority network capacity
trigger: A new control plane configuration rollout on Google's internal backbone, landing alongside repair work and a scheduled network software upgrade, reduced capacity for low-priority traffic between data centers.
impact: Between 19:30 PT on 14 July and 15:02 PT on 15 July 2022, batch, streaming and transfer traffic was constrained in regions including us-east1, us-central1 and southamerica-west1, causing Cloud Storage latency and HTTP 500s on 0.007% of requests and 20-30% egress loss in two South America regions.
detection: Engineers observed Cloud Networking performance degradation at about 02:00 PT on 15 July as the rollout spread to more regions.
fix: Halting the rollout at 03:50 PT did not stop in-flight actions, so engineers rolled back the configuration globally, succeeding by 12:40 PT; follow-ups target better traffic signals, global rollout safety halts and emergency tooling.
summary: A control plane configuration rollout on Google's backbone network reduced capacity reserved for lower-priority classes such as batch and transfer traffic, while user-facing traffic stayed healthy. Stopping the rollout left in-progress actions running, and the reduced capacity itself hampered pushing the rollback, so the first global attempt at 08:40 PT did not reach all nodes. Cloud Storage and BigQuery Storage API users saw elevated latency and errors until the correct configuration landed at 12:40 PT.

title: Partially failed London WAN router causes intermittent packet loss
trigger: A line card on one Microsoft WAN router near London partly failed, with 4 of its 140 ports misrouting about 0.4% of packets without raising any actionable error.
impact: From 02:40 to 20:14 UTC (about 17.5 hours) some customers with traffic through UK West, UK South, Europe West and Europe North, including ExpressRoute and VPN Gateway users, saw packet loss, slow throughput and occasional connection failures.
detection: Traffic-quality alerting missed the gray failure, so engineers had to find it by manual inspection and indirect signals, initially chasing software causes.
fix: Engineers pulled the faulty router out of service at about 20:14 UTC and let redundant routers carry traffic; follow-ups improved low-intensity WAN alerting, got better vendor error signals, replaced the components and plan better VPN and ExpressRoute diagnostics.
summary: On 29 June 2022 one router in Microsoft's wide area network near London began dropping a small fraction of packets because 4 of its 140 physical ports had failed. The fault produced no clear error and only about 0.4% loss, so alerting did not catch it and engineers first suspected recent software changes. Customers in four UK and European regions, especially those using ExpressRoute or VPN Gateway, saw intermittent latency and connection failures for most of a day until the router was isolated.

title: Artifact repository outage in DR test breaks Atlassian scaling
trigger: Atlassian's internal Artifact Repository Manager went down during a scheduled disaster recovery test spanning multiple availability zones.
impact: Customers in all regions saw more Bitbucket Pipelines build failures and degraded Jira, Confluence and Forge from 01:08 AM UTC, with resolution about three hours later and overall impact listed through 05:58 AM UTC on June 22, 2022.
detection: Monitoring detected the incident within two minutes.
fix: Restarting the Artifact Repository service restored access, cloud Pipelines were failed over to an alternative Docker registry, and Atlassian escalated to the vendor and plans DR plan, testing and redundant caching improvements.
summary: During a scheduled disaster recovery exercise simulating availability zone loss, Atlassian's internal artifact repository went down. Products could no longer pull Docker images and other artifacts to scale out, and new service versions could not be built or deployed, so Jira, Confluence and Forge degraded while Bitbucket Pipelines builds stuck in pending or failed when docker-public.packages.atlassian.com was unreachable. A restart of the repository manager brought services back; vendor resilience work and a redundant cache are planned.

title: BGP policy term reorder withdraws prefixes at 19 Cloudflare sites
trigger: A change to prefix advertisement policies on spine routers in Multi-Colo PoP data centers moved a REJECT-THE-REST term ahead of the site-local terms.
impact: Nineteen data centers carrying about half of Cloudflare's HTTP traffic became unreachable for many users from 06:27 UTC, with all sites working again by 07:42 UTC.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem beyond an internal incident being declared at 06:32 UTC.
fix: Engineers reverted the change, using out-of-band access where needed, and planned MCP-aware rollout testing, a policy redesign that prevents term misordering, and automated commit-confirm rollback.
summary: As part of a BGP communities standardization project, Cloudflare reordered terms in the export policy on spine routers in its newer MCP data centers. A REJECT-THE-REST term now came first, so site-local prefixes stopped being advertised and those locations dropped off the internet. The Multimog load balancer also relied on those prefixes, so smaller clusters got overloaded. Only 4% of locations were hit but they served about 50% of HTTP requests. Recovery was slowed by engineers reverting one another's changes.

title: Backbone optical failure causes 20 minutes of inter-region loss
trigger: Part of a fiber route leaving a central US gateway campus on Google's production backbone failed (preliminarily an optical amplification part), cutting bandwidth to several edge locations.
impact: From 13:47 to 14:07 US/Pacific, traffic between many Google Cloud regions saw intermittent packet loss, affecting Cloud VPN, Cloud Router, Cloud Interconnect, Cloud SQL and Cloud Storage, whose errors lasted until 14:17.
detection: Google's automated repair systems detected the bandwidth drop at 13:47 US/Pacific.
fix: Automation rerouted traffic onto alternate links by 14:06 without human action; Google planned to finish the regional topology augmentation by 11 July 2022 and add checks that topologies support fast convergence.
summary: A failed optical component on a fiber path out of a central US gateway reduced Google backbone bandwidth to edge locations. Automated repair moved traffic away, but because an ongoing augmentation had not finished the second-best path, traffic had to shift to the third-best path, lengthening convergence. For about 20 minutes customers saw packet loss on inter-region traffic, VPN and Interconnect latency, delayed routing updates, Cloud SQL operation failures and Cloud Storage HTTP 500 errors.

title: Schema change flips query plan, taking wikis down for logged-in users
trigger: A schema change on the globalblocks table in the centralauth database (s7) led the MariaDB optimizer to pick a new plan, slowing a very frequent query from under a second to about 5 seconds.
impact: For 20 minutes (05:36-05:55 UTC) every wiki was unreachable for logged-in users and for pages not served from cache.
detection: A ProbeDown page for appservers fired at 05:39 UTC alongside latency and PHP-FPM worker alerts, and a user reported on IRC that the site would not load.
fix: DBAs halted ongoing schema changes and rolled back the globalblocks change at 05:50 UTC, with a follow-up to investigate the optimizer behavior for that table.
summary: Right after a schema change to the GlobalBlocking extension's globalblocks table on the s7 centralauth section, MariaDB changed its query plan and a lookup run on nearly every request jumped to around five seconds. MediaWiki app servers stalled on database queries, PHP-FPM workers ran out, and the CDN returned 5xx errors, making all wikis unreachable for logged-in users and uncached pages. Rolling back the small table's schema change restored service within 20 minutes.

title: User search database failover overloads us-east across Atlassian Cloud
trigger: A routine eu-west database cluster scale-up left that cluster with at least 75% less throughput, eu-west traffic was failed over to us-east, and node failures there pushed all load onto a single redundant cluster.
impact: From 13:21 to 14:12 UTC on May 3, 2022, many AMER and EMEA Jira, Jira Service Management and Confluence customers and all Bitbucket Cloud customers could not search, mention or assign users and teams, and some JQL queries failed.
detection: Monitoring detected the problem within one minute and the on-call engineer responded about four minutes after impact began.
fix: Engineers shed load by undoing only the team search failover, then scaled all user search clusters above spec and committed to performance reviews, runbook updates and an architecture change.
summary: Atlassian's central user search service runs two redundant database clusters per region. An eu-west scale-up meant to add 20% throughput instead cut it sharply, so eu-west traffic was shifted to the larger us-east clusters. Hours later, us-east node failures triggered an automatic switch to the redundant cluster, which then carried about four times normal traffic and timed out. User lookups, mentions and assignments failed in Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket until team search was moved back off us-east.

title: Stolen Heroku GitHub OAuth tokens used to clone private repos
trigger: An attacker found a Heroku machine account token in an archived private GitHub repository, apparently reached through a third-party integration, and used it to enter Heroku's environment.
impact: The attacker downloaded customers' GitHub integration OAuth tokens, cloned private repos of some customers and parts of Heroku's own source, and also took hashed and salted account passwords plus the configuration variables customers had set for Review Apps and Heroku CI pipelines.
detection: GitHub spotted the suspicious activity on April 12, 2022 and alerted Salesforce's security team the following day.
fix: Heroku disabled the compromised account within three hours, revoked every Dashboard GitHub integration token and blocked new ones, reset customer account passwords on May 5, 2022, privately warned customers whose config vars leaked, and rotated other critical credentials during a production freeze.
summary: On April 7, 2022 an attacker who had pulled a Heroku machine account token from an archived private GitHub repo accessed a Heroku database and downloaded customers' GitHub integration OAuth tokens. With them the actor enumerated and cloned private repositories of some customers and part of Heroku's own code. They also took hashed customer passwords and the settings and secrets customers stored for Review Apps and Heroku CI. GitHub raised the alarm; Heroku revoked all GitHub integration tokens, forced customer password resets, and had affected customers rotate leaked config secrets.

title: Cleanup script deletes 883 Atlassian cloud sites
trigger: A script meant to remove a legacy Insight app was given site IDs instead of app IDs, and the deletion API accepted them without checks.
impact: 883 cloud sites belonging to 775 customers were deleted, taking down Jira, Confluence, Opsgenie, Statuspage and Atlassian Access for those customers for up to 14 days.
detection: Internal monitoring missed it because the deletions used a normal workflow; a customer support ticket arrived 8 minutes after the script started and the incident was confirmed about an hour later.
fix: Atlassian restored sites from point-in-time backups over two restore approaches finishing April 18, blocked bulk site deletion, and committed to universal soft deletes, automated multi-site disaster recovery and better incident communication tooling.
summary: A maintenance script to retire the legacy Insight asset management app was run with cloud site identifiers rather than app identifiers. The deletion API treated them as valid and permanently removed 883 entire customer sites, including contact details needed to reach those customers. Restoring was manual and slow because tooling was built for single-site recovery, so some customers waited two weeks. Atlassian met its one-hour recovery point objective but missed its recovery time objective.

title: Expired Vault TLS certs and lease backlog take PyPI backends down
trigger: TLS certificates used by PyPI's internal deployment tooling to reach HashiCorp Vault expired at roughly 15:00 UTC.
impact: All PyPI backend services, including pypi.org and files.pythonhosted.org redirects, went down; applications began returning around 15:41 UTC and the incident was resolved at 16:36 UTC.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers manually cleaned up a huge backlog of expired leases so restarted Vault could start; planned work is a Vault upgrade fixing the crash plus better expiry detection and automated unsealing.
summary: PyPI went fully offline when certificates securing access to Vault expired, cutting running pods off from credentials and preventing new instances from launching. Restarting Vault normally would have fetched fresh certificates, but an unusually large pile of expired leases made the new Vault instances crash at startup, so the team had to clear leases by hand before bringing core services, automation and then applications back. The PSF planned to upgrade Vault past the crash bug and automate expiry detection and unsealing.

title: Build Matrix retry bug multiplies jobs and slows Buildkite dispatch
trigger: A latent bug made each failing job in one customer's 8-job build matrix retry the whole matrix, bypassing retry limits and growing job counts exponentially.
impact: Job dispatch latency was unacceptably high for all customers for about 3 hours, with queue latency reaching 250 seconds, and again for about 30 minutes roughly 10 hours later.
detection: Engineers were paged automatically at 01:53 UTC when a critical queue's latency went above 30 seconds, and again at 12:28 UTC.
fix: About 40,000 jobs were moved to an inactive state, automatic retry on build matrices was disabled and then fixed properly by 13:40 UTC, and a per-build job limit was reprioritized.
summary: A Buildkite customer pipeline combined a Build Matrix with automatic retry. Because of a bug, any failing matrix job requeued all eight jobs, and the default retry limit of 2 (and hard cap of 10) was skipped on that path, so jobs multiplied as agents picked them up and failed again. The resulting queue backlog delayed job assignment to agents for every customer. Engineers deactivated the runaway jobs, shipped a guard and then a real fix, and prioritized jobs-per-build limits.

title: Google Traffic Director outage and gRPC bug break Spotify logins
trigger: Google Cloud Traffic Director, an xDS service discovery system some Spotify services used, had an outage that combined with a bug in the gRPC client library.
impact: Users worldwide who were logged out of Spotify apps could not log back in, from about 18:12 UTC until full mitigation at 20:35 UTC.
detection: At 18:12 UTC, users started reporting that the client apps had logged them out.
fix: Spotify pushed configuration changes switching affected services back to its DNS-based service discovery, and is adding monitoring and alerting for service discovery failures while working with Google Cloud.
summary: On 8 March 2022 Spotify had a global login outage. Most of its microservices find each other through DNS-based discovery, but some relied on Google Cloud Traffic Director, an xDS control plane. When Traffic Director failed, a bug in the gRPC client library turned that into broken backend calls, and logged-out users could not sign back in on any app. Starting at 18:39 UTC engineers reverted affected systems to DNS discovery, with gradual recovery and full mitigation at 20:35 UTC. Spotify plans better discovery monitoring.

title: Consul agent rollout empties caches, scatter queries swamp Vitess
trigger: A percentage-based Consul agent upgrade restarted agents on cache nodes, and Mcrib replaced each one with an empty memcached node, lowering the hit rate at peak.
impact: Many users could not connect to Slack and client boot calls were slow or failed from just after 6 a.m. Pacific; exact counts and duration are not stated.
detection: Support tickets, internal user reports, and pages to several engineering teams all arrived at roughly the same time.
fix: Slack paused the Consul rollout, throttled client boots, changed the query to fetch only missing data from Vitess replicas, and raised limits as caches refilled; follow-ups moved the query to a channel-sharded table and changed the rollout process.
summary: Restarting Consul agents during an upgrade caused Slack's Mcrib cache control plane to swap in empty memcached nodes. Group DM membership lookups on cache miss became scatter queries across every Vitess shard, because the keyspace was sharded by user. Database load grew faster than the miss rate, queries timed out before refilling the cache, and client retries plus Mcrib's quick node replacement deepened the cascading failure. Boot throttling, raised too fast at first, eventually let the cache recover.

title: DNS config change breaks name resolution in container cluster
trigger: A DNS configuration change deployed at 00:17 UTC contained a defect, believed to be a dnsmasq misconfiguration, that left every service in the container orchestration cluster unable to resolve DNS.
impact: From 00:22 to 03:14 UTC on 15 December 2021, PagerDuty's web UI, mobile app, REST API and Events API in both US and EU regions could not reliably ingest events or send notifications on time; most US function returned by 01:30 and EU by about 02:00.
detection: Internal monitoring flagged the problem within one minute.
fix: Engineers deployed a fix to a subset of production, verified it, then rolled it out region by region, and planned stronger pre-deploy config testing and better canaries.
summary: PagerDuty pushed a DNS configuration change to the infrastructure behind its container orchestration cluster, and a defect missed in test environments, likely in dnsmasq settings, stopped all containerised services from resolving hostnames. Event ingestion, notification delivery, the web and mobile UIs and the REST API degraded at once in both US and EU service regions for nearly three hours. Monitoring caught it within a minute; a corrected config was canaried and then rolled out sequentially with verification.

title: Internal network congestion cripples US-EAST-1 control planes
trigger: An automated job scaling capacity for a service on the main AWS network provoked a latent client behavior inside the internal network, producing a connection surge whose retries saturated the devices linking the two networks.
impact: From 7:30 AM PST, EC2, ELB, Route 53 APIs, the console, STS, API Gateway, EventBridge, Fargate/ECS/EKS, Connect and support case creation in US-EAST-1 were impaired; network devices fully recovered at 2:22 PM PST and API Gateway largely by 4:37 PM, with Fargate errors normalizing around 5:00 PM.
detection: Real-time monitoring was itself blinded by the congestion, so operators worked from logs and first spotted elevated internal DNS errors.
fix: Operators moved internal DNS off the congested paths by 9:28 AM, then isolated top traffic sources, disabled heavy services and added network capacity; AWS paused the triggering scaling activity, is fixing the client back-off bug and added protective network configuration.
summary: AWS hosts monitoring, internal DNS, authorization and parts of the EC2 control plane on a separate internal network. In US-EAST-1 an automated capacity-scaling action caused many internal clients to open connections at once; latent back-off failures turned this into a retry storm that congested the bridging devices for hours. Running instances kept working, but launching EC2 instances, Route 53 changes, console logins, API Gateway, EventBridge delivery, container restarts and CloudWatch metrics failed or lagged. The outage also hampered AWS's own monitoring, deployment tools and Service Health Dashboard updates.

title: Config pipeline race condition makes Cloud Load Balancing serve 404s
trigger: A six-month-old race condition in the pipeline that ships customer configuration to Google External Proxy Load Balancing fired in a not-yet-patched cluster and pushed a corrupted configuration file.
impact: From 09:35 to 10:08 PT most endpoints behind global GCLB returned 404 errors, hitting Cloud Run, App Engine, Cloud Functions, Apigee and Firebase, and customer config changes were blocked until 11:28 PT for a total of 1 hour 53 minutes.
detection: Automated alerting notified engineers at 09:50 PT, matching incoming customer support cases.
fix: Engineers restored the previous working configuration by 10:08 PT, froze customer config pushes while finishing the fix, and added alerting and stronger automated config correctness checks.
summary: Google found the GCLB configuration race on 12 November and began gradual rollouts of two patches, one closing the race and one adding input validation. On 16 November, with the first patch about 30 minutes from complete, the race corrupted a config in an unpatched cluster, and the corruption took a form the validation patch did not catch. Websites behind Google External Proxy Load Balancing served Google 404 pages until a rollback restored good configuration.

title: Latent load balancer bug breaks Google Front End in Europe
trigger: A newly enabled infrastructure feature activated a latent bug in internal network load balancer code used by Google Front End load balancing.
impact: For about 1 hour 44 minutes (00:30 to 02:14 US/Pacific), mostly European customers could not load Cloud Console and saw failures in Container Registry, Bigtable, Spanner, Endpoints, Cloud SQL, Eventarc and App Engine, with some spillover to us-central1; no customer counts are given.
detection: Automated safety systems caught the errors within about 4 minutes and slowed the rollout.
fix: Engineers pushed a change that disabled the vulnerable code path, and a root cause fix was scheduled to finish rolling out later the same day.
summary: Google Front End, the load balancing layer in front of many Google Cloud services, failed in Europe after a new infrastructure feature exercised a dormant bug in internal network load balancer code. Customers saw the Cloud Console time out, Container Registry API connections fail, Bigtable and Spanner return unavailable errors, and Cloud Run, Cloud Functions and App Engine drop traffic. Automated safety checks noticed within minutes; disabling the buggy code path mitigated the outage after about 1 hour 44 minutes.

title: Incompatible schema change leaves CircleCI jobs stuck not running
trigger: An 18:50 UTC deploy changed a column type in the work distribution database in a way that was not backwards compatible.
impact: Jobs on all executor types sat stuck without starting for about 53 minutes, with queue times staying elevated until 20:19 UTC, especially for machine and Mac executors.
detection: Errors and alerts fired right after the deploy, with error counts spiking and incoming work falling off.
fix: After a rollback failed to help, engineers hand-deployed a change making the distributor ignore the bad field and scaled compute manually, and planned better testing and tolerant handling of unexpected data.
summary: A CircleCI deploy altered a field type in the PostgreSQL database behind its job distribution service. Both new and older work items then broke distribution, and because the distributor halts on bad data and restarts from the beginning, it looped on the same records. Rolling back made rows written in between unreadable, so jobs could not start for nearly an hour. A manual patch to skip the field restored flow, but node health checks and provider rate limits slowed the catch-up.

title: 73-hour Roblox outage from Consul streaming contention and BoltDB
trigger: A newly enabled Consul streaming feature, extended a day earlier to a traffic-routing service, caused heavy contention under high read and write load, compounded by a BoltDB freelist performance problem.
impact: Roblox was fully down for 73 hours from October 28 to October 31, 2021, with no user data lost.
detection: Engineers noticed degraded Vault performance and one Consul server with high CPU, before players were affected.
fix: Streaming was disabled, slow Consul leaders were kept from staying elected, BoltDB was later compacted, and players were let back in via DNS steering; follow-ups removed the telemetry dependency on Consul and added a second datacenter and dedicated Consul clusters.
summary: Roblox depends on a single Consul cluster for service discovery, which Nomad and Vault also rely on. KV write latency jumped from under 300ms to about 2 seconds, and online players fell to half before the whole platform went offline. Swapping hardware, restoring a snapshot and shedding load did not help. Profiling traced kernel spin-lock contention to Consul streaming, and HashiCorp later found BoltDB writing a 7.8MB freelist on each Raft append. Monitoring that depended on Consul made triage harder.

title: Google Meet livestreams rebuffer as message backend hits limit
trigger: An unexpected surge of work on the backend message delivery system for Meet livestreams pushed it into a configured threshold.
impact: Up to 15% of Google Meet livestream viewers saw rebuffering above 5% of viewing time and extra latency for a total of 4 hours, 3 on October 25 and 1 on October 26, 2021.
detection: Engineers diagnosed the problem by monitoring individual viewers who had reported degraded playback.
fix: Google reconfigured the resources processing data and system message delivery, raised the backend's allocation short term, and plans automatic overload detection, real-time livestream quality monitoring and alerts on rebuffering spikes.
summary: Google Meet livestream audiences intermittently saw stalls, extra latency and some frame or audio loss across two days. The final incident report traced it to the backend message delivery mechanism that supports livestream processing: a sudden workload jump hit its configured threshold, degrading playback for at most 15% of viewers for about four hours combined. An earlier preliminary report had blamed a change to the livestream publishing configuration. Google added resources and committed to better overload detection and rebuffer alerting.

title: Maintenance command severs Facebook backbone; DNS withdraws BGP routes
trigger: A routine maintenance command meant to measure global backbone capacity disconnected every backbone link, and a bug in the audit tool failed to block it.
impact: Facebook services were unreachable worldwide; the postmortem does not give user counts or total duration.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers physically went to data centers to restore the backbone, then brought services back gradually using storm drill practice, and planned to add backbone outage scenarios to future drills.
summary: During routine maintenance, a command to assess Facebook's backbone capacity accidentally took down all backbone connections, cutting data centers off from each other and the internet. An audit tool should have rejected the command but had a bug. Edge DNS servers, unable to reach the data centers, withdrew their BGP advertisements, so Facebook's authoritative name servers vanished from the internet. Internal tools also relied on DNS and out-of-band access was down, so engineers had to work on site, slowed by security controls.

title: Frontend bug crashes flag targeting rule attribute selector
trigger: A frontend change shipped on September 30 broke the rule attribute dropdown whenever an environment had private attributes declared in a LaunchDarkly SDK.
impact: Customers in affected environments got an error page when picking an attribute while creating or editing flag targeting rules; status updates ran from 14:00 to 14:30 PDT.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The change was reverted, and LaunchDarkly added unit and integration tests that exercise frontend components with private attributes in use.
summary: A LaunchDarkly web app release introduced a bug in the flag targeting page: opening the attribute selector, the first dropdown in a targeting rule, rendered an error page instead of the list. Only environments where an SDK had declared private attributes were affected, a case the component's tests did not cover. Customers could not create or edit targeting rules there until engineers reverted the frontend change the same afternoon. Follow-up work added unit and integration tests covering private attributes.

title: Slack DNSSEC rollout on slack.com breaks resolution for 24 hours
trigger: Enabling DNSSEC on slack.com exposed a Route 53 bug in NSEC responses for wildcard records, and rolling back signing while resolvers still cached the DS record made validating resolvers return SERVFAIL.
impact: Under 1% of Slack's online users could not resolve slack.com or app.slack.com for about 24 hours, seeing ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED errors.
detection: Customer Experience received user reports of ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED errors; after the rollback, external DNS resolution probes paged the Traffic team.
fix: Slack asked ISPs and public resolver operators to flush cached slack.com records and waited out the 24-hour DS TTL, while AWS Route 53 shipped a fix for the NSEC type bitmap bug.
summary: On 30 September 2021 Slack's third attempt to sign slack.com with DNSSEC caused a day-long outage for a small share of users. Route 53 returned NSEC responses for the *.slack.com wildcard that omitted existing record types, so after an AAAA lookup some resolvers such as Google Public DNS cached that app.slack.com had no A record. Slack pulled the DS record and then removed signing, unaware that .com caches DS records for 24 hours, so validating resolvers began failing outright. Cache flushes and the TTL expiry restored service.

title: Deleted Azure AD group de-provisions all users from GitHub org
trigger: While re-inviting one employee, an admin deleted the Azure Active Directory security group behind GitHub SCIM provisioning instead of removing the user from it.
impact: Employees lost access to the trivago GitHub organization for at least 1 hour 19 minutes and had to accept new invites and re-enable SSH keys and tokens for SSO.
detection: Users reported lost access in Slack within four minutes, and the owning team found the group missing at 16:23.
fix: A new group was created, admins were assigned to the enterprise app directly, and users found via provisioning logs and mail traces were re-added; follow-ups include automated group membership backups and tighter permissions for destructive actions.
summary: trivago syncs GitHub organization membership from an Azure AD security group via SAML SSO and SCIM. After 2FA enforcement removed some accounts, re-inviting one user meant removing and re-adding them to the group, but the whole group was deleted by mistake. SCIM then de-provisioned every synced user from GitHub and sent removal emails. AAD groups cannot be restored, so the team used a sync bot account to restore admins, rebuilt the group, and relied on GitHub to restore previous repository permissions.

title: Network OS defect disrupts AWS Direct Connect in Tokyo
trigger: Customer traffic containing a very specific packet signature hit a latent defect in the network device operating system tied to a new fast-failover protocol, causing devices in one Direct Connect network layer to stop forwarding.
impact: Direct Connect customers reaching AP-NORTHEAST-1 had intermittent connectivity and elevated packet loss from 7:30 AM JST until full resolution at 1:42 PM JST, about six hours; VPN, internet and inter-AZ traffic were unaffected.
detection: Internal alarms flagged elevated packet loss at 7:30 AM JST, and automation noticed an unusually high rate of failed devices that were not being removed automatically.
fix: After removing and resetting devices failed to hold, engineers disabled the new protocol, first in one Availability Zone and then region-wide; AWS added better detection and remediation while rolling the change to other Regions.
summary: AWS Direct Connect traffic into the Tokyo Region suffered packet loss and intermittent connectivity for roughly six hours. Devices in one layer between Direct Connect edge locations and the regional datacenter network kept failing without being pulled automatically, and pulling them by hand just shifted the failures elsewhere. The culprit was a latent bug in a device operating system version, rolled out since January 2021, that enables a faster-failover protocol; a precise set of packet attributes in customer traffic triggered it. Disabling the protocol ended the event.

title: Honeycomb retro on a run of scaling incidents after ingest growth
trigger: Ingest volume grew around 40% in a few weeks, pushing Kafka, the Beagle SLO processor, retrievers and the dogfood environment past previously unknown limits at the same time.
impact: Over September and early October there were five public incidents and more than 20 internal issues, including user-visible data delays of up to about five minutes and an SLO processing outage.
detection: Problems surfaced through redundant alerting, cross-environment component alerts and Beagle's own warnings that it was falling behind.
fix: The team vertically scaled Kafka brokers, tuned Beagle consumer buffers, fixed a runbook typo, and committed to mapping system limits and revisiting each component's scaling model.
summary: This review covers a cluster of Honeycomb incidents driven by fast ingest growth. Kafka brokers hit AWS network allowance limits and were moved to bigger instances; Beagle, which processes SLO data, autoscaled on CPU, a poor signal, and slowed when the Sarama Kafka client shared one connection per broker leader. A retriever scale-up runbook, never tested in production, inserted an SLO record with an underscore instead of a hyphen in a topic name, crash-looping Beagle and causing a public SLO delay outage.

title: Config update triggers DNS bug in Akamai Secure Edge CDN
trigger: At 15:45 UTC, a software configuration update set off a bug in the DNS part of the Akamai Secure Edge Content Delivery Network.
impact: Some customer websites served through the Secure Edge CDN were unavailable for up to an hour.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Akamai rolled back the configuration update to restore service and said it was reviewing its software update process.
summary: On 22 July 2021 a software configuration update to Akamai's Secure Edge Content Delivery Network hit a bug in that network's DNS component, which steers browsers to the right edge servers. As a result, a number of customer websites became unreachable for up to an hour starting at 15:45 UTC. Akamai rolled back the update to recover, said the event was not a cyberattack, later clarified that its standalone DNS service was not affected, and committed to reviewing how software updates are released.

title: Postgres sequence caching makes incident numbers skip by 32
trigger: The team upgraded its database by promoting a follower to primary, and the new primary resumed Postgres sequences up to 32 values ahead.
impact: A significant share of organizations saw gaps of 32 in their customer-facing INC incident numbers, for example jumping from INC-7 to INC-39; no data was lost or misattributed.
detection: Customers reported the skipped numbers, and the team then audited the database and its sequences.
fix: Per-organization sequences were replaced by a before-insert trigger that sets the external ID to the organization's current maximum plus one, backed by an index.
summary: Customers of incident.io noticed their incident identifiers jumping unexpectedly, such as a team with 20 incidents whose newest was numbered 52. The cause was Postgres sequence behaviour: values are pre-logged in blocks of 32, so after a crash or a follower promotion the new primary can start further ahead. A recent database upgrade via failover triggered exactly that. The team switched to computing the next number with a trigger and recommends keeping user-visible IDs separate from internal keys. The exact incident date is not given.

title: Corrupted routing file crashes bunny.net DNS fleet with stack overflow
trigger: An 08:25 UTC update to the SmartEdge optimization database pushed a corrupted file that made the BinaryPack deserializer throw an unhandled stack overflow, killing DNS server processes.
impact: A system-wide outage of more than 2 hours affected over 750,000 websites, cut over 60% of CDN traffic, and also took down storage, the API, dashboard and logging.
detection: Engineers noticed after about 10 minutes that DNS servers were restarting and crashing in a loop.
fix: The team moved deployment files onto a third-party cloud storage provider to redeploy DNS and GeoDNS data by about 11:00 UTC, and plans to drop BinaryPack, decouple internal systems from its own CDN, and keep local backup data on DNS nodes.
summary: bunny.net lost its DNS fleet of close to 100 servers when a corrupted SmartEdge database file, distributed through its own Edge Storage and CDN, caused a stack overflow in the BinaryPack library that bypassed exception handling. Because rollbacks also traveled via the now-broken CDN, servers crash-looped; later fixes pulled bad GeoDNS data that sent all traffic to the small Madrid PoP. Engineers rerouted through Frankfurt, then rebuilt deployment on third-party storage. Follow-ups include removing BinaryPack and making internal tooling independent of bunny.net's own platform.

title: Latent bug triggered by one customer config takes down Fastly edge
trigger: A customer pushed a legitimate configuration change that hit a dormant bug introduced by a Fastly software release rolled out starting May 12.
impact: Around 85% of the Fastly network served errors worldwide from 09:47 UTC; most services were back within about 49 minutes and the incident was mitigated at 12:35 UTC.
detection: Fastly monitoring spotted the global disruption at 09:48 UTC, one minute after onset.
fix: Engineers identified and disabled the triggering customer configuration, then began deploying a permanent code fix at 17:25 UTC and committed to reviewing why testing missed the bug.
summary: A software deployment Fastly started on May 12 carried a hidden bug that only fired under a specific customer configuration. On June 8 a customer made a valid config change matching those conditions, and roughly 85% of Fastly's global CDN began returning errors, knocking many large websites offline. Monitoring caught it within a minute, the offending config was found at 10:27 UTC and disabled, most traffic recovered by 11:00, and a permanent fix rolled out that evening.

title: RabbitMQ upgrade strands VM cleanup queue, blocking CircleCI jobs
trigger: A routine RabbitMQ upgrade introduced a consumer acknowledgment timeout that, contrary to the changelog, applied to all queue types and disconnected consumers of the VM deletion queue.
impact: Docker, machine executor and remote Docker jobs were delayed or blocked for about 12 hours, from 13:30 UTC on May 21 to 01:18 UTC on May 22, and some workflows were cancelled to free resources.
detection: An overnight alert for a queue with zero consumers led only to pod restarts, a later backlog alert was misconfigured and did not page, and the incident was declared after job-start-delay pages at 13:00 UTC.
fix: Engineers obtained a GCP quota increase, manually deleted old VMs, restored queue consumers, scaled up RDS and brought components back one at a time, then planned more robust provisioning, better RabbitMQ observability and batched GCP API calls.
summary: After CircleCI upgraded RabbitMQ, a new acknowledgment timeout kicked consumers off the queue responsible for destroying finished VMs. With nobody consuming it, old VMs piled up and saturated GCP CPU quotas, so new jobs could not get machines, and automatic retries added load. RDS databases then ran out of burst balance, causing connection and I/O failures. Docker, Windows, macOS, Arm and GPU jobs were delayed or stuck for roughly half a day.

title: GCP console bug detaches all Elastic Cloud proxies in us-central1
trigger: An operator used the GCP User Console to scale down six proxies, and a console bug removed every proxy Instance Group from the load balancer Target Pool instead.
impact: All customer deployments in GCP us-central1 (Iowa) lost network connectivity through the proxy layer for 46 minutes, from 18:31 to 19:17 UTC.
detection: An SLA alert fired at 18:37 UTC but did not page on-call; alerts about unavailable monitoring clusters indirectly drew attention, and an incident was opened at 18:51.
fix: After adding new proxies failed, engineers put the proxy Instance Groups back into the Target Pool, made SLA alerts page on-call, filed a GCP bug, and plan safer scale-down tooling and better proxy autoscaling.
summary: On 8 February 2021 Elastic Cloud's gcp-us-central1 region was fully unreachable for 46 minutes. Manually scaling down six proxies in the GCP User Console triggered a Google bug that detached every proxy Instance Group from the load balancer Target Pool, leaving no hosts to route traffic. Detection lagged because the SLA alert did not page, and logging clusters behind the same proxies were unreachable. Adding proxies did not help; reassociating the Instance Groups restored service. Google later confirmed the console bug.

title: Managed Kubernetes upgrade drops security group rule, TaxJar goes down
trigger: A routine minor-version upgrade of the vendor-managed Kubernetes cluster left the cluster security group without the rule allowing control plane and node traffic.
impact: The TaxJar App and the TaxJar API (calculations, rates and transaction push) were unavailable for customers; status updates ran from 13:30 to 15:00 EST.
detection: Right after the production upgrade finished, worker nodes started reporting Not Ready and load balancers marked every workload offline.
fix: Engineers manually re-added the missing rule and repaired other altered CloudFormation-managed security groups; TaxJar moved to blue-green deployments and began auditing vendor managed services lacking rollback.
summary: TaxJar's web app and sales tax API went offline after a quarterly managed Kubernetes upgrade, a procedure it had run 15 times before. Once the upgrade completed, all worker nodes turned Not Ready because the cluster security group no longer permitted traffic between control plane and node groups, so load balancers dropped every workload. Upgrades could not be rolled back and redeploys took 30-50 minutes, so the team patched the rule by hand and fixed other security groups used to reach caches and databases.

title: Overloaded AWS Transit Gateway drops packets on post-holiday Monday
trigger: A surge of returning users with cold client caches overloaded an AWS Transit Gateway that did not scale fast enough, causing packet loss across Slack's VPCs.
impact: Slack became unavailable around 7:00 AM PST on January 4, 2021, stayed degraded after 9:15 AM, and network conditions were normal again by 10:40 AM PST.
detection: An external monitoring service paged on-call as error rates climbed, and Slack's own dashboards and alerting then failed because they depended on the same Transit Gateways.
fix: Slack disabled autoscaling downscaling and repaired provision-service while AWS manually raised Transit Gateway capacity; follow-ups include pre-holiday TGW upscaling requests, colocating monitoring with its databases, and load testing provision-service.
summary: On the first workday of 2021, Slack's traffic spike saturated an AWS Transit Gateway, and the resulting packet loss slowed calls from the web tier to backends. Failing health checks and autoscaling tried to start about 1,200 servers in 15 minutes, but provision-service, on the same degraded network, hit a Linux open-files limit and an AWS quota. Monitoring dashboards lived in a separate VPC from their databases and went dark. Load balancer panic mode and retries kept some traffic flowing.

title: Kinesis front-end capacity add exceeds OS thread limit in us-east-1
trigger: A small capacity addition to the Kinesis Data Streams front-end fleet pushed every front-end server past the operating system thread limit.
impact: Kinesis put and get calls failed in US-EAST-1 for roughly five hours, and dependent services such as Cognito, CloudWatch, Lambda, Auto Scaling, EventBridge, ECS and EKS saw errors or delays, with some not fully recovered until mid-afternoon.
detection: Alarms on Kinesis put and get record errors fired at 5:15 AM PST.
fix: AWS removed the new capacity, changed front-end servers to bootstrap shard maps from the authoritative metadata store and restarted the fleet gradually, then planned larger servers, thread alarms, higher OS limits and a dedicated shard-map cache fleet.
summary: Each Kinesis front-end server keeps threads open to every other front-end server to build its shard-map cache. Adding a few servers raised the per-host thread count beyond an OS limit, so cache construction failed and servers could not route requests to back-end clusters. Kinesis errors spread to CloudWatch, Cognito, Lambda and others, and even status page updates stalled because the posting tool relied on Cognito. Recovery was slow because servers could only rejoin a few hundred per hour.

title: Half-failed switch stalls etcd and overloads auth database
trigger: At 14:43 a control plane network switch entered a partial failure state for six minutes, dropping some forwarded packets while LACP and BGP stayed up, which gave etcd cluster members conflicting views and blocked leader election.
impact: Cloudflare's API and dashboard were degraded for 6 hours 33 minutes, with API success rates dipping to 75% and the dashboard up to 80 times slower than normal; the edge network was unaffected.
detection: Alerts fired when the switch stopped responding to pings.
fix: Engineers shed load from the authentication database and routed API reads to replicas in the secondary data center until a local replica rebuilt; they then fixed the bug forcing replica rebuilds and slowed automatic database promotion.
summary: A partially working switch in Cloudflare's control plane data center left one etcd node able to reach some peers but not the leader, so repeated tied RAFT elections made etcd read-only. The database cluster manager, relying on etcd, promoted new primaries, and a bug then required rebuilding every replica. The authentication database primary, now taking all reads, became overloaded. Cloudflare later noted the fault was better described as an omission fault than a Byzantine one.

title: Local reset script drops the production database
trigger: A developer helper function meant to drop and recreate local tables ran against the production database during late-night coding, for reasons the author had not yet determined.
impact: Every scoreboard and its data was wiped; the site was down about 30 minutes, and roughly 7 hours of scoreboard data created on 17 October 2020 was permanently lost.
detection: The developer realised immediately because the function was run by hand; no monitoring is described.
fix: The site went into maintenance mode and was restored from DigitalOcean's daily managed backup, and the team concluded such a destructive function should not exist.
summary: Keepthescore, a small online scoreboard side project, lost its production PostgreSQL data when a Python helper that drops and recreates tables, hardcoded to connect to localhost, somehow wiped production instead. Around 10:45pm CET every scoreboard disappeared. The site was put into maintenance mode and restored from DigitalOcean's once-daily managed database backup within about 30 minutes, but scores entered between 15:47 and 23:21 CET that day were gone for good. The root cause of the wrong connection was still unknown.

title: DNS query flood topples Datadog's service discovery in US region
trigger: Scaling a small latency-measuring cluster down and up left it briefly missing, and a large intake cluster flooded service discovery with repeated DNS lookups for it.
impact: The US region was degraded from 14:27 UTC on September 24, with web tier error rates of about 60-90% and services recovering between 20:18 UTC and 03:00 UTC the next day.
detection: Engineers noticed intermittent intake cluster failures and opened an internal incident a few minutes later.
fix: The service discovery team isolated the cluster and readmitted clients gradually while other teams switched to static local config, with plans to split control and data planes and cache discovery queries.
summary: A Datadog migration had quietly switched an intake cluster from a local hosts file to a local DNS resolver that does not cache NXDOMAIN answers. When a small latency-measuring cluster was briefly removed, intake clients kept re-querying it, multiplying DNS load tenfold in ten seconds. The consensus-based service discovery cluster lost quorum, and as caches expired a thundering herd followed, so services could not find dependencies or load runtime configuration. Dashboards and APIs failed for hours though incoming data kept being ingested.

title: Buggy migration script marks most Render services as suspended
trigger: A manually run script meant to move one customer's services between teams wrongly modified the suspension status recorded for existing services in the database.
impact: From about 15:14 PDT most HTTPS services on Render showed a suspended-by-owner page until responses normalized around 16:21, and because that page used a 200 status, cached copies kept some static sites showing it until 14:11 the next day.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Render restored the database to its pre-script state, removed the ability to run manual scripts in production, added protection against unintended batch updates, and changed suspended responses to HTTP 503.
summary: An operator ran a one-off migration script on Render's production database to move a customer's services across teams, but a bug flipped the suspension flag on many existing services. The edge then served a suspension notice for most HTTPS apps even though backends were healthy. Rolling the database back fixed live traffic, yet the notice had been sent with HTTP 200, so intermediate proxies cached it for some static sites. Render banned manual production scripts and switched suspension pages to 503.

title: Git server deploy without synced config var breaks git push
trigger: An engineer deployed new Git server code needing a new auth config variable to a production batch after setting the variable but skipping the separate step that pushes config to instances.
impact: Git pushes handled by the updated batch of Heroku Git server instances got 401 responses, because those instances called a private internal API unauthenticated (incident #2105); duration not stated.
detection: An alert fired shortly after the batch was deployed, while the engineer was at lunch.
fix: The engineer ran the config-sync script and killed the affected processes so they restarted with the new variable; Heroku plans to merge config updates and code deploys into one step.
summary: Heroku's Git server, a Go service run as a kernel app on virtual servers, needed a new configuration variable for authenticating to a different internal endpoint. In production the variable was set but never transmitted to instances, so the first deploy batch made unauthenticated calls and returned 401s to users running git push. Syncing the config and restarting processes fixed it, and the blameless review focused on removing the rarely used manual step.

title: Atlanta router policy edit pulls all backbone traffic to one site
trigger: While relieving congestion caused by a lost Newark-Chicago backbone link, an engineer deactivated the prefix-list match inside a BGP export term on the Atlanta router instead of the whole term, so it announced every route to the backbone with local-preference 200.
impact: For 27 minutes (21:12 to 21:39 UTC) around 20 Cloudflare locations in North America, Europe, Russia and Brazil failed, cutting traffic across the network by roughly 50%, with some logs and metrics dropped until 22:10 UTC.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers removed the Atlanta router from the backbone to restore traffic, then lowered the local-preference of local server routes and scheduled maximum-prefix limits on backbone BGP sessions.
summary: A one-line Junos change on Cloudflare's Atlanta backbone router disabled the prefix-list condition of the 6-BBONE-OUT policy term rather than the term itself. The router then advertised all its BGP routes to other backbone routers with local-preference 200, beating the value 100 used for local compute routes, so traffic from many data centers converged on Atlanta and overloaded it. Sites such as San Jose, London, Frankfurt and São Paulo went dark for 27 minutes until Atlanta was pulled from the backbone.

title: Failed EBS volume on file server takes hosted sites offline
trigger: An AWS EBS volume behind the oldest file server, livefile1, suffered multiple component failures that stalled its redundant disk array.
impact: Websites, scheduled tasks and always-on tasks for the roughly 20% of accounts on livefile1 were down for about three to nearly four hours, and nearly all users were affected at some point because the main site slowed and other sites could not be reloaded.
