detection: Monitoring paged the support team at 16:06 UTC with alerts from multiple machines.
fix: The team rebuilt the file server volumes from backup snapshots, cleared stale NFS mounts with a rolling cluster reboot, and planned to script storage rebuilds, detect hung volumes faster, and contain failures to one file server's users.
summary: One of PythonAnywhere's NFS file servers lost its underlying AWS EBS storage when a volume failed in a way AWS later confirmed was unrecoverable. Web app worker processes blocked waiting on storage, so the PythonAnywhere site itself became slow and threw errors, and users across the platform could not start or reload web apps. Engineers restored the volumes from snapshots, then rebooted servers to clear hung NFS mounts. No data was lost, but restored volumes stayed slow for hours while they warmed up.

title: Figma files fail to open after ElastiCache backup chain reaction
trigger: A routine daily forkless backup on the ElastiCache Redis replica consumed its single CPU core, the primary dropped it after hitting its replication buffer limit, then began its own forkless full-sync snapshot while serving traffic.
impact: Many users could not open or create Figma files from 17:25 to 18:04 PDT on June 16, 2020 (39 minutes), though most could keep editing open files.
detection: Monitoring alerted within seconds when the primary began its snapshot at 17:04 PDT.
fix: Service recovered once the primary's snapshot finished; Figma switched backups to the forking method with AWS, scheduled a Redis upgrade for better connection handling, and is removing Redis as an availability dependency.
summary: Figma users could not open or create files for about 40 minutes on 16 June 2020. A daily ElastiCache Redis backup ran in forkless mode on the replica, starving its single CPU core so it fell behind; the primary hit its replication buffer cap, dropped the replica, and refused partial resync, starting a long CPU-bound snapshot of its own. Meanwhile leaked connections grew until the primary hit its connection limit and rejected new clients. A failover request stalled until the snapshot ended.

title: Sessionstore pods OOM-loop on Kubernetes, blocking logged-in edits
trigger: Requests to the sessionstore service rose from roughly 15k to 20k, pushing its four undersized Kask pods in eqiad to their memory ceiling until they crash-looped under the OOM killer.
impact: From 18:36 to 19:20 UTC (44 minutes) editors on every wiki could not edit, log in or log out; about 32 million sessionstore requests were lost and the edit deficit was roughly 24,000, while readers were unaffected.
detection: Automated Icinga monitoring raised an alert on IRC roughly five minutes after the pods first crashed and paged about 30 seconds later, and a user filed task T255179 at 18:44.
fix: Responders depooled eqiad to codfw, added pods, raised the memory limit from 300Mi to 400Mi and dropped pod affinity rules before repooling, then followed up by expanding Kubernetes node capacity and planning resource alerts and SLOs.
summary: Wikimedia's sessionstore, a Kask service on Kubernetes, ran with only four pods in eqiad when session requests rose from about 15k to 20k. The pods hit their memory limit, entered CrashLoopBackOff and dragged Kubernetes nodes and kube-proxy down with them, so logged-in users across all wikis lost the ability to save edits or sign in for 44 minutes. Engineers switched sessionstore to codfw, raised pod counts and memory limits, and later grew cluster capacity and investigated iowait problems on the nodes.

title: Bitcoin hitting $10,000 overwhelms Coinbase API web servers
trigger: When BTC crossed USD $10,000 around 16:05 PDT, traffic jumped fivefold within 4 minutes, faster than autoscaling could add capacity.
impact: Request error rates hit 50% on coinbase.com, the mobile apps and the API between roughly 16:05 and 16:58 PDT, including an extra 2-minute outage during a redeploy.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; the status page began investigating rising latency at 16:14 PDT.
fix: Engineers redeployed the API on more machines at 16:20 PDT, then changed the health endpoint so saturated instances stay in rotation, with pre-scaling, caching and deploy-process improvements planned.
summary: On 1 June 2020 a fivefold surge in traffic as Bitcoin reached $10,000 outran Coinbase autoscaling. Slower inter-service calls saturated the worker processes on API web servers, so requests queued, timed out or failed and errors reached 50%. Because health checks ran on those same saturated processes, the load balancer pulled instances out of service, worsening the overload. A redeploy to add machines briefly caused another two-minute outage when old instances left rotation. Coinbase fixed the health endpoint and is pursuing pre-scaling, caching and safer deploys.

title: Expired cross-signing CA takes down MongoDB Cloud control plane
trigger: A cross-signing certificate authority that internal certificate chains still trusted for legacy systems reached its expiry date, so critical internal services began rejecting certificates.
impact: From about 10:50 to 13:15 UTC cloud.mongodb.com, MongoDB University and support portal logins were down, Atlas clusters could not be created or changed, alerts were not sent and metrics for the window were lost, though running clusters kept serving.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; MongoDB says it pinpointed the root cause around 10:54 UTC, four minutes after impact began.
fix: Starting at 11:38 UTC, operations stripped the expired cross-signing elements out of internal certificate chains, and MongoDB will extend its certificate monitoring to inspect full chains.
summary: On 30 May 2020 the MongoDB Cloud control plane failed after an intermediate CA used to cross-sign internal service certificates expired. Internal systems began rejecting those chains, making cloud.mongodb.com, MongoDB University and support portal logins unreachable for roughly two and a half hours. Atlas and Cloud Manager clusters stayed reachable but could not be modified, alerting stopped, and metrics for the period were lost. Engineers stripped the expired cross-signing links from internal chains, and full-chain inspection is being added to certificate expiry monitoring.

title: Expired mTLS client certificate cuts SCORM Cloud off from secrets
trigger: The hand-generated client TLS certificate used by app servers to talk to the internal secrets and configuration service expired.
impact: SCORM Cloud's website and API were fully down for 40 minutes, from 04:21 PM to 05:01 PM UTC.
detection: The monitoring system detected the outage at 04:21 PM UTC and paged engineers, who acknowledged within a minute.
fix: Engineers reissued the client certificate, pushed it to running servers and baked it into the base machine image; client certificates will now be provisioned dynamically at build time and the confusing errors will get clearer alerts.
summary: SCORM Cloud relies on an internal security service that rotates database credentials and hands out third-party secrets, reachable only over mutual TLS. When the application servers' client certificate expired, that service rejected them, the servers could not fetch the secrets they needed, and the whole web application failed. The team traced the issue through misleading error messages to the certificate in 28 minutes, reissued it, and plans to generate client certs automatically during image builds.

title: Stale HAProxy backend slots cause Slack outage after scale-down
trigger: Evening scale-down of the webapp tier removed the older instances that were the only backends most HAProxy servers still knew about.
impact: Slack users saw failures from about 4:45pm Pacific as HTTP 503 errors rose; the post does not give the total duration.
detection: Engineers were alerted to an elevated rate of HTTP 503 errors, and noticed that only a subset of webapp hosts were heavily loaded.
fix: Restarting the HAProxy fleet in rolling fashion restored correct backend lists, and Slack is moving ingress load balancing to Envoy with xDS endpoint discovery after finding its alerting for this case was broken.
summary: On 12 May 2020 Slack's webapp tier had scaled up 75% after a morning database incident, exceeding the fixed number of HAProxy backend slots. A Slack-built program that syncs Consul host lists into HAProxy via the Runtime API tried to place new hosts before freeing dead ones, so it kept failing and HAProxy state went stale. When autoscaling terminated older instances in the evening, most HAProxy servers pointed at mostly deprovisioned hosts and users got 503 errors. Rolling HAProxy restarts fixed it; monitoring meant to catch this was not working.

title: Flowdock DB crash reuses user IDs, exposing flows across orgs
trigger: A surge in usage, attributed to more people working remotely, pinned the database CPU and hung it, and the restart left the table holding user ID sequences corrupted and reset to a value almost 80 days old.
impact: Flowdock was unavailable for about 22 hours within a roughly 32-hour incident, some users from one organization could see other organizations' flows, and activity created during the incident window was lost after database restores.
detection: Customers reported odd behavior such as missing users, login failures and strangers from other organizations appearing in their flows.
fix: Flowdock restored a pre-crash database snapshot twice, invalidated all sessions and verified isolation end to end; follow-ups added database capacity, finer response-time monitoring, secondary database failover, DBA review before restarts and session and cache invalidation on restore.
summary: CA Flowdock, Broadcom's team chat SaaS, hung when database CPU maxed out under a jump in remote-work usage. After a restart, a corrupted sequence table handed out recently used user IDs again, so new logins were mapped onto other organizations' accounts and could see their flows and 1-1 chats. A snapshot restore helped, but cached IDs kept the leak alive until a second restore and full session invalidation. Users lost flows, user changes and Rally integrations created during the incident window.

title: Stale Postgres planner stats and wraparound risk degrade Buildkite
trigger: An ANALYZE on Buildkite's largest table led the planner to stop using the primary key index for a key query, and long-running vacuums holding locks prevented later ANALYZE runs from correcting it.
impact: From late April into May 2020 customers saw intermittent latency and request timeouts, often HTTP 502s on artifact upload/download, plus several maintenance windows including an emergency Postgres upgrade on 7 May that kept the site in maintenance far longer than the expected 15-30 minutes.
detection: Monitoring paged on-call engineers on 21 April 2020 for high database CPU and slow queries and API responses.
fix: Buildkite upgraded to PostgreSQL 12, used VACUUM INDEX_CLEANUP and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, ran the missed ANALYZE (which fixed the bad plan), and cut transaction ID usage by moving subsystems out of the primary database.
summary: Buildkite's RDS PostgreSQL database hit a chain of problems: an unexpected 16 TiB storage cap from a 2015-era 32-bit filesystem, high CPU from a query that switched to an inefficient index after an ANALYZE, and interrupted vacuums that left bloated indexes and brought transaction ID wraparound close. Instance upsizing only partly helped. An urgent PostgreSQL 12 upgrade enabled a fast emergency vacuum, and once engineers remembered to run ANALYZE post-upgrade, query plans and API latency returned to normal.

title: Technician unplugs core DC patch panel, taking down dashboard and API
trigger: During planned removal of retired equipment at a core data center, a technician also pulled the cables from a patch panel that carried all of the site's redundant external connectivity.
impact: From 15:31 to 19:52 UTC (about 4 hours 21 minutes) the Cloudflare Dashboard and API could not be reached, blocking config changes, cache purges, Workers updates, load balancer health checks and log access, while edge proxying kept working.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers restored the connections, starting with a 10Gbps backup link at 19:44 UTC, while weighing a failover to the disaster recovery site; follow-ups spread connectivity across multiple patch panels, label critical cabling and flag do-not-touch cables in work instructions.
summary: Cloudflare's control plane lives in one of two core data centers, and every diverse external fibre link there ran through a single patch panel. When technicians decommissioning an unused cabinet disconnected that panel, the Dashboard and API went dark for over four hours, along with DNS record edits, cache purges, Argo Tunnel setup, Stream encoding and log delivery, though customer traffic kept flowing. Teams restored links while debating DR failover, and committed to removing the single physical point of failure.

title: Cron job silently runs schema updater, drops Wikidata sitelinks table
trigger: A weekly dumps cron called sql.php, which quietly ran extension schema update hooks in production; with wb_terms freshly renamed, Wikibase's years-old updater code treated the database as outdated and dropped the 70M-row wb_items_per_site table.
impact: For about 20 minutes most content page parses failed with a DBQueryError, hitting many logged-in page views and edits; for 19 hours pages rendered since the start showed wrong Wikidata-derived metadata, and hundreds of duplicate Wikidata items were created.
detection: A user reported a fatal DBQueryError on IRC at 23:03:57 UTC and an Icinga exceptions alert followed about a minute later, but no page was sent.
fix: The table was recreated empty so pages rendered again and its data was later recovered from backups; follow-ups remove DROP and ALTER grants from the automated wikiadmin user, stop sql.php running schema update hooks and move the cron to mysql.php.
summary: Wikidata's wb_items_per_site table, needed to render every Wikidata-connected page, vanished when a weekly dumps cron used sql.php, which unexpectedly executed Wikibase schema updaters without update.php's production guard. Because wb_terms had just been renamed, a 7.5-year-old migration path wrongly listed this live table for deletion. Page parses threw DBQueryError for about 20 minutes until an empty table was created, interlanguage links and infobox data were wrong for 19 hours, and duplicate-sitelink checks failed until data was restored from backup.

title: Empty etcd service discovery key crash-loops Discord Elixir nodes
trigger: A newly autoscaled API node's etcd announce request lost its body to a connection reset, and etcd's Go net/http handler stored an empty value that Elixir service watchers could not parse.
impact: Most users could not use Discord for about an hour, from 14:18 to 15:32 PDT.
detection: Internal alarms on key metric drops and cluster utilization anomalies fired at 14:21, triggering a SEV1.
fix: Engineers restarted lost capacity, throttled reconnections and paused ScyllaDB repairs, then made etcd clients send announcements in one TCP packet and made watchers ignore corrupt entries.
summary: When Discord's API cluster scaled in a new node, its announce to etcd v2 sent headers but lost the body after a connection reset. Go's ParseForm did not check Content-Length, so etcd saved an empty value. Elixir services watching discord_api failed to deserialize the JSON, crash-looped, and hit max restart intensity, restarting about half the watching nodes across clusters and cascading into a near-total outage. Discord throttled reconnects during recovery, then shipped single-packet announces and tolerant handling of corrupt discovery keys.

title: Let's Encrypt halts issuance over CAA rechecking bug in Boulder
trigger: A bug in the Boulder CA software, apparently introduced on 2019-07-25, rechecked one domain N times instead of each of N domains when CAA had to be rechecked before issuance.
impact: Certificate issuance was halted from 03:10 to about 05:22 UTC, and about 3 million certificates (2.6% of active ones) were marked for revocation, of which over 1.7 million were replaced within 48 hours.
detection: Not stated how it was found; Let's Encrypt confirmed the bug at 03:08 UTC and halted issuance two minutes later.
fix: Let's Encrypt deployed a fixed Boulder at 05:22 UTC and resumed issuance, then revoked replaced and highest-risk certificates while deferring revocation of more than 1 million others to avoid breaking sites.
summary: On 29 February 2020 Let's Encrypt found that its Boulder CA software mishandled CAA rechecks for authorizations older than 8 hours: with N domains needing recheck, it checked one domain N times. Domains could therefore get certificates despite newer CAA records forbidding it. Issuance was paused for about two hours while a fix was deployed. Around 3 million affected certificates were slated for revocation; over 1.7 million were replaced quickly and 445 high-priority ones revoked, while revocation of the remainder was deferred to avoid widespread site breakage.

title: Destiny 2 servers skip hotfix config, wiping currency again
trigger: When Hotfix 2.7.1.1 launched, some WorldServers crashed on startup from too many servers booting at once, and after manual restarts they silently skipped both the configuration override fixing the January inventory bug and version verification.
impact: A small share of Destiny 2 players lost currency and materials, the game was taken offline at 10:30 AM PST after several hundred thousand unique players had already logged in, and all characters were rolled back to their 8:30 AM PST state.
detection: Players reported lost currency soon after the game came back online following the 2.7.1.1 deployment; manual test logins had happened to land only on healthy servers.
fix: Bungie restored all character data from the pre-patch backup and added hot-patch safeguards so servers cannot start on an unexpected version, with fixes planned for the startup crash and config-skipping issue and a code-level fix for the corruption bug.
summary: Destiny 2 needed its second character rollback in two weeks. A January change to inventory clean-up, meant to fix quest sorting, miscalculated stack caps so currencies and materials above the cap vanished; it was patched via a server configuration override. During the Crimson Days update some WorldServers crashed at startup because of the huge server count, and after manual restarts they ran old code without the override or version checks. Players hitting those servers lost items, so Bungie took the game down and restored every account from backup.

title: Stale conntrack entries after CoreDNS scale-down break in-cluster DNS
trigger: Under low load the CoreDNS autoscaler cut CoreDNS pods from 3 to 2, and kube-proxy failed to remove the old UDP conntrack entry for the deleted pod.
impact: Some services inside the Kubernetes cluster had a partial DNS outage lasting 26 minutes to mitigate, with 15000 events dropped across three services.
detection: Prometheus caught an elevated 5xx rate on the affected services and paged on-call through VictorOps.
fix: A later deploy added nodes, the autoscaler brought CoreDNS pods back and the conntrack table was rewritten; action items were disabling the CoreDNS autoscaler, adding a DNS cache on production and monitoring conntrack usage.
summary: Preply engineering shared a postmortem of a partial in-cluster DNS failure on Kubernetes. When the CoreDNS autoscaler removed one of three pods during quiet traffic, kube-proxy logged an error deleting conntrack entries for the kube-dns service, so some pods kept sending DNS queries over UDP to a pod that no longer existed. Services A, B and C returned 5xx errors and dropped about 15000 events. Recovery came after a deploy triggered new nodes and DNS pods; the team acknowledged the underlying conntrack bug remained unexplained.

title: Kernel panic drops LogDNA nodes, delaying search and live tail
trigger: A group of production nodes fell out of the cluster after an OS kernel panic, partially taking down the ingestion and indexing pipeline.
impact: Customers saw delayed search, live tail, alerting and graphing plus generally degraded performance, with indexing lag around 50 minutes at one point across January 27-28.
detection: The infrastructure team was notified immediately when the nodes dropped out.
fix: Engineers rebooted the failed nodes, verified pod health and rolled the Kubernetes pipeline to work off the log backlog, and hardened the infrastructure against nodes leaving the cluster.
summary: LogDNA, now Mezmo, had a partial outage when a kernel panic knocked several production nodes out of its cluster, removing capacity from the log ingestion and indexing pipeline. Customers experienced lagging search results, delayed live tail and alerts, and slow graphs while a backlog of logs built up, with lag fluctuating over the following hours. The team rebooted the nodes and rolled the Kubernetes pipeline to catch up, continued to investigate the panic, and made the platform more tolerant of nodes dropping out.

title: RDS Multi-AZ failover loses writes and breaks MySQL replicas
trigger: An AWS RDS MySQL Multi-AZ failover hit a primary configured with innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit set to 2, so recently committed transactions had not been flushed to EBS and never reached the standby.
impact: The main API app could not reach its database for about 110 seconds, about 5 seconds of transactions vanished from the new primary, all 5 read replicas failed with duplicate-key errors, and rebuilding them took about six hours.
detection: The internal monitoring tool alerted on an unusual spike in 5xx errors.
fix: Replica traffic was shifted to the primary while replicas were rebuilt, the lost rows were rebuilt from binary logs in an 8-hour session, and innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit was changed from 2 to 1.
summary: Razorpay's primary MySQL instance on RDS failed over to its standby in another AZ. Because InnoDB logs were flushed only once per second while sync_binlog was 1, replicas had already applied writes the standby never got; when the new primary reissued the same auto-increment IDs, replication broke with duplicate-key errors. Reads moved to the primary, raising its CPU by 50%, and the first snapshot from the replaced host took hours. Binary logs allowed the missing data to be restored.

title: Memory leak crashes Honeycomb ingest workers in synchronized waves
trigger: A slow memory leak in a code change grew at the same rate on every ingest backend, so all of them ran out of memory and crashed within minutes of each other.
impact: Honeycomb rejected 1-3% of incoming customer telemetry during four separate 20-minute periods, with resolution taking several hours.
detection: An SLO burn alert on ingest response codes caught the brownout within minutes, though it was not set to page and was seen by an off-duty engineer.
fix: The team reverted the leaking commit and shipped a fixed release, and is making SLO alerts page on-call, surfacing crash and OOM rates during debugging and considering backpressure.
summary: On 6 November 2019 Honeycomb's ingest tier went through repeated brownouts, dropping 1-3% of customer events for four 20-minute windows. A memory leak made every ingest worker hit its limit and crash at nearly the same time, so in-flight requests failed and load balancers found no healthy backends. An SLO alert spotted it quickly, but the team fixated on an AWS ALB fault and waited on a support ticket. An engineer with fresh eyes found the restarts and leak; reverting the commit ended the incident.

title: Penny stock order filled in 100k+ trades overloads Zerodha OMS
trigger: A single 10 lakh quantity order on a sub Rs 1 BSE stock placed around 9.40 AM executed as more than 1 lakh separate trades, overloading the order management system.
impact: Order placement failed between 10.00 and 10.40 AM, and clients whose older open orders filled during that window saw extra margin blocked until positions were reconciled with the exchanges.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Zerodha capped equity orders at 20,000 quantity while vendor Refinitiv works on an OMS fix, with basket orders on Kite planned to ease splitting large orders.
summary: Zerodha's order management system, supplied by Thomson Reuters (now Refinitiv), normally sees big orders fill in up to a few hundred trades. On August 29, 2019 one huge order in a BSE penny stock was matched in over a lakh individual fills, which the OMS could not process, halting order placement for 40 minutes and leaving some clients with incorrect margin blocks until reconciliation. Zerodha added a 20,000 per-order quantity limit, affecting under 0.02 percent of clients.

title: Cooling control system bug overheats servers in a Tokyo AZ
trigger: During a control host failover, a bug in third-party datacenter control software flooded devices with traffic, the system hung, and cooling units shut down instead of falling back to maximum cooling.
impact: A small share of EC2 servers in part of one AP-NORTHEAST-1 Availability Zone overheated and shut down from 12:36 PM JST, degrading EBS and dependent services like RDS, Redshift and ElastiCache, with most recovered by 6:30 PM JST and some hardware retired.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Operators manually reset the control equipment and PLCs and forced maximum cooling, restoring cooling by 3:21 PM JST, then disabled the failover mode and changed controls so purge mode can bypass the PLCs.
summary: In the AWS Tokyo Region, the datacenter control system that manages cooling was failing over between hosts when a bug in vendor logic caused excessive device communication and the system became unresponsive. Air handlers in part of one Availability Zone shut off rather than going to safe maximum cooling, and the manual purge fallback also failed because PLCs hung. EC2 servers overheated, EBS volumes slowed, RunInstances calls errored, and some multi-AZ ALB users with WAF or sticky sessions saw extra errors.

title: Cassandra auto_bootstrap misunderstanding hides Monzo customer data
trigger: Engineers added six servers to the 21-node Cassandra cluster with auto_bootstrap set to false, and the empty nodes immediately took ownership of data ranges and served reads.
impact: From 13:10 BST customers had trouble logging in, making payments, withdrawing cash, seeing correct balances and contacting support; most recovered by 15:08 and all by 23:00.
detection: Automated alerts flagged failing Mastercard transactions at 13:14 and customer operations reported broken support tooling; later 404s from the internal edge led engineers to missing configuration data.
fix: Monzo decommissioned the six new nodes one by one, then replayed stored events and ran reconciliation, corrected its auto_bootstrap use and wrote fuller Cassandra runbooks and metrics.
summary: On 29 July 2019 Monzo scaled its Cassandra cluster from 21 servers by adding six. Because auto_bootstrap had been set to false, the new nodes joined fully active, claimed partition ranges without holding data, and answered quorum reads with nothing. Configuration keys, transactions and balances appeared missing, breaking app logins, payments, the internal edge and support chat. Engineers found reads coming from new nodes and removed them one at a time, restoring most service by 15:08 BST, then reconciled data written during the incident.

title: Kubernetes pod priority preemption evicts Grafana Cloud ingesters
trigger: A new Cortex cluster launched without explicit priorities got the new default medium priority and preempted production Ingesters that had no priority set.
impact: The Grafana Cloud Hosted Prometheus service was down for 26 minutes with failed writes, though no data was lost.
detection: New error-budget-based Prometheus alerts paged on-call within 4 minutes of the outage starting.
fix: Engineers scaled up the Kubernetes cluster, then fixed OOMing auth proxies hit by a retry surge; they set high priority on production Ingesters and now require design docs and wider review for cluster-global config.
summary: On 19 July 2019 Grafana Cloud's Cortex-based Hosted Prometheus went down for 26 minutes. A day after adding Kubernetes priority classes with medium as default, an engineer created a dedicated Cortex cluster for a customer; its pods outranked production Ingesters, which had no priority yet, and preempted one. The replacement pod got medium priority and preempted another, cascading until all production Ingesters were evicted and writes failed for lack of replicas. Scaling the cluster restored service, then retries overloaded auth proxies briefly.

title: Stripe API degraded twice by database election bug and config clash
trigger: A shard's primary failed while two stalled nodes were present, hitting a latent failover bug from a database minor-version upgrade so no new primary could be elected.
impact: Most Stripe API requests failed from 16:35 to 17:02 UTC and again from 21:14 to 22:47 UTC on 10 July 2019.
detection: Automated monitoring caught the failed election within a minute, and alerts fired again at 21:14 UTC for the second episode.
fix: Stripe restarted the cluster to force an election, then fixed a config setting that clashed with its election-protocol rollback; it added replication-lag and election-state alerts, more circuit breaking and fault isolation.
summary: On 10 July 2019 the Stripe API was severely degraded twice. A database upgrade from three months earlier had a hidden failover fault that surfaced when two stalled nodes stopped reporting replication lag; one shard then could not elect a primary, writes timed out, and the widely used shard starved API compute. Restarting the cluster recovered it after 27 minutes. Later, rolling back the election protocol clashed with a recent configuration change and starved shards of CPU, causing a second outage until the configuration was updated.

title: WAF regex with catastrophic backtracking pins CPU globally
trigger: A new WAF Managed Rule for XSS was pushed globally at once and included a regular expression prone to catastrophic backtracking, which pinned CPU on the edge.
impact: CPU on every server handling HTTP and HTTPS spiked to nearly 100% worldwide, so customer sites returned 502 errors for about 27 minutes and the dashboard and API were also unreachable.
detection: External synthetic WAF tests failed and paged on-call about three minutes after the deploy, followed by a global traffic-drop alert and reports of CPU exhaustion.
fix: Engineers ran a global WAF kill, then re-enabled it after testing in one location, then restored a removed CPU safeguard and inspected all WAF rules for backtracking; performance tests for every rule and a move to re2 or Rust regex were planned with target dates, and staged rule rollouts were announced as an SOP change.
summary: A WAF Managed Rule meant to detect cross-site scripting was deployed to Cloudflare's entire edge in one step. Its regular expression caused catastrophic backtracking, and although the rule was in simulate mode it still ran, consuming every CPU core serving HTTP and HTTPS traffic. Sites behind Cloudflare returned 502 errors and the dashboard was down too. A previously removed CPU-limit protection would have contained it. A global WAF termination restored traffic in about 27 minutes.

title: Maintenance automation deschedules network control plane in US regions
trigger: A bug in maintenance automation descheduled network control plane jobs across several physical locations at once, and after a few minutes of fail-static operation BGP routes between those sites were withdrawn.
impact: For about four hours, six GCP regions including us-central1 and us-east1 saw heavy congestion: Cloud Storage errors reached 96% in us-west2, Spanner was down in three regions, Compute Engine saw up to 33% packet loss, and Interconnect saw 50-100% loss.
detection: Engineers were paged two minutes after the failure began, but debugging was slowed because monitoring tools ran over the same congested network.
fix: Engineers halted the automation, rebuilt lost control plane configuration and restored capacity, then hardened cluster management to reject multi-location deschedules, made the control plane persist its config and lengthened fail-static time.
summary: Maintenance automation meant for one location had a bug that let it deschedule logical clusters in several locations together, and the network control plane jobs there were configured to stop during maintenance. The network ran in fail-static mode briefly, then BGP routes were withdrawn and capacity collapsed. Compute Engine, App Engine, Cloud VPN, Interconnect, Pub/Sub, Spanner, Cloud Storage and BigQuery all degraded in several US and South American regions. Recovery was slow because control plane config had been lost and monitoring shared the congested network.

title: Expired signing certificate disables Firefox add-ons
trigger: The intermediate certificate used to sign Firefox add-ons was allowed to expire because its owners believed Firefox did not check expiration dates.
impact: Add-ons stopped working for many Firefox users; the post gives no user counts or exact duration, and fixes rolled out over weeks through eight system add-on versions and six dot releases.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Mozilla pushed a fix through the Studies (Normandy) system and later dot releases, and committed to documenting certificate behaviour, testing expiry and future dates in QA, and building a fast update channel independent of Telemetry.
summary: In 2019 the certificate that signs Firefox add-ons expired, and Firefox rejected extensions it could no longer verify. The signing team knew the date was coming but misunderstood how Firefox validated intermediate certificates, partly because of an earlier change to end-entity checks. QA had never tested certificate expiry or clocks set in the future. The quickest fix path ran through Studies, which required Telemetry, so some users had to enable data collection to get the patch.

title: Cloud API rate limits stall Travis CI Linux and Windows builds
trigger: A rise in build traffic created many VMs that stalled shortly after creation, and the cleanup job deleting stopped instances older than 3 hours flooded the cloud provider API until it was rate limited.
impact: All Linux and Windows builds on travis-ci.com and travis-ci.org were delayed for about 20 hours across 27 and 28 March 2019.
detection: Users reported long VM boot times around 14:45 UTC, and monitoring showed the shared infrastructure was over capacity.
fix: Travis CI cut its own API call volume so deletions could proceed and the backlog drained, then changed cleanup to delete stopped instances immediately and added rate-limit metrics and logging.
summary: Starting 27 March 2019 Travis CI builds on both travis-ci.com and travis-ci.org were delayed for about 20 hours. Higher job volume spawned many VM instances that quickly stalled, and the cleanup system, which only removed stopped instances after 3 hours, then sent bursts of delete calls that got the account rate limited by the cloud provider. Unable to create or delete VMs, the fleet hit quotas such as SSD limits, and requeued jobs made more API calls. Tuning the self-imposed rate limit restored progress.

title: MongoDB lock contention stalls CircleCI builds for two weeks
trigger: Each service instance redeclared every MongoDB index at startup, taking database-level locks that, together with exhausted WiredTiger tickets and memory allocator stalls, repeatedly froze the jobs replica set.
impact: Between March 26 and April 10, 2019 CircleCI suffered repeated incidents of delayed or stuck jobs and workflows, API outages and Out of Memory crashes in API containers, including read replicas unresponsive for about 10 and 42 minutes.
detection: Workflow processing delays were seen at 21:29 UTC on March 26, and on April 10 an alert fired on sharp growth in job and workflow queues at 13:25 UTC.
fix: CircleCI removed the redundant index creation, enlarged MongoDB hosts, failed over degraded primaries, applied MongoDB-recommended TCMalloc settings, began tracking tcmalloc.spinlock_total_delay_ns, and planned a MongoDB upgrade and data access refactoring.
summary: Over about two weeks CircleCI builds repeatedly queued up because the MongoDB replica sets behind its builds queue slowed or stalled outright. A concurrent JVM upgrade that shrank thread pools via Docker awareness initially looked like the cause. With MongoDB support, the team found that every service start redeclared all indexes, each check needing a database-level lock, starving WiredTiger read and write tickets. Later stalls tied to TCMalloc memory behavior and failed cache evictions were handled by failovers and allocator tuning.

title: Config change overloads blob lookup service, Cloud Storage errors
trigger: A configuration change meant to cut metadata storage use in Google's internal blob service overloaded the component that locates blob data.
impact: For about 4 hours 10 minutes, internal blob storage averaged 20% errors (31% peak), Cloud Storage averaged 4.8% errors across all locations, App Engine deployments hit 90% errors, and Gmail, Photos and Drive saw elevated errors.
detection: SREs were alerted at 18:56 PDT, about 16 minutes after impact began.
fix: SREs halted the job applying the config and manually throttled traffic so blob service tasks could restart without crashing, then planned better regional isolation, faster provisioning, config-change safeguards and load shedding.
summary: After noticing growing metadata storage in Google's internal blob service, SREs pushed a config change to shrink it. The change unexpectedly piled load onto the blob location lookup component and set off a cascading failure. Google Cloud Storage returned elevated errors and tail latency in every region and storage class, App Engine Blobstore and deployments failed heavily, Stackdriver struggled to read historical metrics, and Gmail, Drive and Photos saw errors softened by caching. Recovery required stopping the change and manually reducing traffic.

title: Postgres transaction ID wraparound halts Mandrill email sending
trigger: A hot Postgres shard (shard4) ran out of transaction IDs because autovacuum fell behind or failed, and the database entered its protective shutdown mode.
impact: Mandrill email sending was impaired for about 33 hours from 05:35 UTC on February 4, only 80% of queued mail went out during the outage, and app servers nearly filled their disks with queued jobs.
detection: The first exception was buried among unrelated errors; engineers began investigating at 11:58 UTC and identified XID wraparound at 12:56 UTC.
fix: After slow VACUUM and dump-and-restore attempts, the team truncated the huge Search and Url tables so the vacuum could finish, resumed sending at 21:36 UTC on February 5, added wraparound alerting and refunded customers.
summary: Mandrill stores data in Postgres shards acting as one key/value store, and uneven hashing made shard4 the busiest. Its autovacuum did not keep up, the 32-bit transaction ID counter neared wraparound, and Postgres stopped accepting writes. Failed jobs piled up on app server disks while retries added load. A plain VACUUM was estimated to take up to 40 days, so after a day of attempts engineers dropped the terabyte-scale Search and Url tables, letting the vacuum finish and sending resume.

title: ZooKeeper patching collapses Elastic Cloud us-east-1
trigger: Routine replacement of hosts in the ZooKeeper coordination ensemble for AWS us-east-1 left it under heavy connection load, its leader shut down and quorum could not be held, compounded by a runc bug causing kernel OOPS and CPU softlocks.
impact: Elasticsearch Service deployments in us-east-1 were partly or fully unreachable from 02:50 to 09:28 UTC, with every cluster seeing some failures, most Kibana instances down until 09:28 and some until 18:44 UTC, and the Cloud console degraded until 07:17 UTC.
detection: A rise in HTTP 5xx errors at the load balancer was noticed at 02:50 UTC, while the engineer doing the maintenance had hit an unfamiliar error.
fix: Engineers cut client load to restore ZooKeeper quorum, raised initLimit to steady the observer layer, scaled out the proxy fleet, and restarted TLS proxy containers and Kibana with sysctl limits; Kibana connection-leak bugs were identified.
summary: Patching the three-node Apache ZooKeeper ensemble behind Elastic Cloud in AWS us-east-1 went wrong even though the same procedure had worked in 12 other regions. Connection storms overloaded the leader, quorum was lost, and every component depending on the coordination layer failed, including the proxy routing layer. A runc bug triggered kernel softlocks when entering a TLS proxy container's network namespace. Once routing returned, a threefold reconnect surge hit the proxies, and leaking Kibana sockets filled the nf_conntrack table, prolonging Kibana outages.

title: ZooKeeper bug desyncs Kafka, blocking Grafana Cloud queries
trigger: ZooKeeper pods lost connectivity and elected a new leader, hitting bug ZOOKEEPER-2985, which left some Kafka pods no longer replicating.
impact: Customer queries in the HM-US-West2 hosted metrics region went unserved for about an hour (12:21 to 13:14 UTC on January 29, 2019) while ingestion continued.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers restarted the active Kafka controller (kafka-5) and then the two out-of-sync pods (kafka-3, kafka-12), after which replication completed and Metrictank recovered.
summary: Grafana Cloud's HM-US-West2 metrics region could not answer most customer queries for roughly an hour on 29 January 2019. A ZooKeeper connection timeout triggered a leader change that hit the known bug ZOOKEEPER-2985, causing some Kafka pods to stop replicating. Metrictank instances consuming those partitions stopped ingesting, their partition lag grew past a threshold, and they marked themselves not ready, so queries failed. Restarting the Kafka controller and the two lagging brokers restored replication and querying.

title: ZooKeeper overload cascades into Elastic Cloud eu-west-1 proxy outage
trigger: The leader node of the three-node ZooKeeper ensemble backing the coordination layer in AWS eu-west-1 hit very high CPU and began dropping client connections.
impact: Elastic Cloud customers in AWS eu-west-1 had badly degraded cluster access for about three hours, including roughly 20 minutes (12:42 to 13:02 UTC) when every deployment in the region was unreachable.
detection: On-call SREs were alerted to coordination-layer degradation at 09:35 UTC, about 26 minutes after the CPU spike began.
fix: SREs scaled the proxy layer up and out, forced a ZooKeeper leader election to stabilize the ensemble, and accelerated replacing Curator TreeCache with an in-house TreeWatcher in the proxies.
summary: In Elastic Cloud's AWS eu-west-1 region, the ZooKeeper leader ran hot and clients disconnected. The routing proxies used Apache Curator TreeCache, which on every reconnect re-reads and re-watches every znode in one huge batch, so flaky connections made proxies flood ZooKeeper, deepen its GC pauses and run out of memory themselves. Proxies degraded, customer Elasticsearch and Kibana clusters became hard to reach for about three hours, and the whole region was down for around 20 minutes before recovery.

title: Config update shrinks EC2 DNS resolver fleet in Seoul region
trigger: A configuration update dropped the minimum healthy host setting for the EC2 DNS resolver fleet in AP-NORTHEAST-2, so a very low default took effect.
impact: DNS lookups made from inside EC2 instances in the Seoul region failed for about 84 minutes, from 8:19 to 9:43 AM KST, while external DNS and network connectivity kept working.
detection: Engineers were alerted at 8:21 AM KST, two minutes after impact started.
fix: AWS stopped healthy hosts from being taken out of service and rebuilt resolver capacity, then audited capacity settings in all regions and began adding semantic config validation and hourly limits on capacity removal.
summary: In the AWS Seoul region, a configuration change to the EC2 DNS resolver service lost the value defining how many healthy hosts must stay in service. The system fell back to a very low default and removed hosts, leaving too little capacity, so recursive DNS queries from EC2 instances started failing. Outside resolution and instance networking were unaffected. The cause was found within half an hour, but restoring fleet capacity took most of the 84-minute outage. Follow-ups include semantic validation and throttled scale-down.

title: Events table hits 32-bit ID limit, Basecamp 3 goes read-only
trigger: The primary key on the events table, which logs nearly every user action, reached the 32-bit integer maximum of 2,147,483,647.
impact: Basecamp 3 was read-only for about five hours, from 7:21am to 12:11pm CST, so users could view content but not create or edit anything.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The team widened the table key to a 64-bit integer, and acknowledged it had underestimated how fast headroom was shrinking and missed the earlier Rails 5.1 default change as a warning.
summary: Basecamp 3 stores almost all user activity in a single events table whose primary key was a signed 32-bit integer. When the ID sequence hit 2,147,483,647, inserts failed and nearly every write path stopped, leaving the app in a read-only state where messages, to-dos and files could be viewed but not changed. Work to widen the column was already in progress but too late. Migrating the key to bigint restored writes after about five hours.

title: Azure DevOps outages from sync-over-async thread starvation
trigger: Brief slowdowns in the SPS authentication service made thousands of build and release agents reconnect, and new code that blocked on async calls exhausted the thread pool on application tier machines.
impact: On 3, 4 and 8 October 2018 several scale units went down, SU3 for up to 75 minutes; on 10 October most units had about 15 minutes of impact and one West Europe unit longer.
detection: Not clearly stated; a hot-path health alert fired on 10 October at roughly the same moment the first customer escalation came in.
fix: Microsoft disabled the async agent-online code path and recycled the application tiers, and plans to isolate the message queue service in its own app pool, run fault injection and gate VIP swaps on SPS health.
summary: In October 2018 Azure DevOps suffered a series of outages. Short latency spikes in the SPS identity service caused build agents to reconnect en masse; code added in Sprint 140 made synchronous calls over async ones, and with all threads waiting on queued completions, application tier servers deadlocked and failed health probes. A dump showed 1202 threads stuck in SetAgentOnline. A 10 October incident added deployment-driven SPS database contention and uneven load across recovering servers, mitigated by recycling them.

title: Database connection queue buildup slows Duo DUO1 authentications
trigger: Load on the DUO1 deployment, already above acceptable levels, caused requests to queue waiting for database connections until the database could not recover.
impact: All customer applications on DUO1 saw slow authentications, intermittent timeouts and degraded push, phone call and SMS delivery from 14:11 to 15:13 UTC.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Duo flushed application server queues, added a maximum queue size with queue-depth alerting and moved some customers off DUO1, then scheduled a doubling of database capacity and a database tier redesign.
summary: Duo's DUO1 deployment was running hot after an earlier outage, and on August 29 rising load caused application servers to queue requests while waiting for database connections. The backlog grew to the point that the database could not catch up even after traffic eased, so authentications, push notifications, phone calls and SMS codes were slow or timed out for about an hour. Request limits did not help; flushing the queues did. Duo added queue caps and planned a capacity upgrade.

title: Jenkins leaks GitHub token with push rights to core Homebrew repos
trigger: A GitHub personal access token whose scopes had recently been widened was exposed through Homebrew's Jenkins instance, granting git push to Homebrew/brew and Homebrew/homebrew-core.
impact: Anyone holding the token could have pushed to the two main Homebrew repositories, but GitHub confirmed it was not used for any pushes, so no packages were tampered with and users needed to do nothing.
detection: A security researcher discovered the exposed token and reported it via Homebrew's HackerOne program.
fix: Within hours the token was revoked, replaced and scrubbed from Jenkins output; branch protection, required reviews and mandatory CI checks were added, and maintainers were asked to prune their access tokens and turn off SMS fallback for 2FA.
summary: On 31 July 2018 a researcher reported via HackerOne that Homebrew's Jenkins was leaking a GitHub personal access token with freshly elevated scopes, enough to push directly to Homebrew/brew and Homebrew/homebrew-core. A volunteer maintainer revoked and replaced the token within hours and stopped Jenkins from revealing it again. GitHub verified the token had made no pushes, so no packages were compromised. Homebrew then locked master against direct pushes by non-admins, required passing CI on most repos, and had maintainers audit their tokens.

title: PLN 1 phone promotion overloads Allegro's service cluster
trigger: A noon promotion selling 100 Honor 7C phones for PLN 1 drew a traffic spike two to three times the prior day's level, much of it from bots.
impact: The marketplace was largely unavailable for roughly 20 minutes around midday, with many users getting blank pages and some buyers having their transactions aborted.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers scaled Listing and Search, added cluster resources and shut down non-critical services, then planned to fix oversized resource reservations, tune pools, retries and circuit breakers, and extend rate limiting.
summary: A PLN 1 phone flash sale at Allegro pushed traffic to 200-300% of normal. Misconfigured services had reserved far more CPU and RAM than they used, so new instances could not be scheduled despite free cluster capacity. Thread pools, connection pools and file descriptors saturated, a circuit breaker threshold was too high to trip, and the slow autoscaler fought a watchdog that killed unresponsive Opbox frontend instances. Retries added load, rate limiters served blank pages, and the site was down about 20 minutes.

title: Hijacked npm account publishes token-stealing eslint-scope release
trigger: An attacker logged into an ESLint maintainer's npm account with a reused password (no 2FA was enabled), created an auth token and published malicious package versions.
impact: eslint-scope@3.7.2 and eslint-config-eslint@5.0.2 carried a postinstall script that fetched code from pastebin.com and sent the installing machine's .npmrc file, typically holding npm publish tokens, to the attacker.
detection: A user opened issue eslint/eslint-scope#39 at 11:17 UTC, about 37 minutes after the eslint-scope release, alerting the ESLint team.
fix: The bad versions were unpublished, the pastebin payload was taken down, a clean eslint-scope@3.7.3 was released, and npm invalidated all access tokens issued before 2018-07-12 12:30 UTC; maintainers were urged to use unique passwords, npm 2FA and lockfiles.
summary: On July 12, 2018 an attacker took over an ESLint maintainer's npm account using a password reused from elsewhere, minted an auth token and published eslint-config-eslint@5.0.2 and eslint-scope@3.7.2. Their postinstall hook pulled a payload from pastebin.com that exfiltrated users' .npmrc files containing npm access tokens. eslint-scope is a dependency of packages such as babel-eslint and webpack. A user report triggered unpublishing, and npm revoked every access token created before 12:30 UTC that day, so affected developers had to re-authenticate.

title: Runaway ChangeProp topic creation takes down Kafka main-eqiad
trigger: A small config deploy to production ChangeProp caused an outdated dev ChangeProp instance, missing a known bug fix, to resubscribe to every topic and endlessly create retry topics on the production Kafka main-eqiad cluster.
impact: From about 14:37 UTC until the brokers came up cleanly at 21:13 UTC, Kafka main-eqiad repeatedly failed, EventBus saw produce errors and EventStreams was heavily disrupted, with services failed over to codfw; 2086 new topics were added during the event.
detection: Icinga logged EventBus errors producing to Kafka at 14:38 UTC, one minute after brokers began logging the creation of new topic partitions.
fix: Operators raised the open-file limit and the broker heap from 1G to 2G, stopped ChangeProp, failed EventBus over to codfw and finally hard-deleted the bogus topics from ZooKeeper and broker disks; follow-ups include isolating dev ChangeProp from production Kafka and reconsidering automatic topic creation.
summary: A stale development copy of Wikimedia's ChangeProp, reading from production Kafka, reacted to an unrelated config deploy by subscribing to all topics and spawning retry-of-retry topics every few seconds. The flood exhausted file descriptors and JVM heap on the kafka100x brokers, which logged OutOfMemoryError and Too many open files, and an attempt to delete the long-named topics hit Kafka bug KAFKA-7156. EventBus and EventStreams were moved to codfw; recovery came only after manually purging the topics from ZooKeeper and disk.

title: Guessed admin password lets attacker seize Gentoo GitHub org
trigger: The attacker obtained an organization admin's password, apparently guessable from a pattern after a disclosure on an unrelated site, and logged into the Gentoo GitHub organization.
impact: All developers were removed from the org and malicious commits adding rm -rf payloads were force-pushed to gentoo/gentoo, gentoo/musl and gentoo/systemd for roughly ten hours, leaving GitHub unusable for Gentoo for about 5 days and breaking pull-request CI and history.
detection: Developers noticed within minutes because removal from the organization triggered notification emails, and the first report reached Infra at 20:36 UTC.
fix: GitHub froze the org, Gentoo identified and cut off the compromised account, reverted the bad commits, rotated its credentials, and followed up with mandatory 2FA, fewer org owners, audit-log streaming and hardware 2FA keys for developers.
summary: On June 28, 2018 an attacker used a guessed password for a Gentoo GitHub organization administrator, created extra admin accounts, removed every legitimate developer and force-pushed commits inserting rm -rf commands into ebuilds and a systemd configure script. Gentoo's primary repositories on its own infrastructure were unaffected, but anyone who freshly cloned the GitHub mirrors in the affected windows was told to reclone. GitHub froze the organization; Gentoo regained control, reverted content, required 2FA to join the org and gave developers hardware 2FA keys.

title: VSTS outage spreads as throttled health probes reroute traffic
trigger: A routine deployment left the tfs-weu-2 scale unit unhealthy, and Azure Front Door rerouted its traffic to other scale units that proxied it back.
impact: Visual Studio Team Services was disrupted across multiple regions from 15:00 to 16:55 UTC on 22 May 2018, affecting an estimated 20,800 users.
detection: Automated deployment health checks caught the failing tfs-weu-2 application tiers and rolled them back at 15:10 UTC.
fix: Engineers disabled the concurrent anonymous request block so health checks passed, exempted health probes and proxied ARR traffic from throttling, and changed Front Door to stop rerouting away from unhealthy units.
summary: On 22 May 2018 a deployment broke the tfs-weu-2 scale unit of Visual Studio Team Services. Azure Front Door sent its traffic to other scale units, which used Application Request Routing to proxy it back to the dead unit. The resource utilization service counted those slow proxied requests and load balancer health probes as anonymous traffic, hit its concurrency cap and returned 429s, so probes failed and each unit was marked offline in turn. Disabling the anonymous request limit stopped the chain reaction.

title: Test suite truncates production database via stale DATABASE_URL
trigger: A developer ran a test suite using the Database Cleaner gem in an old terminal whose DATABASE_URL still pointed at the production primary, truncating its tables.
impact: travis-ci.com was unusable for about 5.5 hours from 12:14 UTC plus about 3.5 hours of build backlog; users saw blank profiles, some were logged in as other accounts because reused IDs collided, and about 15 minutes of data was lost.
detection: Alerts fired right after the truncation, and customer reports of missing data at 12:45 UTC confirmed it.
fix: Apps were taken offline and the database restored from that morning's snapshot, affected tokens were revoked, and follow-ups included revoking truncate rights, DATABASE_URL guards in spec helpers and shell prompts, and an easy follower alias.
summary: A Travis CI developer had pointed a terminal at the production PostgreSQL primary days earlier to inspect data and later ran tests there; Database Cleaner truncated all tables. The API kept serving a nearly empty database for about 30 minutes, and because truncation does not reset sequences, new user rows got IDs belonging to old users, so some people logged in as someone else and could have seen build logs. The team restored from a snapshot, revoked sessions and notified affected customers and GitHub admins.

title: Test run against production DB truncates all travis-ci.com tables
trigger: A developer ran the test suite in an old terminal that still had DATABASE_URL pointed at production, and the Database Cleaner gem truncated every table.
impact: travis-ci.com was down for about 5.5 hours from 12:14 UTC with 3.5 more hours of build backlog, about 15 minutes of data was lost, and users who logged in during a 30-minute window were later signed in as the wrong accounts.
detection: The team responded to alerts right after the truncation, but the API kept serving from the near-empty database for about 30 minutes.
fix: Travis CI took apps offline, restored the database, revoked mismatched tokens, and removed the truncate permission, added DATABASE_URL guards and shell warnings, and made the read-only follower easy to reach.
summary: On 13 March 2018 a test suite run in a stale tmux shell with DATABASE_URL set to travis-ci.com's production PostgreSQL truncated all tables. The API stayed up for about 30 minutes on the empty database, creating new user records that reused id sequences, so after restore some users were logged in as other accounts and build logs were potentially exposed. The site was offline about 5.5 hours. Travis CI revoked affected tokens, notified customers, dropped truncate permissions and added safeguards against using production credentials locally.

title: Fortnite services buckle at 3.4M concurrent players
trigger: Record load of 3.4 million concurrent players over February 3 and 4 exposed MongoDB write queuing, Memcached saturation and a memory leak in the XMPP cluster.
impact: Six incidents caused partial and full Fortnite disruptions, including matchmaking failures, blocked sign-ins from 18:30 to 20:20 UTC on February 4 and friends showing offline from 22:00 UTC to 00:15 UTC.
detection: Not stated for most incidents; the post says monitoring alerted the team quickly to AWS instance limits, and CPU sampling diagnosed thread pool starvation.
fix: Engineers repeatedly failed over the matchmaking database, rolled back a thread pool change and switched XMPP clusters, then planned to route traffic around Nginx, add Memcached capacity, fix subnet sizing, monitor cloud limits and rearchitect MCP and messaging.
summary: When Fortnite hit 3.4 million concurrent players, several backend systems failed. The MongoDB shard holding matchmaking data began queuing writes until it hung, forcing manual failovers several times an hour. Memcached instability tied up Nginx workers in front of the Account Service, so health checks failed and the load balancer pulled every node, blocking logins. A blue-green switch of a leaking XMPP cluster overloaded the Friends Service load balancer, whose subnet lacked spare IPs, so everyone appeared offline.

title: Spam-detection false positive pulls 106 npm packages from the registry
trigger: npm's automated spam and malicious-code detection flagged a legitimate publisher, and staff reviewing the flag wrongly blocked that publisher's packages.
impact: 97 packages could not be downloaded for about 30 minutes and another 9 for about three hours.
detection: npm says it spotted the mistake within five minutes, but the post does not describe the detection mechanism.
fix: Staff reversed the block through the normal process, verified package integrity after community members published lookalike replacements, and made immediate process changes pending a full review.
summary: On a Saturday in January 2018 the npm registry made 106 packages temporarily unavailable after its security tooling, which runs static analysis to flag suspicious code and authors before human review, produced a wrong block decision against a legitimate publisher. Dependent installs failed for 30 minutes for 97 packages and roughly three hours for 9 more. Recovery was slowed because community members, fearing a breach, published their own substitute packages that npm had to clean up. npm said no account or package integrity was compromised.

title: AWS network trouble exhausts connections on self-hosted load balancers
trigger: An AWS connectivity incident in us-east1 and us-west2 made EC2-hosted clients send requests very slowly to Hosted Graphite's non-AWS load balancers.
impact: From 23:28 to about 01:46 UTC the website and graph render API were intermittently unreachable, HTTP API ingestion failed from every location, and overall ingestion traffic dropped.
detection: External monitoring checks against the website and render API began timing out, followed by internal and external canaries showing ingestion loss.
fix: Service recovered once AWS resolved its incident; afterwards the team enforced tighter client timeouts, raised load balancer connection limits, and adopted new log-based visualizations for troubleshooting.
summary: Hosted Graphite's site, render API and HTTP ingestion became intermittently unavailable even though its frontend runs outside AWS. An AWS networking problem slowed EC2 clients in affected regions so much that each took up to 5 seconds to finish a request, and those lingering connections filled the self-hosted load balancers to their connection limit. New clients elsewhere then stalled in SSL handshakes. Disabling Route53 health checks did not help; recovery came when AWS recovered, and the fix was stricter client timeouts plus higher connection limits.

title: GCP networking bug triggers cascading Discord sessions cluster outage
trigger: A Google Cloud Platform networking stack update caused 16 brief network loss events on nodes in Discord's sessions cluster.
impact: Over 24 hours on November 17 and 18 Discord went fully offline twice, for 30 minutes each time, and had fourteen smaller partial interruptions.
detection: Engineers noticed service impact and escalated it in incident chat, and on-call was paged by low-memory alerts on sessions nodes.
fix: Discord force-terminated wedged nodes and restarted core services twice while Google rolled back its change, then fixed an Erlang net_kernel instability and began replacing its HTTP library and service discovery parts.
summary: A Google Cloud networking change caused short connectivity losses on Discord's network-heavy sessions cluster. Those blips overloaded Erlang's net_kernel, wedging the distribution port and causing runaway memory growth, and forced node terminations eventually triggered cascading failures that required restarting core services and reconnecting millions of clients twice. A degraded service discovery component and an unstable internal HTTP library slowed recovery. Google rolled back its update after more than 24 hours; Discord fixed the net_kernel issue and is replacing weak components.

title: Monzo outage from etcd timeout bug and linkerd empty-service crash
trigger: A routine deploy of a payments service exposed a Kubernetes and etcd client bug, triggered by an earlier etcd cluster resize, that stopped linkerd receiving updated endpoint locations.
impact: Current account payments failed from about 14:10 to 15:31, roughly 1.5 hours, escalating after 15:13 into a full platform outage affecting the app, prepaid cards and internal tools.
detection: Requests to the newly deployed service failed immediately after the 14:10 deploy and an outage was declared internally at 14:16.
fix: Engineers deleted a Kubernetes service with zero endpoints so linkerd could parse discovery data again, and planned to fix the Kubernetes timeout bug, upgrade linkerd and add better health checks and alerts.
summary: On 27 October 2017 a Monzo payments service deploy started failing because linkerd had not learned the new pod addresses, a result of a Kubernetes and etcd client bug that caused timeouts after an etcd cluster expansion. Restarting all linkerd instances made it far worse: the new linkerd hit a NullPointerException parsing a Kubernetes service that had been scaled to zero replicas, so no service could route traffic. Deleting that empty service restored the platform about 1.5 hours after payments first failed.

title: crossorigin attribute and CORS headers blank the Buildkite web UI
trigger: A deploy added crossorigin=anonymous to script tags for CSP reporting, but assets from buildkiteassets.com (S3 behind Cloudflare) lacked the needed CORS response headers, so browsers blocked the JavaScript.
impact: The buildkite.com web interface rendered blank for most non-Safari browsers until a revert restored it about 5 minutes later, and a later redeploy caused blank pages again for users whose browsers held cached assets without CORS headers.
detection: Internal staff reported the blank UI first, followed by customer reports.
fix: Buildkite reverted the attribute twice, corrected the S3 CORS setup, and is moving assets to a CloudFront and Lambda@Edge host with planned canary deploys and full-browser post-deploy checks.
summary: While preparing Content Security Policy support, Buildkite added crossorigin=anonymous to its script tags so CSP reports would include stack traces. That made browsers send CORS requests to the separate asset host, whose S3 bucket did not return the expected headers due to a misread S3 CORS quirk, so the dashboard JavaScript failed to load. After fixing S3, a second rollout still broke for some users because immutable asset URLs without Vary: Origin let browsers reuse cached responses missing the headers.

title: Redis failover and bad cache rule cascade into full Discord restart
trigger: Google Cloud live-migrated the Redis primary of a key API cluster, which wrongly dropped offline and failed over, and API instances mishandled the failover due to a known bug.
impact: Users saw guilds appear unavailable and connection problems from about 14:01 to 16:52 PDT, and a full service restart reconnected millions of clients over roughly 20 minutes.
detection: Real-time metrics and monitoring alerted engineers at 14:01, and user reports were escalated at 15:42.
fix: Engineers restarted API instances, fixed the caching rule, recovered Cassandra, removed bad guilds nodes and restarted the whole service, then prioritized the Redis failover fix and added monitoring for early cascade signals.
summary: A Google Cloud migration knocked a Redis primary offline and API servers handled the failover badly. A misconfigured edge caching rule then let clients hammer an expensive API route, overloading a Cassandra cluster, while faulty nodes in the guilds and sessions clusters ran out of memory. A mistyped reconnection setting made things worse. Guilds showed as unavailable and Discord had to restart the entire service. The postmortem says the exact path to full system failure was not determined.

title: Pacemaker fails to promote Postgres replica after disk failure
trigger: The RAID controller on the primary Postgres node reported three disks lost at once, and the filesystem went read-only.
impact: Every GoCardless API and Dashboard request failed for 1 hour 50 minutes, from 15:09 to 16:59 BST, with no data corruption found afterward.
detection: Monitoring caught the complete outage at 15:09.
fix: After automatic promotion failed, engineers manually promoted the synchronous replica and repointed apps, then rebuilt the cluster and planned app-side proxies and more failure game days.
summary: GoCardless ran a three-node Postgres cluster managed by Pacemaker with virtual IPs. When the primary's disks failed, Pacemaker should have promoted the synchronous replica within a minute or two, but did not. The team later reproduced the failure only with a combination of non-zero default-resource-stickiness, a Backup VIP with a -INF colocation rule, and a Postgres subprocess crashing on the replica at the same moment. After an hour of trying, engineers promoted the replica manually and pointed Rails apps at it.

title: Impersonator slips malicious packages into JCenter
trigger: Someone posing as Jake Wharton submitted a technically valid but malware-laced package for JCenter inclusion, and support reviewers approved it without catching the impersonation.
impact: Malicious artifacts under a look-alike namespace, including copies of timber, bitcoinj, litecoinj and async-http libraries, stayed available through JCenter from July 2017 until December 2018.
detection: Community abuse reports filed in February 2018 never reached Bintray due to a technical fault in the reporting pipeline; the team only acted after Marton Braun blogged about it publicly in December 2018.
fix: Bintray banned the fake user, deleted the uploaded files and their JCenter links, added monitoring and logging to the abuse reporting system, and set up a dedicated moderation team to vet authors and namespace claims.
summary: In July 2017 a user impersonating Android developer Jake Wharton asked for a package to be included in JCenter; it looked legitimate but contained malicious code, and Bintray support approved it. Abuse reports sent in February 2018 were silently lost because of a failure in Bintray's reporting path. After a public blog post in December 2018, Bintray banned the account, removed the rogue artifacts, which mimicked timber, bitcoinj and async-http packages, and tightened inclusion review and abuse-report monitoring.

title: Load balancer master pushes stale config, causing 502 errors
trigger: Mastership of the HTTP(S) Load Balancer config pipeline moved to a replica that could not read Google's distributed file system, and after its first test push failed it reverted all load balancers to a badly out-of-date configuration.
impact: From 01:13 to 01:35 PDT, 25% of requests to the Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancer got 502 errors (100% for some recently changed balancers), and a 3 hour 41 minute config freeze broke App Engine Flexible deployments.
detection: An on-call page went out to Google engineers at 01:22 PDT.
fix: Engineers moved the update process to another master at 01:34 and froze changes until 05:16; follow-ups reject configs older than a few hours, improve testing and fix the file system read and garbage collection health check problems.
summary: Google's HTTP(S) Load Balancer config master failed over to a server that had lost access to the distributed file system. When its first push test failed, it rolled every load balancer back to the newest config it could see, which was very old. Deleting the many removed configs set off heavy garbage collection on Google Frontend servers, which then failed health checks and restarted, returning 502 errors for 22 minutes.

title: Misconfigured instance after EU maintenance causes H10 routing errors
trigger: During scheduled EU maintenance, a remote reconfiguration step silently hit a new security timeout, leaving one instance misconfigured so the routing fleet could miss dyno start and stop updates.
impact: From April 3 17:20 UTC to April 6 10:00 UTC, about 12% of EU apps (only those that created new releases) saw H10, H19, H21 and H26 errors and became unreachable at times, affecting under 1% of EU requests.
detection: Engineers noticed elevated H10 errors, but a 30-minute router connection cycling window made symptoms move between apps and led to false leads.
fix: Engineers repeatedly flushed routing caches to limit impact, eventually traced the stale routing data to one instance via internal logs and corrected its config, and planned better monitoring, an H99 error for this case, and timeout-aware automation.
summary: A trusted automation tool used during Heroku's EU database maintenance timed out on one instance because of a newly added strict timeout for admin sessions, and the tool did not surface the failure. The misconfigured instance fed stale state to the routing layer, so web dynos looked crashed and apps that deployed or changed config vars got H10 App Crashed and related errors. Because routers reconnected every 30 minutes, errors hopped between apps, making diagnosis take about three days.

title: Bad Puppet config change restarts and kills all authoritative DNS
trigger: A merged Puppet change carried an invalid authdns config file, and scheduled Puppet agent runs automatically restarted gdnsd on all three authoritative servers within about four minutes, leaving each daemon stopped.
impact: Authoritative DNS was completely unavailable for 2m43s (13:34:43-13:37:26 UTC) and partly degraded for 8m19s, causing secondary failures in internal services and a small spike of public 5xx responses from about 13:35 to 13:40.
detection: An Icinga Auth DNS check on the first failed server alerted at 13:32 UTC and operators began responding on IRC a minute later.
fix: The faulty commit was corrected and Puppet's ability to automatically restart the authdns daemons on config change was removed, with follow-ups to spread out agent run timing and refactor authdns CI.
summary: Wikimedia's three gdnsd authoritative DNS servers went down after an invalid configuration file, which CI could not lint, was merged into Puppet. Puppet was allowed to restart gdnsd on config change, and the move to systemd had removed the old pre-restart validation, so each agent run stopped the daemon. Because all three hosts happened to run Puppet within a five-minute window, DNS was fully dark for under three minutes, with knock-on alerts across internal services. Auto-restart was disabled afterward.

title: Presence cluster split-brain stalls Discord connections
trigger: A presence service node on Google Cloud suffered CPU soft lockups, and a known but undeployed bug made the presence cluster split-brain when it lost that node.
impact: About a third of user connections stalled and stopped receiving messages and events, direct messages went undelivered for a time and message sending was disabled globally at points, across two episodes from about 11:38 until the afternoon.
detection: Engineers noticed service degradation at 11:39, one minute after impact began.
fix: Discord patched the API to limit connections and sending, restarted the whole service, rebooted the faulty VM onto another host, deployed the split-brain fix overnight and added a cap on in-flight session-to-presence connections.
summary: Discord's presence service, which tracks who is online, lost a node to hypervisor-level CPU soft lockups on Google Cloud. A known bug caused the presence cluster to split-brain, and session servers holding client websockets all tried to reconnect at once, overloading it. Without presence data, sessions stalled and buffered events in memory until many ran out of memory and crashed. A third of users stopped receiving messages, and the failure recurred later in the day before the VM was moved.

title: Unbounded Redis transaction retries overload Square auth service
trigger: A deploy of the Roster identity service in one datacenter coincided with the Multipass authentication service retrying Redis optimistic transactions up to 500 times with no backoff, saturating its Redis.
impact: Most Square products, including payments, Point of Sale, Dashboard, Appointments and Payroll, were down from 10:02 to 11:55 a.m. PDT, and SMS 2FA codes failed until 1:12 p.m.
detection: Multipass began reporting timeouts to on-call at 10:02, and external monitoring reported api.squareup.com down at 10:08.
fix: Engineers deployed a Multipass change to cut Redis transaction retries and relaxed cgroup limits for critical services; follow-ups audit retry logic and cgroup limits, add a Redis runbook, and review SMS capacity.
summary: Square's merchant authentication service, Multipass, became unrecoverably overloaded right after a Roster deployment. Rolling back Roster and restarting Multipass did not help. Redis SLOWLOG and MONITOR pointed to a code path retrying optimistic transactions up to 500 times without backoff, a feedback loop that maxed out Redis. A fix reducing retries restored payments at 11:48. A burst of logins then overwhelmed outbound SMS for two-factor codes until the vendor rebalanced sending numbers.

title: Mistyped playbook command takes down S3 in us-east-1
trigger: While debugging slow S3 billing, an engineer ran a playbook command with a wrong input that removed far more servers than intended, including capacity for the index and placement subsystems.
impact: S3 in US-EAST-1 was unavailable or impaired for about 4 hours 17 minutes, which also broke the S3 console, new EC2 launches, EBS volumes restoring from snapshots, Lambda and the AWS Service Health Dashboard.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: AWS fully restarted the index subsystem and then the placement subsystem, and afterwards slowed the removal tool, blocked removals below minimum capacity, audited other tools, and accelerated partitioning into smaller cells.
summary: An authorized S3 engineer mistyped a parameter in a capacity-removal command, pulling servers that backed the index and placement subsystems for the whole US-EAST-1 region. Both had to be fully restarted, and their metadata integrity checks took far longer than expected because the region had grown massively since its last full restart. GET, LIST, PUT and DELETE requests all failed during the restarts. AWS could not even update its own status dashboard, which depended on S3, so it posted updates on Twitter.

title: AWS outage traffic and SMS provider limits delay PagerDuty alerts
trigger: A traffic surge from customers hit by the AWS US-East-1 disruption coincided with a degraded voice/SMS provider, and failover volume tripped rate limits at a backup provider, overloading an internal component that could not scale elastically.
impact: Between 20:15 and 22:30 UTC, 32 percent of notifications were delayed by an average of 12 minutes, affecting 3.2 percent of users, while the API, web and mobile apps stayed available.
