detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: PagerDuty throttled some customers' inbound events to relieve the overloaded component, then committed to removing bottlenecks, making components elastic or pre-scaled, capacity planning, lifting provider rate limits and adding another voice provider.
summary: On the day of the large AWS US-East-1 disruption, PagerDuty, which does not run there, received a flood of events from affected customers. At the same time one of its SMS and voice carriers degraded; automatic failover to secondary providers worked but hit rate limits on one of them. The combined load made an internal notification component unhealthy, and it could not be scaled on demand. Phone, SMS, push and email alerts were delayed or duplicated for over two hours until inbound throttling stabilized delivery.

title: HTML parser buffer overrun leaks memory into responses (Cloudbleed)
trigger: A pointer overrun in Cloudflare's Ragel-based HTML parser, exposed when the new cf-html parser changed buffer handling, caused pages ending in an unfinished tag to read past the buffer end.
impact: About 1 in 3.3 million HTTP requests could have leaked uninitialized memory such as cookies, headers, POST bodies and tokens between September 2016 and February 18, 2017, with 770 URIs on 161 domains cached by search engines.
detection: Tavis Ormandy of Google Project Zero reported corrupted HTTP responses to Cloudflare.
fix: Cloudflare disabled Email Obfuscation, Automatic HTTPS Rewrites and Server-Side Excludes within hours, shipped a bounds-check fix globally, purged search engine caches, and added pointer checks, fuzzing and code review of the generated parser.
summary: Three Cloudflare features that rewrite HTML, Email Obfuscation, Server-Side Excludes and Automatic HTTPS Rewrites, shared a parser chain whose generated code checked buffer end with equality instead of greater-or-equal. When malformed pages ended mid-tag, the parser ran past the buffer and wrote neighbouring process memory into responses, exposing other sites' cookies, API keys and OAuth tokens. Some leaked pages were cached by search engines. Cloudflare killed the features within hours, purged caches and found no evidence of malicious use.

title: MySQL table hits RDS ext3 2TB file limit, 31-hour outage
trigger: The bookmarks table in Instapaper's Amazon RDS MySQL database grew past the 2TB per-file limit of the ext3 filesystem used by RDS instances created before April 2014, so inserts started failing.
impact: Instapaper was fully down for 31 hours from February 9 to February 10, then ran with limited archive access until a full restore on February 14, about five days in total.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; it notes RDS offered no monitoring, alert or log warning about the approaching limit.
fix: The team launched a temporary instance with partial archives, then AWS engineers rsynced the data onto an ext4-backed instance and replicated recent changes before promoting it, with follow-ups for faster escalation to Pinterest SRE and monthly backup tests.
summary: Instapaper's MySQL database on Amazon RDS descended, through a 2015 read-replica upgrade, from an instance created in 2013, so it kept an ext3 filesystem capped at 2TB per file. When the bookmarks table crossed that size, new saves failed, and every snapshot backup carried the same limit. A dump of the 2.5TB database took 10 to 24 hours, so the team brought up a limited service after 31 hours. AWS staff later copied data to ext4 storage, restoring everything without loss.

title: Bad worker release and failed rollback mark container builds failed
trigger: Worker v2.6.2 began running build scripts under a bash login shell, which changed exit code handling, and the rollback to v2.5.0 stalled because that image was never tagged on Docker Hub, where hosts now pulled from.
impact: From the 2 February rollout until about 00:31 UTC after emergency maintenance on 5 February 2017, jobs on the container-based Linux infrastructure were wrongly marked as failed, with reduced capacity during the maintenance.
detection: Reports of jobs incorrectly marked failed surfaced on 3 February; the stalled rollback was found on 4 February, since no alert covered the image pull errors.
fix: The on-call engineer created the missing v2.5.0 tag and emergency maintenance forced all EC2 hosts onto v2.5.0; follow-ups include alerts on image pull failures, faster instance replacement and more diverse staging tests.
summary: Travis CI rolled worker v2.6.2 onto its sudo: false, container-based EC2 fleet. The release ran bash as a login shell, altering exit codes so builds were reported as failed. The rollback silently stalled: v2.6.0 had moved image pulls from quay.io to Docker Hub, but v2.5.0 had only ever been tagged on quay.io, and nothing alerted on the pull errors. Slow host recycling stretched the outage across a weekend until emergency maintenance.

title: Apt pinning ignored, dynos lose write access to /dev/null
trigger: An upstream apt patch release caused Heroku's custom source policy to be skipped, so stock upstream packages replaced the pinned in-house ones and altered dyno filesystem permissions.
impact: From 14:29 to 20:18 UTC (nearly six hours) apps in the EU and US that wrote under /dev, such as /dev/null, hit permission failures that crashed them (H10) or stopped them booting (R10), with the affected count growing over the window.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Heroku paused new instance creation in its slack pools, rolled packages back on affected hosts and told users to restart dynos, then rewrote the apt policy file so both newer and older versions resolve to its own repository and planned stronger validation of new instances.
summary: A patch-level update to apt on Heroku's runtime hosts stopped honoring the platform's package pinning policy, so default upstream packages were installed instead of Heroku's customized builds. Those packages changed filesystem permissions, and dynos could no longer write to paths under /dev, including /dev/null. Apps crashed with H10 errors or failed to boot with R10 for almost six hours in both regions. Engineers froze new instance creation, rolled back packages, asked customers to run heroku ps:restart, and fixed the apt policy file.

title: Engineer wipes GitLab.com primary database during replica rebuild
trigger: While rebuilding a PostgreSQL secondary that had lost replication under heavy load, an engineer ran the data-directory wipe on the primary host instead of the secondary.
impact: GitLab.com was unavailable for about 18 hours and lost roughly six hours of database records, including about 5,000 projects, 5,000 comments and 700 user accounts; Git repositories and wikis were not lost.
detection: The engineer realized within seconds that the wrong host was being wiped, after about 300 GB was already gone.
fix: The team restored from an LVM snapshot taken about six hours earlier, copying it over slow disks for roughly 18 hours, then moved to hourly LVM snapshots, started a backup monitoring dashboard, and opened tracked issues for automated restore testing and an owner for data durability.
summary: A spike in database load pushed GitLab.com's PostgreSQL secondary so far behind that WAL segments it needed were gone, forcing a manual rebuild. During that work an engineer deleted the primary's data directory by mistake. Recovery then exposed silently broken safety nets: pg_dump backups had been failing because of a PostgreSQL version mismatch, failure emails were rejected by DMARC, and Azure disk snapshots were off. A staging LVM snapshot saved most data, but about six hours of issues, comments, projects and accounts were lost.

title: Stuck network canary leaves new GCE VMs unreachable
trigger: A big batch of changes to a seldom-touched load balancer setup hit an inefficient code path, so the canary test for public address changes timed out.
impact: New or live-migrated Compute Engine instances, new Cloud VPN tunnels and new network load balancers had no public IP reachability for about 2 hours 8 minutes, while existing resources were fine.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; the first public notice went out at 11:13 Pacific and new metrics and alerting were listed as a follow-up.
fix: Engineers restarted the jobs that program the load balancers so the queue drained in a batch avoiding the slow path, rolled out zone by zone, and planned a longer canary timeout, code fixes, broader tests, and a move to decentralized routing.
summary: Google Compute Engine sends inbound traffic through shared layer 2 load balancers whose address changes are canaried before global rollout. A large set of edits to an uncommon config made the canary time out, and that blocked every queued public address change behind it. As a result, VMs created or live-migrated during the window, along with new VPN tunnels and network load balancers, could not be reached via public IPs and could not send outbound traffic. Europe-west1 was the last region to recover.

title: Primary SQL Server bugcheck takes Stack Exchange offline
trigger: At 17:53 UTC the SQL Server process on primary database NY-SQL02 hit a bugcheck, with logs pointing to a possibly faulty DIMM.
impact: The Stack Exchange network was read-only for about 5 minutes and then fully offline for 12 minutes, and roughly 3.5 seconds of uncommitted transactions may have been lost.
detection: The team noticed the problem within 2 minutes and located the source within 5 minutes.
fix: Restarting SQL Server on NY-SQL02 brought sites back read-only, then read-write after health checks, and the server was pulled for memory testing while NY-SQL01 took all load and the cluster moved to 2016 SP1 CU1.
summary: Stack Overflow and the wider Stack Exchange network depend on a primary SQL Server, NY-SQL02, with standbys used for read-only fallback through application logic rather than automatic failover. When SQL Server crashed with a bugcheck, possibly due to bad memory, a bug had disabled the application-level failover, so sites went from read-only to fully offline. A service restart restored read-only access, then writes after checks. The 384GB memory dump was skipped to shorten downtime to about 17 minutes.

title: Unbounded memoize cache in AWS library exhausts JVM heap twice
trigger: An unbounded, never-evicting memoize cache in the Amazonica library kept piling up AWS SDK client objects for short-lived credentials until the JVM heap ran out.
impact: Customers could not deploy through Skyliner for 27 minutes on January 19 and 7 minutes on January 23, 2017, with their own infrastructure unaffected.
detection: External monitoring alerted on the first outage; on the second, automated exception reports showed heap exhaustion before the monitoring alarm fired.
fix: Instances were restarted, then a heap dump located the leak and a patch was deployed on January 24; follow-ups add latency and GC-failure alerting and PagerDuty paging.
summary: Skyliner, a multi-tenant deploy service, uses brief AWS credentials across 14 regions. A clojure.core/memoize cache inside Amazonica stored a client object per credential set and never evicted, so hundreds of thousands of objects built up until garbage collection spiraled and requests timed out. The first outage lacked forensic data; the team then enabled GC logging, fixed jmap tooling, enlarged disks to capture a full heap dump, found the cache, patched it and reported it upstream.

title: MongoDB connection surge and botched rollback cause Mailgun errors
trigger: MongoDB configuration changes made the previous day were followed by a steady rise in connections that overloaded the secondaries serving most reads.
impact: In one region the Control Panel, API, SMTP, website and click and open tracking saw timeouts and errors for about six and a half hours, with the API at roughly 75% of normal throughput for part of it.
detection: Alerts fired at 14:09 UTC on the click and open tracking services and the primary MongoDB clusters.
fix: Engineers rolled back the config, resized MongoDB servers and added server and per-service connection limits, then ran tracking in two regions and permanently enlarged the primary cluster.
summary: In one Mailgun region, MongoDB secondaries handling most reads became overloaded after a gradual connection increase that followed configuration changes made the day before. While rolling those changes back, a human error pointed API and SMTP reads at the primary, which could not cope, so error rates climbed across the API, SMTP and website. Engineers resized the cluster, imposed connection caps and restored secondary reads, and the region was healthy again at 20:35 UTC.

title: Leap second makes Go DNS server panic on negative duration
trigger: The leap second at midnight UTC on New Year's Day 2017 moved the wall clock backwards on Cloudflare's RRDNS servers.
impact: For up to about 6 hours 45 minutes, CNAME lookups failed on some machines, peaking at around 0.2% of DNS queries and under 1% of HTTP requests returning errors.
detection: The issue was escalated to engineers at 00:10 UTC and confirmed at 00:34 UTC.
fix: A patch that rejects negative timings and resets upstream performance data was canaried and rolled out globally within about two hours, servers were restarted, and Cloudflare began reviewing all code that measures time intervals.
summary: Cloudflare's Go-based authoritative DNS server, RRDNS, timed upstream resolvers by subtracting two time.Now() readings. Because that clock was not monotonic, the leap second produced negative durations that were smoothed into stored averages. When weighted server selection passed a negative value to rand.Int63n, the function panicked, breaking CNAME resolution for customers who used CNAME records. Only a small number of machines across 102 data centers were hit, and the most affected ones were patched within about 90 minutes.

title: Mirai botnet DDoS overwhelms Dyn Managed DNS in two waves
trigger: Large floods of TCP and UDP traffic to port 53, mostly from Mirai-based botnets, targeted Dyn's Managed DNS points of presence.
impact: Customers and their end users saw significant DNS disruption from about 11:10 to 13:20 UTC and again from 15:50 to 17:00 UTC, with residual effects until roughly 20:30 UTC.
detection: Dyn observed abnormally high bandwidth on its Managed DNS platform across several regions, matching a DDoS pattern.
fix: Engineers applied traffic shaping, anycast policy rebalancing, internal filtering and scrubbing services, then extended those defenses globally and are scaling them further.
summary: On October 21, 2016 Dyn's Managed DNS was hit by two multi-vector DDoS attacks, first concentrated on US-East and then globally distributed, using masked TCP and UDP packets aimed at port 53 from up to 100,000 malicious endpoints, largely Mirai botnet devices. Recursive resolvers retrying legitimate queries added 10-20X normal traffic, obscuring which sources were hostile. Dyn mitigated with traffic shaping, anycast rebalancing, filtering and scrubbing, recovering from the second wave by 17:00 UTC, and kept those protections in place for later probing attacks.

title: GlobalSign OCSP error marks intermediates revoked, breaking HTTPS
trigger: A failure at certificate authority GlobalSign caused its OCSP service to report its intermediate signing certificates as revoked, so some browsers stopped trusting Wikimedia's main site certificates.
impact: Starting around 10:00 UTC and lasting until a fix deployed at 17:36 UTC, certain newer clients, notably Safari and Chrome on macOS Sierra, could not trust Wikimedia sites; smaller sites were fixed by 19:05 and the OCG PDF service broke until 21:26.
detection: A trickle of user reports on IRC from about 11:30 UTC, with internal staff reproducing the problem at 14:20 UTC.
fix: Wikimedia deployed an alternate intermediate CA certificate supplied by GlobalSign and force-refreshed OCSP caches, and planned to run redundant unified certificates from a second vendor.
summary: A process failure at GlobalSign led its OCSP responders to declare the CA's intermediate certificates revoked, so browsers that check intermediate OCSP, especially Safari and Chrome on macOS Sierra, rejected Wikimedia's TLS certificates. Engineers initially investigated the leaf certificate's OCSP stapling before finding the real cause. With cached revocations able to persist for days, Wikimedia deployed GlobalSign's alternate intermediate after testing on a canary, which in turn broke the OCG PDF renderer's node.js until a rebuilt package shipped.

title: Developer Story CV pages leak emails and phones in HTML source
trigger: A view originally built to render PDF CVs was reused for HTML Developer Story pages during the Careers 2.0 port, and a bug placed users' email addresses and phone numbers in the page markup for all visitors.
impact: Contact details of users who filled out a Developer Story were present in public page source between 2016-10-11 and 2016-11-28 and got indexed by search engines, though only findable by searching an already-known email or phone number.
detection: On 2016-11-28 a user reported that searching their phone number returned their public Stack Overflow Jobs CV as the top hit.
fix: The bug was fixed at once, search engines and the Internet Archive were asked to suppress or purge the cached data, and the team adopted regular PII audits and tagging of PII in code and databases; users were told no action was needed.
summary: When Stack Overflow ported legacy Careers 2.0 code, it reused a PDF CV view for HTML Developer Story pages, and a bug embedded each user's email address and phone number in the HTML source even though it was not displayed. After the public beta opened on 2016-10-11, crawlers indexed the data until a user reported it on 2016-11-28. Stack Overflow fixed the view, got major search engines and the Internet Archive to purge or suppress the pages, and introduced PII code audits; users did not need to act.

title: Datadog PagerDuty and Opsgenie alerts skipped after deploy
trigger: A deployed update contained a circular import that only surfaced under certain conditions once processes were recycled, causing some notification types to be skipped.
impact: PagerDuty, Opsgenie and Flowdock notifications were skipped or delayed from 19:13 to 21:27 UTC on October 11, 2016 (about 2 hours 14 minutes).
detection: Detection took about two hours because notification monitoring only watched aggregate traffic rather than each notification class; the issue was caught at 21:10 UTC.
fix: A fix was deployed at 21:27 UTC and recent notifications were replayed; Datadog added per-class notification monitors, changed deploys to restart the affected processes promptly, and extended its replay cut-off to 4 hours.
summary: For over two hours on 11 October 2016, Datadog failed to deliver some monitor alerts to PagerDuty, Opsgenie and Flowdock. A code release included a circular import that tests and pre-flight checks missed; it broke notifications only after certain processes were later recycled, which also gave false confidence in the deploy. Aggregate-only monitoring hid the drop in one notification class. After a fix, only recent alerts were replayed, a choice Datadog later reconsidered by widening its replay window.

title: Datadog web app down after Postgres master fails
trigger: The master of the Postgres cluster holding user data failed, and a bootstrap misconfiguration meant most services were connected to the master rather than read replicas.
impact: The Datadog web app crashed from 13:40 until about 14:06 UTC on September 1, 2016, metric processing backed up, dashboards showed delays and gaps, and alerting stayed suspended until 15:51 UTC.
detection: Datadog was alerted to a critical failure in the database cluster at 13:40 UTC.
fix: Responders failed over to the standby (after first mistakenly targeting a replica) and added processors to clear the backlog; follow-ups audit connections to the master, review failover procedures and remove the metrics pipeline's dependency on this cluster.
summary: On 1 September 2016 the Datadog web application went down and metric ingestion stalled when the master of its Postgres user-data cluster failed. A bootstrap misconfiguration had most services, including metric processors needing metric names and units, talking to the master instead of read replicas. The scripted failover was first run against a replica by mistake, delaying recovery; a post-failover config error also briefly broke dashboards. Alerts were paused to avoid false positives, and backlog was replayed newest first.

title: Database downgrade and DB-coupled health checks take down Buildkite
trigger: To save AWS costs, the production RDS PostgreSQL instance was downsized without load testing, and its CPU maxed out under US peak traffic.
impact: The Buildkite dashboard, login, build logs and docs were unavailable or very slow for about 5 hours 50 minutes, although builds kept running and PR statuses still updated.
detection: The paging alert never reached anyone because of misconfigured PagerDuty settings and silenced phones; the team learned of the outage from customer emails, tweets and Slack after waking up.
fix: The team moved servers between load balancers, upgraded the database again, reverted to per-host pgbouncer and switched Auto Scaling to EC2 health checks, then planned load testing, simpler health checks, alert testing and storing the deploy revision in S3.
summary: Buildkite shrank its RDS PostgreSQL instance and added a central pgbouncer without load testing. Under peak load database CPU hit 100%, and because web health checks queried the database, load balancers pulled every server. Auto Scaling replacements booted from a stale AMI pointing at a retired shard, failed checks too, and churned until EC2 request limits were hit. With on-call paging misconfigured, nobody responded for hours; users could not log in or view build logs for nearly six hours.

title: EU region down 4 hours after gateway restart during upgrade
trigger: During a maintenance upgrade, gateways were restarted before the orchestration software had fully started, wiping their in-memory application list with no way to reload it.
impact: Websites in the Platform.sh EU region were down from 19:30 to 23:30 UTC, about 4 hours, with git servers and the UI also unavailable from 19:00, though no data integrity issue occurred.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers patched the Kazoo ZooKeeper client with a semaphore to stop pipe overflow and raised ZooKeeper's max buffer size, then added automated startup checks for upgrades and alerts when nodes reach 90 percent of the size limit.
summary: Platform.sh upgraded the orchestration software for its EU region, then restarted the gateways, which lost the cached list of applications and could not fetch it because orchestration was not up. Orchestration kept losing its ZooKeeper connections: with about a million nodes, the Kazoo library filled its 64k internal pipe buffer and hit EPIPE errors. After patching Kazoo, one ZooKeeper node still exceeded the maximum size. Raising the buffer limit brought sites back after four hours.

title: Puppet re-enables autoscaler mid-ZooKeeper migration, killing servers
trigger: During a ZooKeeper migration, the configuration management system restored the manually stopped autoscaler, which read half-migrated data and terminated application and cache servers.
impact: Reddit and its API were down on every official platform from 15:24 to 16:52 PDT and degraded until 18:19 PDT, about 3 hours in total.
detection: Engineers saw servers being shut down at 15:24 PDT, roughly a minute after the autoscaler came back on.
fix: The site was put in down mode while servers were rebuilt, then recovered as empty caches warmed; follow-ups include limiting how many servers the autoscaler may terminate at once.
summary: Reddit stopped its autoscaler by hand while moving ZooKeeper, which tracks server health, to new AWS infrastructure. Puppet saw the manual change as drift and turned the autoscaler back on. Seeing only half-moved ZooKeeper state, it shut down a large share of app and cache servers within 16 seconds, taking the site and API offline. After servers were restored, cold caches pushed heavy load onto the databases, so latency stayed high for another 1.5 hours.

title: Image cleanup service deletes all stable GCE build VM images
trigger: A re-enabled image cleanup service fetched only the 100 newest names from the image catalog, so the oldest, stable images looked unused and were deleted from Google Compute Engine.
impact: Builds on the sudo-enabled GCE infrastructure stopped for about 90 minutes, and the forced switch to new, not fully tested images broke many users' builds for weeks afterward.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Travis CI rolled forward to its development images and cleared the backlog in under two hours, then disabled automated cleanup, added deletion checks, made image builds reproducible and added automated image tests.
summary: Travis CI had been publishing many new GCE images while building a new provisioning pipeline, and its cleanup service queried the image catalog with a hard-coded limit of 100 names sorted newest first. When cleanup was switched back on, the nine-month-old stable images fell outside that window and were permanently deleted. They could not be rebuilt identically, so the team shipped development images, which lacked tools such as docker-compose and broke builds, and devoted the whole engineering staff to support for over a week.

title: Runaway free-block log fills disk after repeated S3 write failures
trigger: A background job that frees unreferenced blocks kept aborting on S3 write failures and restarting, so its on-disk change log grew until it filled the filesystem.
impact: For 85 minutes (about 10:15 to 11:40 UTC) no Tarsnap archives could be created or retrieved, in-progress backups failed, and no data was lost.
detection: Monitoring sent a text and phone call within minutes, but the operator only woke on a second call over an hour later.
fix: The runaway log was deleted and the server restarted; follow-ups include hourly repeat alerts, planned internal metrics like free disk space, and more S3 failure logging.
summary: From late June, retried Amazon S3 requests were failing far more often, with InternalError responses after about 4.88 seconds. Tarsnap's block-freeing job logged every change to disk, aborted 142 times in a week because of these failures, and restarted each time. The log eventually filled the filesystem, other writes failed, and the server code shut itself down as designed. The operator missed the first alerts, then removed the log and restarted service, and credited affected users two days of storage.

title: Whitespace-trim regex on a malformed post takes Stack Overflow down
trigger: A post with about 20,000 consecutive whitespace characters made a trim regular expression run in quadratic time on every home page view.
impact: Stack Overflow was unavailable for 34 minutes starting 14:44 UTC on July 20, 2016.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The regex was replaced with a substring function; follow-ups included auditing regexes and post validation, a way to disable the load balancer health check, and an outage checklist.
summary: A malformed Stack Overflow post on the home page contained roughly 20,000 spaces that were not at the end of a line. The regular expression used to trim Unicode whitespace backtracked through about 200 million character checks per render, an O(n squared) blowup, pinning web server CPU. The home page also served as the load balancer health check, so every server was pulled from rotation and the whole site went down. Diagnosis took 10 minutes, the fix 14, and rollout 10.

title: Telia backbone packet loss causes spike in Cloudflare 522 errors
trigger: Massive packet loss on the backbone of transit provider Telia Carrier (AS1299) began at 12:10 UTC, following a smaller intermittent episode on June 17.
impact: Cloudflare saw a large jump in HTTP 522 errors, meaning its edge could not reach customer origins, across many PoPs from 12:10 UTC until it shut its Telia ports at 12:30 UTC; full recovery time is not stated.
detection: Cloudflare's own systems detected and recorded the packet loss as it started.
fix: Cloudflare took down its ports with Telia so other transit providers carried the traffic, and planned to extend its automatic packet-loss detection and failover from small PoPs to all PoPs within two weeks while improving status page communication.
summary: On June 20, Cloudflare traffic relying on Telia Carrier's backbone suffered heavy packet loss, so edge servers frequently failed to connect to customer origin servers and returned 522 errors. Because BGP has no built-in sense of path loss, engineers had to manually shut the Telia ports at 12:30 UTC to shift traffic to other tier 1 providers. Cloudflare admitted it initially misjudged the scope as Europe-only, and committed to rolling out its automated loss-based reroute system, then active only at small sites, everywhere.

title: Misconfigured S3 ACL exposes database backup bucket
trigger: Two conflicting S3 bucket policies meant the bucket holding partial database backups was readable and writable by any authenticated AWS account that knew its name.
impact: Backups containing user accounts, bcrypt password hashes, API tokens and integration settings were exposed, users had to re-authenticate SSO and had passwords force-expired, but the investigation found no evidence of third-party access.
detection: An external security report arrived at 10:13 PDT on 12 June 2016 and was confirmed seven minutes later.
fix: Sentry revoked bucket credentials, rotated SSO provider secrets, moved to unguessable bucket names with correct ACLs and pre-encrypted backups, and planned MFA, encrypted tokens, OAuth integrations and a HackerOne bounty program.
summary: A researcher told Sentry that one of its S3 buckets had wrong permissions. The bucket stored partial database backups, and conflicting ACL policies let any logged-in AWS user read or modify it if they guessed the name. Sentry locked the bucket within minutes, rotated Google and GitHub SSO credentials, forced password resets, alerted integration partners such as Atlassian because JIRA plugin passwords were stored in plaintext, and began encrypting backups before upload. Two days later it confirmed no outside access had occurred.

title: Sydney storm voltage sag drains DRUPS and drops an AZ
trigger: A storm-related substation failure produced a long voltage sag, and breakers isolating the DRUPS units opened too slowly, so their stored energy drained into the grid before generators took over.
impact: A significant number of EC2 instances and EBS volumes in one Sydney Availability Zone lost power from 10:25 PM PDT; over 80% returned by 1:00 AM, nearly all by 8:00 AM, and under 0.01% of EBS volumes were unrecoverable.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Technicians manually re-engaged power at 11:46 PM PDT and engineers recovered hosts and shifted API traffic away, with follow-ups for faster breakers, a fix for a latent recovery bug, and more resilient launch APIs.
summary: A severe weather event cut a regional substation feeding several AWS Sydney facilities. In one, the utility fault was a sustained voltage sag rather than a clean loss, and slow breakers let DRUPS energy flow back to the grid, so instances lost both primary and backup power. Internal DNS errors lingered, a latent bug in instance management slowed recovery, launch and Auto Scaling calls failed until traffic moved, and a few EBS volumes were lost when both replicas' drives failed.

title: Config bug withdraws all GCE IP blocks from BGP
trigger: Removing an unused GCE IP block left two config files inconsistent, and the management software responded by dropping every GCE IP block from the new configuration.
impact: Inbound internet traffic to Compute Engine saw over 95% loss for 18 minutes until 19:27 PT, also breaking Cloud VPN and L3 network load balancers; Google offered service credits.
detection: Internal monitoring alerted on an asia-east1 VPN failure and rising latency, then dozens of alerts fired once traffic loss became visible.
fix: Engineers reverted recent network config changes and froze changes, and planned announcement comparisons, semantic config checks and monitoring for lost redundancy.
summary: Google engineers removed an unused IP block from Compute Engine's network configuration. A timing issue made two config files disagree, and a bug in the management software reacted by stripping all GCE IP blocks rather than falling back to the last good config. A canary flagged the result as unsafe, but a second bug stopped that verdict reaching the rollout system, so sites progressively stopped announcing GCE prefixes over BGP. Inbound traffic to VMs, VPNs and network load balancers failed for 18 minutes.

title: Database overload backs up Linux build queue for 17 hours
trigger: Rising demand pushed CircleCI's primary database into overload, with queued operations it could not catch up on; no single definitive trigger was identified.
impact: Linux builds were delayed or blocked for roughly 17 hours, the site was down for about an hour, all builds were cancelled at one point, and some builds were left in a broken state.
detection: Operations staff saw that usual capacity tools were not shrinking the backlog and escalated to engineering; customer reports after a premature all-clear prompted further work.
fix: The team rolled back recent changes, failed over the database primary, added capacity, force-promoted builds to runnable, fixed throttle logic, and planned a rebuilt queue model plus further database isolation.
summary: On October 14, 2015 CircleCI's Linux build queue stopped draining as the primary database became overloaded. Builds could not move to the runnable state, and scheduling throttles kept backing off even as conditions normalised, which slowed recovery. Engineers failed over the database, cancelled everything in the queue, and pushed builds through manually and then with batch tooling, leaving some builds inconsistent. An early all-clear proved premature. The company noted a similar load incident in July of that year.

title: DynamoDB metadata service overload cascades through US East
trigger: A short network disruption made some DynamoDB storage servers re-request their partition membership from the metadata service at the same moment.
impact: DynamoDB request errors in US East reached about 55% for several hours, and dependent services including SQS, EC2 Auto Scaling, CloudWatch metrics and Console sign-in degraded, with a small residual error rate lasting into the following Monday.
detection: Not stated for the initial spike; the lingering Monday error rate was recognized late, after customers opened support cases.
fix: Engineers paused metadata requests to stop the retry load, added metadata service capacity and let storage servers rejoin, then planned membership-size monitoring, longer processing allowances and splitting the metadata service into multiple instances.
summary: After a brief network blip, DynamoDB storage servers in US East asked the metadata service for their membership lists. Those lists had grown large as Global Secondary Index adoption added partitions, so replies exceeded the servers' time limits and the servers dropped out of service. Their retries overloaded the metadata service, causing even healthy servers to fail renewals. DynamoDB error rates hit about 55%, breaking SQS, Auto Scaling, CloudWatch and Console logins until capacity was added and requests resumed.

title: Lightning strikes cause Persistent Disk errors and data loss
trigger: Four consecutive lightning strikes on the local power grid briefly cut power to storage systems backing Persistent Disk in zone europe-west1-b.
impact: About 5% of Standard Persistent Disks in the zone saw at least one failed read or write over several days, and a tiny fraction of disk space (under one millionth of a percent) suffered permanent data loss.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; the first public notice reported customers seeing read errors.
fix: Engineers ran manual data recovery and told customers to restore from snapshots, with follow-ups to move to storage hardware more resilient to power loss and to add further durability schemes for Persistent Disk.
summary: Repeated lightning strikes near a Google Compute Engine data center in europe-west1-b caused short power interruptions to the storage layer. Power came back automatically, but recently written blocks held on storage vulnerable to repeated battery drain were not all safely committed. Standard Persistent Disks returned I/O errors and snapshot operations failed for days, and a very small amount of data was lost for good. SSD disks, Local SSDs and snapshots were not affected, and Google urged multi-zone designs.

title: Expired vSphere password lets OS X build VMs leak for days
trigger: vSphere credentials were rotated on 31 July under a 90-day password policy but the vsphere-janitor config was not updated, so finished build VMs were never deleted.
impact: OS X builds on travis-ci.com and .org were queued, paused and run at reduced capacity from 4 August 17:45 UTC until resolution on 7 August, with over 6,000 VMs on a cluster expecting about 200 peak.
detection: Operators noticed unusually high build re-queue rates and power-on errors in VM creation logs; alerts stayed silent because the janitor kept reporting its last known VM count.
fix: The team updated janitor credentials, ran an aggressive cleanup that deleted 6,326 leaked VMs, replaced vSphere CPU reservations with VM sizing, load tested, and planned better VM lifecycle metrics.
summary: Travis CI runs OS X builds as VMs on a vSphere cluster hosted at MacStadium, and a vsphere-janitor service deletes finished VMs. After a scheduled password rotation, the janitor could no longer authenticate and silently stopped cleaning up, while its metric froze at a normal-looking value. Over four days thousands of VMs leaked until new builds failed to power on. Cleanup exposed a second problem: CPU reservation settings stopped the cluster from booting its configured maximum of VMs under backlog load.

title: Postgres wraparound autovacuum plus DROP TRIGGER locks Manta shard
trigger: A PostgreSQL autovacuum launched to prevent transaction ID wraparound held a shared lock on one Manta metadata shard while a DROP TRIGGER statement queued for an exclusive lock, blocking every later query on the table.
impact: From about 10:30 to 20:45 UTC the Manta object store returned 500 errors on roughly 19 to 23 percent of requests, peaking near 27 percent, across PUT, GET and DELETE for objects and directories.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: After a restart and hours of speeding up the vacuum failed to hold, engineers raised the threshold that triggers wraparound autovacuum, then planned to stop dropping and recreating the trigger, run manual VACUUM FREEZE and monitor vacuum statistics.
summary: Manta keeps object metadata in sharded PostgreSQL clusters managed by Manatee. On one shard, a wraparound-prevention autovacuum that does not back off under contention held a shared lock for hours. A component reconnecting to the database issued DROP TRIGGER, which waited for an exclusive lock, and PostgreSQL then queued all new shared-lock reads and writes behind it. API requests timed out with 500 errors for about ten hours until Joyent tuned the autovacuum freeze threshold to stop the operation.

title: Postgres transaction ID wraparound protection halts Sentry writes
trigger: Autovacuum did not keep pace on the write-heavy primary database, so Postgres hit its transaction ID (XID) wraparound safeguard and refused writes.
impact: Hosted Sentry was unavailable for much of a business day in the US, ran read-only from replicas, and the queued event backlog was discarded.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: After roughly three hours of autovacuum left one huge event-mapping table unfinished, the team truncated it and service returned in about five minutes; follow-ups included more memory and vacuum workers, retuned autovacuum settings, and plans to split relations across databases.
summary: Sentry's main Postgres database, with very large and heavily written tables, reached the transaction ID wraparound limit, where Postgres stops accepting commands to avoid reusing XIDs. The site ran read-only off replicas while the team let in-progress autovacuums finish on newly provisioned hardware, and dropped the event backlog to protect Redis buffers. One very large table that maps events to rollups still blocked recovery, so it was truncated. Settings such as autovacuum_freeze_max_age and vacuum delays were changed afterward.

title: EVE Online down 699 minutes as cluster nodes hang on startup
trigger: After deploying a follow-up patch to Aegis Sovereignty, writing to the sovereignty campaign logging channel during startup degraded Tranquility nodes so badly that dozens stalled at stage -1 or dropped out of the cluster.
impact: EVE Online's Tranquility server was unavailable to players for 699 minutes on July 15, 2015, its longest downtime in years.
detection: Startup monitoring showed 12 of roughly 250 nodes stuck shortly after the first start attempt at 11.46, with later attempts leaving 41 to 53 nodes stuck.
fix: After hours of experiments with data removal and hotfixes, Hotfix #5 stripped all logging from the campaign system, allowing a clean start and reopening at 22.41; work continued on why that log channel only misbehaves on Tranquility.
summary: A routine patch for EVE Online's new sovereignty system left the Tranquility cluster unable to finish its staged startup, with dozens of its roughly 250 nodes hanging before the ready stage. Restarts, swapping the Polaris coordinator node and disabling an IBM USB Remote NDIS interface did nothing. Emptying sovereignty campaign tables let it boot, pointing at campaign loading. Live Python console experiments then showed that bursts of messages on the campaign log channel alone stalled nodes until they fell out of the cluster, though test servers never reproduced it.

title: GitHub hook surge overwhelms CircleCI build queue database
trigger: GitHub push hooks paused and then resumed at several times normal peak volume during US daytime, flooding the database-backed build queue with inserts.
impact: The build queue nearly stopped, dequeuing about one build per minute instead of many per second, so builds across the platform were delayed or cancelled until stuck work was cleared the next day.
detection: Engineers saw the familiar pattern of missing GitHub hooks, then a growing queue while build throughput stayed far below capacity.
fix: After throttling and a failed database failover, the team live-patched slow queries, drained the queues with scripts and moved to larger database hardware, with unspecified architectural and capacity work to follow.
summary: CircleCI's build queue lived in its main shared database. When GitHub hooks came back in a burst far above normal peak, rapid build inserts created heavy write contention and some queries with poor plans degraded as the queue grew, taking the database from healthy to unresponsive in about two minutes. Throttling at the load balancer briefly made the site unreachable, and promoting a secondary failed under the same load. Recovery required live REPL patches, queue draining and new database hardware.

title: StackEgg April Fools game exhausts HAProxy session limit
trigger: Turning on the StackEgg game for all logged-in users added an extra AJAX request per page, and with 15-second HTTP Keep-Alive this pushed concurrent sessions past the HAProxy cap of 40,000.
impact: Stack Overflow had a 6-minute public outage plus a period of general slowness across the network.
detection: Site slowness was observed at 11:32 UTC, SREs spotted load balancer traffic bouncing at 11:55, and Pingdom later reported Stack Overflow offline.
fix: The team raised the HAProxy session limit via Puppet, embedded game data in pages and leaned on websockets, briefly disabled StackEgg, and the next day cut Keep-Alive from 15s to 5s.
summary: Stack Exchange's StackEgg April Fools game generated up to 3,444 extra requests per second. Because HAProxy kept connections open for 15 seconds, this implied around 51,660 more concurrent sessions, against a frontend cap of 40,000. New TCP connections queued and load oscillated, causing slowness and a 6-minute Stack Overflow outage. Engineers raised the cap, reduced the game's requests, and the following morning shortened Keep-Alive, dropping sessions from about 59,500 to roughly 19,000.

title: DNS provider migration causes NXDOMAIN answers and stale cache records
trigger: Moving the algolia.io zone from Route 53 to NSOne exposed a bug in a custom NSOne routing module that returned NXDOMAIN for some EDNS-capable resolvers.
impact: Search was down for a subset of customers for a total of about 5 hours, with failed DNS resolution of their APPID hostnames.
detection: Customers began reporting failed DNS lookups once NSOne traffic reached roughly 1,000 queries per second.
fix: Algolia rolled back to Route 53, then returned to NSOne after the vendor fixed the bug, moved affected customers to algolia.net or created new records to sidestep stale caches, and committed to stronger DNS rollback planning.
summary: During a cutover of algolia.io from Amazon Route 53 to NSOne, a custom filter module built for Algolia returned NXDOMAIN to some EDNS resolvers, so certain customers' search endpoints stopped resolving. Rolling back made things worse for others: the module had cached rewritten names with a one-day TTL that did not exist in Route 53, and AAAA lookups were mis-translated because no IPv6 records existed. Algolia re-migrated after NSOne's fix, pointed users at algolia.net or fresh records, and noted the need for a tested DNS rollback path.

title: Azure Storage config pushed everywhere at once hits Blob infinite loop
trigger: A storage performance config change, tested for weeks on some Table front ends, was rolled to most production regions at once and exposed a bug that put Blob front ends into an infinite loop.
impact: From 00:51 UTC on 19 November 2014, Blob, Table and Queue customers in 12 regions saw timeouts and connection failures until about 11:45 UTC, with dependent services such as VMs, Websites, Service Bus and SQL also affected and a subset hit until 22 November.
detection: The bug surfaced during the rollout after the change had already reached many regions; the status dashboard itself was impaired for about three hours.
fix: The change was reverted and storage front ends were restarted, and Microsoft committed to enforcing incremental batch deployment in tooling, fixing the loop bug and hardening the Service Health Dashboard.
summary: Azure Storage shipped a config change to cut CPU on Table front ends. Contrary to standard practice it went to nearly all regions in a short window rather than in batches, and it triggered an infinite loop in Blob front ends so they stopped taking traffic. Reverting the config did not help until front ends were restarted. Storage outages cascaded to Virtual Machines, which lost RDP and SSH access, plus Websites, Service Bus, HDInsight and others, while the status dashboard was also down.

title: Shellshock on stale server exposes AWS keys and user emails
trigger: An unpatched, unused prototype EC2 machine running since before 2012 was breached via Shellshock, and it held BrowserStack's AWS API access and secret keys.
impact: The attacker created an IAM user, mounted a backup disk holding the database password, partially copied a table of emails, hashed passwords and last tested URLs, and used SES to email roughly 5,000 users (under 1%) false claims of a shutdown.
detection: The attacker's table copy locked the database table, which fired monitoring alerts; engineers then found an unknown IP in the logs and blocked it.
fix: BrowserStack took the service down, revoked and regenerated all AWS keys and passwords, audited SSH, web and CloudTrail logs, moved to encrypted backups, added alerts on AWS actions, and suggested users change their passwords.
summary: On 9 November 2014 an attacker exploited Shellshock on a forgotten BrowserStack prototype server that still stored AWS access keys. With those keys they made an IAM user, launched an instance, mounted a backup containing the database password, whitelisted their IP and began copying user records with bcrypt-hashed passwords. A table lock triggered alerts and the IP was blocked, but SES credentials were used to email about 5,000 users. BrowserStack rotated all AWS keys and passwords and recommended users change their passwords.

title: Wrong server reboot stalls Allegro's async task processing
trigger: At 4:19 AM an operator rebooted the wrong side of a blade server in the active data center that hosted Gearman, Redis and the task-fetching daemons, which lost their settings and did not restart cleanly.
impact: Multi-offer cart purchases and bulk offer editing stopped working, part of the daily newsletter and some admin panels failed, and task processing was delayed until about 7:00 PM on 24 October, with a backlog of several million tasks.
detection: Poor monitoring meant the problem went unnoticed until 8:40 AM, more than four hours after the restart.
fix: SRE roughly doubled processing throughput, cancelled a release and offer alerts, dropped unprocessable tasks and reset the task counter to the 23 October start; follow-ups include monitoring the subsystem, supervised restarts and removing the single point of failure.
summary: Allegro's asynchronous task system, built on Gearman, Redis and Oracle, went down when someone rebooted the wrong blade server half. After restart the fetching daemons inexplicably began pulling tasks dating back to 11 September 2014, flooding the queue with several million items that would have needed about 84 hours to process. Engineers boosted throughput, pruned tasks such as stale cart purchases and moved the task counter forward, ending delays the next evening. The suspected counter bug was never confirmed.

title: Bad deploys trigger mass reconnects that overwhelm Slack databases
trigger: An automation fault during routine maintenance pushed corrupted code to web servers and job queue workers, and a day later a buggy build of the message servers made for the SSLv3/POODLE change caused a heavily used server to crash.
impact: All users were locked out for 14 minutes and 13% then had poor or no service for up to two hours, with 5% disconnected that long; a second incident the next day affected a subset of users for about an hour.
detection: The bad deploy was spotted internally right away; detection of the second incident is not stated.
fix: The bad code was fixed within 14 minutes and the affected database cluster recovered; Slack added database capacity and optimized how clients reconnect.
summary: Two separate October 2014 incidents disconnected large groups of Slack users, and both were made worse by reconnection surges. Corrupted code from a maintenance automation fault knocked 13% of users offline, and their simultaneous reconnects exhausted database capacity, so the failures cascaded. The next day, a message server build for disabling SSLv3 contained a crash bug, and a client change that cleared caches and reloaded full history added more database load during the reconnect wave.

title: Misleading iptables comment leads to change that blocks load balancers
trigger: A Puppet-managed iptables change on the HAProxy load balancers, prompted by an inaccurate note in the rules file, blocked SYN/ACK replies from the IIS web servers.
impact: All Stack Exchange Q&A sites and Careers were down for about 6 minutes, from 19:26 to 19:32 UTC.
detection: The on-call pager fired and staff noticed within a minute of the primary load balancer applying the change.
fix: The commit was reverted and Puppet reapplied rules to both load balancers; follow-ups were cleaning up comments, enabling changes to hit the inactive balancer first, and moving rules to the Puppet firewall module.
summary: Stack Exchange engineers wanted web servers to reach internal API endpoints directly instead of through ASA firewalls. An inaccurate note in the HAProxy load balancers' iptables rules prompted a change that dropped the SYN/ACK return traffic from IIS web servers, so HAProxy could not complete connections. The rule was pushed via Git and applied by Puppet about 25 minutes later, taking every Stack Exchange site offline. A revert propagated through TeamCity and Puppet within six minutes.

title: Metadata database overload and cache failure take down iPlayer
trigger: Load on the database behind the programme metadata service spiked sharply on Saturday morning for reasons not yet isolated, and almost simultaneously one pool in the caching layer in front of BBC Online failed.
impact: BBC iPlayer, iPlayer Radio and media playback across bbc.co.uk failed over the weekend, the BBC homepage repeatedly fell back to an emergency version, and iPlayer was effectively unusable through Saturday afternoon and evening and down on some devices until a Monday restoration.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The team first stabilized the caching layer, then did major remedial work on the metadata system and ran in a degraded state until a full restore on Monday morning; forensics on root causes were still ongoing.
summary: Over a July weekend BBC iPlayer and other bbc.co.uk video and audio broke when the metadata system feeding programme and clip data, 58 application servers and 10 database servers across two hot-hot data centres, saw database load surge and requests fail. Older apps that used metadata without caching broke first. At nearly the same time a cache pool fronting iPlayer and the homepage failed repeatedly, forcing the simplified emergency homepage. The BBC had not yet pinned down the source of the extra database load or the cache fault.

title: GitLab.com reboot leads to services starting on the wrong filesystem
trigger: An I/O brownout on the primary server caused its hardware watchdog to force a reboot, after which neither node of the DRBD pair was primary and the production filesystem was not mounted.
impact: GitLab.com was down for most of the night, roughly 01:00 to 09:29 CEST on July 8, with background jobs not processing until later and some repositories corrupted.
detection: Pingdom and PagerDuty raised alerts at about 01:13 CEST, but the pages were missed because of phone and notification settings, and user reports arrived by email and Twitter.
fix: Engineers stopped the database, rsynced the data directory and restarted unicorn, Sidekiq and Redis on the production filesystem; follow-ups changed the failover script to restart services and added a mountpoint check so services refuse to start without the production volume.
summary: GitLab.com ran on two servers replicated with DRBD. Disk lockup on the primary triggered an HP watchdog hard reset, leaving both nodes secondary. Responders ran gitlab-ctl start, which brought up PostgreSQL and other services against empty staging data on the root filesystem, so the app returned 502 errors and the database looked like 6 MB. Promoting the node mounted production data underneath processes that still held old files, prolonging the confusion for hours. Missed PagerDuty pages also delayed the response.

title: Host network maintenance partitions cluster, delaying exceptions
trigger: Planned hosting provider maintenance to move servers onto new network infrastructure left Yeller's internal network split into several partitions.
impact: For roughly 18 to 19 hours, 42 exceptions were delayed by up to 7 hours and users could not sign up, change passwords or billing, or invite teammates, though the site stayed readable.
detection: Alerting paged the operator within seconds of the partition, while he was already watching the maintenance.
fix: A rolling restart of the whole cluster cleared the partition and timed-out writes were reprocessed by hand; follow-ups include a hosted status page, scheduled outage updates, better retry logic, and keeping a broken node for forensics.
summary: After the hosting provider moved Yeller's servers to new network gear, the cluster ended up partitioned. Riak writes for some exceptions timed out and needed manual replay, and the Datomic store for user and billing data lost write capacity, blocking account changes. The operator assumed the fault was the provider's and waited about 17 hours before a suggested rolling restart fixed it, possibly by clearing cached routes. Because every node was restarted, the root cause could not be found.

title: Supermarket launch overloads undersized app servers behind ELB
trigger: About two hours after Supermarket replaced the old community site, real traffic overwhelmed three single-core m3.medium app servers whose launch had skipped load planning.
impact: supermarket.getchef.com, community.opscode.com, cookbooks.opscode.com and api.berkshelf.com became slow or intermittently unresponsive, breaking cookbook browsing, uploads and downloads, the Supermarket API and Berkshelf v3.x dependency solving.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Chef moved production to five m3.xlarge instances, and corrective actions include pointing Berkshelf API servers at the new /universe endpoint, tuning unicorn workers, non-blocking metrics on downloads and alerts when nodes leave the ELB.
summary: Chef's new Supermarket cookbook site, a Rails app under unicorn behind nginx and an AWS Elastic Load Balancer, became sluggish and intermittently unreachable soon after replacing the old community site. The three m3.medium instances lacked CPU for the load, and ELB health check timeouts were so tight that slow nodes were ejected, pushing more traffic onto the rest until they timed out too. Cookbook downloads and Berkshelf dependency resolution failed. Chef held its postmortem meeting publicly and scaled to larger instances.

title: Botched Redis credential roll leaves Heroku dynos unmanageable
trigger: During scheduled maintenance, faulty runbook instructions led operators to change credentials on all four Redis servers used by the dyno manager at once, and a rolling restart of runtime agents then cut them off from the dyno manager.
impact: From 18:14 to 19:43 UTC the US API was locked so no customer could deploy and US customers could not scale, stop or restart dynos, and H99 errors hit 3.4% of the apps that were serving HTTP traffic between 17:00 and 21:00 UTC, with PX dynos affected longer.
detection: Elevated error rates across the platform were posted at 18:06 UTC, followed by dynos failing to start.
fix: Two Redis servers were reverted to the old credentials so the dyno manager could reach every runtime, and fixes landed for an exception-handling bug and PX fleet config; Heroku corrected the runbook, began reviewing all operational docs and improved rollback plans and team communication.
summary: Heroku planned a maintenance window to rotate credentials on the four Redis servers that link its dyno manager to runtime agents. The procedure should go one server at a time, but incorrect documentation had all four changed together. Restarting runtime agents then severed their status reporting, so instances were flagged lost and the dyno manager could not start, restart or replace crashed dynos, causing H99 routing errors. Heroku locked its US API for about 90 minutes while reverting credentials and patching bugs surfaced by the incident.

title: SimpleDB down two hours after lock service handshake timeouts
trigger: Power was lost to servers in one data center, and de-registering the many failed storage nodes overloaded the internal lock service so healthy nodes timed out on handshakes and dropped out of the cluster.
impact: SimpleDB in US East rejected essentially all API calls with HTTP 500 errors from 9:16 PM to 11:16 PM PDT, apart from some eventually consistent reads, and CreateDomain and DeleteDomain stayed error-prone until 1:30 AM.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers manually raised the handshake timeout and restarted some metadata nodes so storage nodes could be re-authorized, then throttled CreateDomain and DeleteDomain; follow-ups were a longer timeout and having nodes retry later rather than leave the cluster.
summary: Amazon SimpleDB in the US East Region went dark after a power loss took several storage nodes down simultaneously in one data center. The rapid de-registration spiked load on the replicated lock service, so healthy storage and metadata nodes missed a too-short handshake timeout and removed themselves from the cluster. Storage nodes need metadata nodes to approve their return, but those were down too, leaving the API returning 500 errors for two hours. Recovery required manual timeout increases and metadata node restarts.

title: Mistyped command reboots every server in Joyent us-east-1
trigger: An operator upgrading new capacity mistyped a remote reboot command, and the tool, lacking input validation, rebooted all servers in the us-east-1 data center at once.
impact: Customer instances were down between 20 and 149 minutes, with 80 percent recovered in 32 minutes or less and more than 90 percent within 59, and the us-east-1 API was unavailable for 1 hour 17 minutes until 21:30Z.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers lifted throttles on the TFTP boot service, re-rebooted nodes hit by a legacy NIC DHCP bug and manually recovered stateful control plane services, then committed to strict validation in operator tooling and unattended control plane recovery.
summary: At 20:13 UTC an operator using SmartDataCenter's remote execution tooling to reboot a handful of new servers accidentally targeted the whole us-east-1 data center, rebooting every compute node and the control plane together. Simultaneous PXE boots overloaded the throttled DHCP/TFTP boot service, some older machines failed to get DHCP leases because of a network driver bug, and stateful control plane components needed hand recovery. Most instances returned within about 30 minutes; the API took 77 minutes.

title: Hijacked repo account exposes offsite backup keys and user database
trigger: An intruder got into an employee's account on the hosted source code repository, which held the credentials for Bitly's offsite database backup storage, and pulled data from those backups.
impact: A static backup of the user database was taken, exposing salted password hashes (MD5 for older accounts, BCrypt with HMAC for those active after January 8th, 2014) plus linked Facebook and Twitter credentials, while production systems and Bitlinks were untouched.
detection: Another technology company's security team alerted Bitly on May 8, and Bitly then spotted unusual outbound traffic from its offsite backup storage that it had not initiated.
fix: Bitly invalidated all Facebook and Twitter credentials, rotated backup storage credentials, SSL certificates and deploy credentials, forced two-factor authentication on the code host and every third-party service, and sped up two-factor login for bitly.com.
summary: In May 2014 Bitly found that an attacker had used a compromised employee account on its hosted source code repository to obtain credentials for offsite database backup storage, then downloaded a backup of the user database. Production servers were not breached. Exposed data included salted password hashes and connected Facebook and Twitter tokens, which Bitly invalidated. The company rotated storage keys, SSL certificates and deploy credentials, mandated two-factor authentication on all third-party services, added storage logging, and encrypted sensitive credentials with GPG.

title: 20Gbps DDoS takes Basecamp offline
trigger: Attackers launched a mixed SYN flood, DNS reflection, ICMP flood and NTP amplification attack exceeding 20Gbps against Basecamp's network.
impact: Basecamp and its sibling services were fully down for 45 minutes and flaky or slow for the rest of the attack from 8:32 to about 10:12 central time, and some users could not connect until 11:08 because other providers quarantined Basecamp's network; no data was compromised.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; the team notes a 20-minute gap between learning of the attack and telling customers.
fix: Traffic was routed through a single provider that filtered out the bogus packets; follow-ups include evaluating DDoS mitigation vendors, a five-minute target for public notice, and upgraded, load-tested status site servers.
summary: Basecamp suffered a distributed denial-of-service attack lasting one hour and forty minutes that combined SYN floods, DNS reflection, ICMP floods and NTP amplification at more than 20Gbps. The apps were completely unreachable for 45 minutes and intermittent otherwise, and upstream providers placed the network in quarantine, delaying full access until 11:08. Mitigation came from funnelling traffic through one provider to scrub it. The company also found its off-site status page buckled under record traffic and that customer notification took 20 minutes.

title: Varnish VCL restart sends npm registry traffic to the wrong backend
trigger: A simplification of the Varnish VCL on Fastly set req.backend in vcl_fetch and then called restart, which reset the backend to Manta for every request.
impact: Package metadata requests meant for CouchDB went to Manta and returned 403 Forbidden, and uncached errors caused a thundering herd; duration and user counts are not stated.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The team found the cause with Fastly support, and committed to always setting req.backend explicitly in vcl_recv and staging VCL changes on a separate Varnish instance.
summary: The npm registry served tarballs from Joyent Manta and package metadata from CouchDB behind Fastly's Varnish CDN. A VCL cleanup chose the backend in vcl_fetch and then used restart, but a restart resets req.backend to the first listed backend, Manta. Requests for package names like /pkgname therefore hit Manta, which answered 403 Forbidden. Since Fastly did not cache error responses, the flood of misses created a thundering herd that took time to calm down.

title: Faulty generated config breaks Gmail, Calendar and Docs
trigger: A bug in an internal configuration generator produced a bad configuration at 10:55 a.m. PST that rolled out to live services over about 15 minutes.
impact: Most users could not reach logged-in services such as Gmail, Google+, Calendar and Documents for about 25 minutes, and about 10% of users were affected for up to 30 minutes longer.
detection: Internal monitoring alerted the Site Reliability Team at 11:02 a.m. PST.
fix: The generator produced and pushed a correct configuration starting at 11:14 a.m., live everywhere by 11:30, and Google planned to fix and audit config generators, validate configs and add targeted monitoring.
summary: An internal Google system that generates configuration for other services hit a bug and emitted a wrong configuration, which spread to production within about 15 minutes. The bad config caused services to ignore users' requests for their own data, so Gmail, Google+, Calendar and Docs returned errors to most logged-in users for around 25 minutes. The generator later produced a correct config on its own, which fully propagated by 11:30 a.m. Follow-ups include input validation for configs.

title: Utility fault and generator failures black out an SA-EAST-1 AZ
trigger: A fault at the local utility substation cut power to one SA-EAST-1 Availability Zone at 10:05PM PST, and during failover one generator's breaker opened and a second generator failed mechanically, overloading and tripping the rest.
impact: Instances in the affected Availability Zone lost power, and instances in both SA-EAST-1 AZs saw network connectivity degraded for 20 minutes in total; total outage duration is not stated.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The facilities team bypassed a malfunctioning automated generator control system to bring generators up manually, the misconfigured network device was removed from service, and AWS committed to hardening the AZ against similar power failures.
summary: Utility power to an AWS Availability Zone in São Paulo failed and the load moved to backup generators, but a breaker opened on one and another broke down, leaving too few to carry the facility. Restoration was slowed because the automated system that aggregates generator output was not working, forcing manual startup. During network recovery a technician brought up a device with a bad configuration that advertised an invalid route, degrading Internet connectivity for both SA-EAST-1 zones.

title: MongoHQ breach exposes CircleCI database of keys and tokens
trigger: CircleCI's hosted database at provider MongoHQ was accessed by an IP linked to an intrusion at MongoHQ late on October 27 UTC.
impact: The database held customer SSH keys, GitHub OAuth tokens, Heroku API tokens, AWS IAM keys and API tokens stored in env vars, all of which had to be treated as exposed, though CircleCI saw no evidence they were abused.
detection: CircleCI saw an unexpected IAM key deletion on October 28, MongoHQ announced its breach on October 29, and at 5:03pm that day MongoHQ confirmed CircleCI's database had been accessed.
fix: CircleCI shut down the site and all builds, had GitHub revoke every CircleCI OAuth token and SSH key, had Heroku and Amazon revoke API tokens and IAM keys, cleared caches and cycled its own keys, and told customers to secure anything reachable with credentials stored in CircleCI.
summary: In October 2013 attackers who breached database host MongoHQ reached CircleCI's database, which stored customer SSH keys, GitHub OAuth tokens, Heroku API tokens and AWS IAM keys. Once MongoHQ confirmed the access, CircleCI took its website and builds offline and worked with GitHub, Heroku and Amazon to revoke all affected OAuth tokens, SSH deploy and user keys, API tokens and IAM keys within hours. Customers were told to secure systems reachable via those credentials, verify git SHA1s, and check Heroku config vars.

title: Cassandra cluster crash backs up shared queues, stalls alerting
trigger: Most nodes of the 36-node Cassandra cluster holding time series data ran out of memory after days of leaking and crashed almost simultaneously around 9:45 AM ET.
impact: Charts showed a data gap from 9:45 AM to 1:30 PM on October 23 and partial data until the historical restore finished at 9 AM on October 26, alerting was delayed about an hour, and some false alerts fired afterwards.
detection: Around 8:45 AM the team found many Cassandra nodes had been leaking memory for days, a trend its own Stackdriver monitoring had captured.
fix: Engineers decoupled other consumers from the stuck Cassandra queue, built a new 36-node cluster on upgraded Cassandra and Java, restored history from the archive, and planned stronger isolation between pipelines in the queueing layer.
summary: Stackdriver's gateways publish incoming metrics to a message broker feeding archiving, Cassandra indexing and alerting consumers. When the Cassandra cluster crashed from memory exhaustion, its queue grew, and the gateways' overload protection spilled all data to disk, starving healthy pipelines, including alerting. Two full cluster restarts failed to converge. Engineers rerouted data to the other subsystems around 11 AM, triggering some bad alerts from hour-old data, then stood up a replacement cluster and backfilled from S3 archives with no data lost.

title: Data update triggers double free, crashing all ad servers
trigger: A database update deleting a rarely changed in-memory object hit an old double-free bug in the impression bus, and because the crash only happened after a deferred memory-reclamation delay it passed validation and shipped to every server.
impact: All roughly 900 impbus servers worldwide crashed together at 17:54 UTC, stopping all ad serving; direct traffic was fully restored by 20:00 UTC and remaining supply over the next hour or so, about two and a half hours in total.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; two engineering teams were working the outage within three minutes.
fix: AMS1 was restored from a fresh, tested data snapshot and a fixed impbus build was rolled out as a rolling deploy after a global deploy failed; follow-ups hold data changes past the deferred-deletion window and add a second validation tier under production traffic.
summary: AppNexus lost all ad serving when every instance of its impression bus (impbus), the auction and ad delivery tier, crashed within moments. A data change removing a rarely edited object hit a latent double-free in code using time-based memory reclamation. The Validation Engines approved the change because the crash fired only after the delayed free executed. Recovery used fresh data snapshots per data center plus a patched binary, slowed further when the deployment system could not handle a simultaneous push to all six data centers.

title: Redis billing balance loss triggers repeated customer card charges
trigger: Billing Redis replicas lost contact with the master and all requested full resyncs at once, and a restart of the overloaded master loaded a wrong config that wiped all balances.
impact: About 1.4% of customers with auto-recharge were charged repeatedly or suspended, and billing was offline for much of July 18-19, 2013.
detection: Monitoring alerted on the Redis cluster failure at 2:42 AM PDT and on a billing anomaly at 3:28 AM PDT.
fix: Billing was shut off, balances were rebuilt from the separate double-entry relational database and erroneous charges refunded; follow-ups disabled master restarts in favor of replica promotion and added fail-safes against charging on missing balances.
summary: Twilio's billing system kept in-flight account balances in a Redis cluster. After a network blip, replicas simultaneously requested full resync and overloaded the master. Engineers restarted it on a misdiagnosis, and it came up with a bad configuration, tried to recover from a nonexistent AOF file, lost all balance data, and became a read-only replica of itself. Zero balances made auto-recharge bill customer cards again and again, and some accounts were suspended. Affected customers were refunded and credited.

title: Client retries and new dependency overload Popcount, hitting Europe
trigger: A Discovery feature rollout added an unintended dependency from the Bartender service to an underprovisioned Popcount, while legacy desktop clients retried Popcount on every timeout without backoff.
impact: A large share of European users had slow playback and some could not log in for a few hours on a busy Saturday night.
detection: Engineers chatting on IRC noticed Popcount was unhealthy again.
fix: A hotfix removed the Bartender dependency, Accesspoints were hard-reset and firewalled off so clients backed off, and follow-ups added Discovery data caching with a TTL, fixed client retry logic, and rate-limited Accesspoint logging.
summary: Spotify's Popcount service, which stores subscriber lists for over a billion playlists, became slow after the Discovery rollout added load from Bartender. Desktop clients retried without backoff, requests piled up on the Accesspoints that clients connect to, and verbose error logging saturated their disk I/O. The cascade caused high playback latency and login failures across Europe. Engineers firewalled the Accesspoints so client exponential backoff could relieve them, then reopened traffic. A similar but smaller Popcount incident had occurred two months earlier.

title: Shared peering point takes out two AWS regions, halting notifications
trigger: A degraded network peering point in Northern California cut connectivity for the two AWS regions PagerDuty treated as independent datacenters.
impact: Notification dispatch was fully stopped for 18 minutes (8:35 to 8:53 am Pacific) after a period of higher latency and errors, while the events API kept accepting events.
detection: The on-call engineer was paged at 8:11 am about a failing notification dispatch node, and monitoring flagged multi-provider notification failures at 8:18 am.
fix: The dispatch cluster regained quorum once latency eased and drained queued notifications; follow-ups included better logging, auto-restart of coordinator processes, an inter-host connectivity dashboard, Cassandra and ZooKeeper training, and evaluating a move off one AWS region.
summary: PagerDuty ran across three datacenters (two AWS regions plus Linode) and was built to survive losing one. Both AWS regions, however, relied on the same Northern California peering point, and when it degraded, high inter-node latency kept the notification dispatch system from forming a quorum. Alerts slowed and then stopped entirely for 18 minutes while API intake continued. A misconfigured coordinator service slowed recovery, and many coordinator processes had to be restarted by hand.

title: Filesystem corruption on git.kde.org propagates to all anongit mirrors
trigger: After a host reboot for security updates, the git.kde.org VM came up with ext4 corruption, including a corrupt projects file listing its repositories.
impact: git.kde.org went down and every anongit mirror deleted or corrupted its copies of the roughly 1500 KDE repositories, leaving one newly built server as the only intact copy.
detection: The VMs showed file system corruption immediately on restart, and checks of the anongit mirrors then found them corrupted or missing repositories.
fix: KDE restored git.kde.org from the one clean server after git fsck checks, rebuilt Gitolite on version 3, added a 1% change guard on the projects file, and planned delayed syncs, ZFS snapshots and more fsck runs.
summary: When the git.kde.org VM rebooted after host security patching, ext4 corruption damaged its projects list. The mirroring design trusted the main server, so each anongit removed repositories missing from the corrupt list and some re-cloned corrupted repos, since git mirror clones copy objects without validation and still exit with code zero. Only a new projects.kde.org server, whose sync happened to time out during the reboot, kept clean copies of all 1500 repositories. KDE re-provisioned from it and added safeguards against mass deletions.

title: MySQL ORDER BY bug silently diverges Kickstarter replicas
trigger: A later unsafe query switched MIXED-mode replication to row-based events, which collided with backer sequence rows that had quietly diverged between master and replicas.
impact: All MySQL read replicas, which serve most Kickstarter traffic, stopped applying updates with duplicate-key error 1062 on the backings table; the post gives no duration or user numbers and notes the problem then recurred.
detection: Engineers noticed the replicas had stopped updating, and SHOW SLAVE STATUS reported the duplicate entry error.
fix: The team kept the site stable, limited the effect of stale replicas and recovered, but the post does not describe the specific remediation beyond tracing the cause to a MySQL bug.
summary: Kickstarter used Amazon RDS MySQL with the default MIXED replication mode. A background job numbered backers per project with a user variable and an ORDER BY, replicated as a statement.
