Hung transactions committed out of order, and a MySQL bug that sometimes ignores ORDER BY meant master and replicas assigned different sequence numbers. The divergence sat unnoticed for weeks until an unsafe query forced row-based replication, which then hit unique-key conflicts and halted replication on every replica at once.

title: Flowspec rule crashes Cloudflare's Juniper edge routers worldwide
trigger: While fighting a DDoS attack on a customer's DNS, an operator pushed a Flowspec rule to drop port 53 packets sized around 99,971 to 99,985 bytes, larger than any packet the network could carry.
impact: Every Cloudflare service and customer site went offline across 23 data centers in 14 countries for about an hour, from 09:47 to 10:49 UTC, with users seeing DNS errors and no route to host.
detection: Internal and external network monitoring alerted the ops and network teams immediately.
fix: The rule was removed and staff hard-rebooted routers that could not be reached remotely, and Cloudflare planned to work with Juniper, test Flowspec filters more, scope rules to needed sites, and issue SLA credits.
summary: Cloudflare used Flowspec over BGP to distribute a packet filter targeting an attack on a customer's DNS servers. The rule matched impossible packet sizes, yet when the Juniper routers at the edge received it they exhausted RAM and crashed, dropping the whole Anycast network. Sites behind Cloudflare returned DNS errors and pings failed with no route to host. Automatic reboots did not recover every router and management ports were unreachable, so data center staff power-cycled devices by hand. Some sites briefly failed again when traffic returned.

title: Expired SSL certificates break HTTPS to Azure Storage worldwide
trigger: The shared wildcard certificates for blob, queue and table storage expired between 12:29 and 12:32 PM PST because the release carrying the renewed certs was never flagged as certificate-critical and got delayed.
impact: HTTPS requests to Windows Azure Storage failed in all regions from 12:29 PM PST until most customers were restored at 22:45 PST, with the dashboard green at 00:09 the next day; HTTP access kept working and affected customers got 25% service credits.
detection: Normal monitoring caught the incident at 12:44 PM PST.
fix: A tested procedure updated the certificate on each storage node region by region, followed by a full storage service rollout; Microsoft will monitor certificates on production endpoints, treat any cert within 3 months of expiry as an incident and partition certificates across regions.
summary: Windows Azure Storage lost HTTPS globally when the *.blob, *.queue and *.table.core.windows.net certificates expired within minutes of each other. The storage team had updated them in the Secret Store in January, which silenced further expiry alerts, but the build containing them was not marked as a certificate update and slipped behind higher-priority releases. Fixing nodes was complicated by the Fabric Controller reverting them to goal state, so the manual fix took hours to validate before US West and then all regions recovered.

title: Maintenance job deletes ELB state data on Christmas Eve
trigger: A developer with standing production access accidentally ran a maintenance process against live Elastic Load Balancing state data, logically removing part of it.
impact: Up to 6.8% of running ELB load balancers in US East were misconfigured and served errors or degraded performance, while others could not be scaled or changed, from 12:24 PM PST on December 24 until normal operation at 12:05 PM PST on December 25.
detection: Engineers first saw rising ELB API errors and latency, and only later linked degraded load balancers to the missing state data.
fix: AWS paused scaling and other control plane workflows, restored a usable snapshot of the state data and merged in later changes before re-enabling APIs, then required per-incident change approval for production data access and planned automatic reconciliation of load balancer state.
summary: On Christmas Eve a maintenance process was mistakenly executed against production Elastic Load Balancing state data in US East, deleting part of it. Because the ELB control plane relied on that data, every scaling action or customer modification applied bad configuration to the affected load balancers, which then returned errors. A first restore attempt took hours and failed; a second method recovered a snapshot early on December 25. AWS removed persistent developer access to the data and tightened change management.

title: EBS volumes stuck after agent memory leak in one US-East zone
trigger: After a failed data collection server was replaced, the DNS change did not reach every internal resolver, so some EBS storage servers kept retrying the dead host and their reporting agent slowly leaked memory.
impact: EBS volumes in one of five US-East Availability Zones degraded or got stuck from 10:00AM PDT until about 4:15PM, knocking out Single-AZ RDS databases until about 6:35PM and some ELB load balancers until 9:50PM, while aggressive API throttling hit many customers from 12:06PM to 2:33PM PDT.
detection: Volumes began degrading at 10:00AM PDT; aggregate memory monitoring on the EBS servers had not alarmed on the leak, and the root cause was only identified at 3:10PM PDT.
fix: The team slowed the EBS failover rate and then freed the memory held by the misbehaving agent; follow-ups included a leak fix, per-process memory alarms and resource limits, reliable internal DNS propagation, retiring the aggressive throttling policy and reserving extra Elastic IP capacity for ELB.
summary: Amazon EBS in one US-East Availability Zone saw volumes stall when many storage servers ran out of memory at once. A latent leak in an operational data collection agent was triggered because an internal DNS update, made after replacing failed hardware, never fully propagated. Mass failover found too few healthy servers, so more volumes got stuck. Side effects included Single-AZ RDS outages, Multi-AZ RDS failover bugs, ELB recovery stalls from Elastic IP exhaustion, and overly strict EC2 API throttling on DescribeInstances-style calls.

title: Netflix rides out AWS US-East EBS degradation by evacuating a zone
trigger: An AWS service degradation involving EBS in one US-East Availability Zone surfaced at Netflix as network problems in that zone.
impact: From around 11am some Netflix customers had intermittent streaming problems, though most did not notice, and service was fully restored after a 20 minute zone evacuation.
detection: Engineers saw other AWS-hosted sites failing at 8:30am but no internal impact; customer issues began near 11am and an internal alert was opened at 11:15am, which the team says should have come sooner.
fix: Netflix stopped routing traffic to the bad zone and removed instances via Asgard while Cassandra routed around it, and planned to make Chaos Gorilla zone evacuation a one-click operation.
summary: When AWS suffered an EBS-related degradation in US-East, many popular sites went down for hours, while Netflix saw only intermittent customer errors. Symptoms first looked like a network fault, which slowed diagnosis. Once the problem was isolated to a single Availability Zone, Netflix used Asgard to drain traffic and instances from it in 20 minutes. Running every service across three zones, Cassandra with a replication factor of three spread across zones, and regular evacuation drills kept the impact small.

title: Misapplied DDoS rate limit knocks out Cloudflare's European traffic
trigger: While manually fending off a large DDoS that peaked above 65 Gbps, ops staff applied a new network rate limit meant for one customer that instead hit many customers, at a time when an upstream provider issue had already concentrated traffic in Europe.
impact: Around 16:36 GMT inbound and outbound traffic at Cloudflare's eight European data centers dropped almost to zero, with some spillover to North America and Asia Pacific, and some BGP announcements were disrupted; the total duration is not stated.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The team reverted the rate limit, after which routing rebalanced over the following hour, and built additional smoke tests to catch this kind of manual mitigation change before it reaches production.
summary: Cloudflare's European network briefly collapsed after a day spent mitigating a DDoS against one customer. An upstream provider problem had already pushed extra traffic into some European facilities, and when the attacker changed vectors around 16:30 GMT, operators deployed a rate limit that was applied far more broadly than intended. Traffic across the region fell off nearly entirely and some BGP route announcements were affected. Reverting the limit restored service, and new smoke tests now guard similar manual changes.

title: Partial deploy revives dead Power Peg code, losing $460M
trigger: A manual rollout of new SMARS order-router code for the NYSE Retail Liquidity Program missed one of eight servers, and a repurposed flag switched on long-dead Power Peg logic there.
impact: In about 45 minutes Knight sent millions of child orders, executing around 4 million trades in 154 stocks for over 397 million shares, built roughly $3.5B long and $3.15B short positions, and lost about $460M.
detection: SMARS sent 97 automated emails mentioning Power Peg before the open but they were not treated as alerts; abnormal volume was noticed by 9:31 AM, and there was no kill switch.
fix: Staff removed the new code from the seven updated servers, which made things worse by enabling Power Peg everywhere, before the system was finally halted; Knight then needed emergency capital and was acquired months later.
summary: Knight Capital's high-speed router SMARS was updated to support a new NYSE program by reusing a flag that once enabled Power Peg, test code unused for years whose fill tracking had been removed. One server never received the new build, so when trading opened it kept firing child orders without noticing parents were filled. With no written deploy procedure, no second reviewer and no kill switch, the firm took 45 minutes to stop it, and its rollback spread the fault to all eight servers.

title: Storm and failed generators knock out a US East-1 AZ
trigger: An electrical storm caused a voltage spike, and generators in one datacenter failed to stabilise and carry load, so UPS batteries drained and servers lost power at 8:04pm PDT.
impact: About 7% of EC2 instances and a similar share of EBS volumes in the Region lost power, region-wide launch and volume APIs failed for about an hour, and most instances returned between 11:15pm and just after midnight.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Staff manually started generators and UPS units, EBS volumes were checked before release, and follow-ups included generator repair, longer stabilisation waits, an automated control plane datastore failover and splitting the ELB control plane queue.
summary: On 29 June 2012 a severe storm in Northern Virginia disrupted utility power to one US East-1 Availability Zone. In one facility the generators never stabilised voltage, UPS batteries ran out, and servers went down. Beyond lost EC2 and EBS capacity, region-wide control planes stalled because the datastore failover needed manual steps, some RDS Multi-AZ failovers hit a bug, and an ELB scaling bug after power return flooded a shared queue, delaying traffic shifts for Elastic Load Balancers.

title: Hong Kong router misconfig pulls global traffic to an offline site
trigger: During maintenance of the offline Hong Kong data center, outbound routes covering Cloudflare's whole address range were entered on the inbound interface, so the Hong Kong router announced itself as the destination for all Cloudflare traffic and upstreams propagated it.
impact: Beginning at 20:19 GMT about 75% of traffic to Cloudflare's network was affected, with downtime of up to roughly 15 minutes depending on region; traffic from direct peers, about 25% of inbound, was spared.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Cloudflare announced corrected routes, and planned a verification layer that checks all routing changes before announcement plus upstream checks against propagating major routing changes without confirmation.
summary: While Cloudflare's Hong Kong facility was offline for upgrades, a network engineer optimizing its routing put the outbound routes, which describe the company's entire IP space, onto the inbound interface. The Hong Kong router then claimed all Cloudflare traffic, and the upstream provider relayed the BGP announcement onward, sending worldwide visitors to a dark data center. About three quarters of traffic failed for up to 15 minutes until corrected routes propagated. Direct peers were unaffected because they preferred Cloudflare's own routes.

title: Leap day certificate bug cascades across Azure compute
trigger: The Guest Agent inside VMs built a transfer certificate expiring one year later by bumping the year, producing the invalid date February 29, 2013, so it crashed.
impact: For about 34 hours Windows Azure Compute and dependent services such as Access Control Service, Service Bus and the SQL Azure Portal were disrupted, service management was disabled worldwide, and seven clusters lost VM networking in a secondary outage; customers received a 33% credit.
detection: Critical alarms on clusters being updated halted the rollout and alerted operations, and on-call developers pinpointed the bug at 6:38 PM PST.
fix: Microsoft disabled service management globally, shipped a fixed Guest Agent, redeployed a corrected host agent package to the seven clusters, and committed to better date testing, separating agent faults from hardware faults, and finer-grained management controls.
summary: On February 29, 2012 the Azure Guest Agent failed to generate a certificate because adding one year yielded a date that does not exist. Host agents timed out waiting for it, and after three failures the Fabric Controller wrongly marked servers as having hardware faults. Service healing moved VMs to new hosts where the same bug fired, spreading the failure. A rushed rollback package then cut network access to every VM in seven clusters. Azure Storage and SQL Azure were unaffected.

title: Primary DNS database deleted during rollout of new DNS system
trigger: While debugging a minor data-push problem during a rollout of new instant-propagation DNS infrastructure, the primary DNS database was deleted and the empty state spread to the 10 of 14 data centers already upgraded.
impact: Customer sites resolving through those 10 data centers got invalid DNS answers from about 07:30 GMT, with most back by 8:00 GMT as resolver caches cleared, and two data centers serving bad results until about 8:10 GMT, hitting some visitors in Europe and Asia longer.
detection: Engineers recognized the problem within about 5 minutes; the post does not say what signal alerted them.
fix: The database was restored from backup and re-pushed, two data centers that failed to apply the corrected data were pulled from rotation, stray TLD entries were removed, and additional safeguards were added.
summary: During a late-night push of new Cloudflare DNS infrastructure designed to propagate record changes almost instantly, the primary DNS database was deleted while the team chased a small replication glitch. The fast pipeline promptly distributed the bad state, so authoritative DNS answers from 10 data centers became invalid and customer websites went offline. Restoring the backup took minutes, but ISP resolver caching stretched the outage, two data centers choked on the large correction, and fewer locations weakened DDoS mitigation, producing a small number of 500 errors.

title: Multicast rsync test for Solr indexes overloads core switches
trigger: An engineer tried distributing Solr search indexes to replicas in production with mrsync, a multicast UDP rsync tool that had worked well in development.
impact: The entire Etsy site was unreachable for several minutes.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Multicast rsync was dropped, and Etsy instead built BitTorrent-based index replication into Solr using a modified ttorrent library.
summary: Etsy's Solr HTTP replication was too slow for growing indexes, so the team experimented with mrsync, which sends index files over multicast UDP. In production the multicast flood saturated the CPU on Etsy's core network switches and took the whole site offline for several minutes. The episode pushed the team toward peer-to-peer replication: they integrated BitTorrent into Solr, cutting replication of the largest index from 60 minutes to 6 minutes.

title: Expired front-end certificate blocks new PageKite tunnel connections
trigger: The SSL certificate for frontends.b5p.us, which front-end relays use to prove their identity to PageKite clients, expired at 15:27 GMT.
impact: For about 8.5 hours most users on the default secure setup could not start new kites, getting a could-not-connect-to-front-end error, and Icelandic users had about 30 minutes of total unavailability after a troubleshooting restart.
detection: The team learned of the problem around 22:30 GMT when notified, hours after the expiry.
fix: A freshly signed certificate was deployed to all front-ends by 23:00 with automated scripts; follow-ups were fewer certificates overall plus monitoring of certificate expiry and end-to-end availability.
summary: The localhost tunneling service PageKite suffered a holiday-season outage when the certificate on its front-end relays lapsed. The team had been renewing certificates but missed that this one expired a few days before the rest. Existing tunnels kept working, but new connections in secure mode failed with a front-end connection error until a new certificate from StartCom was rolled out; users could temporarily run with --nossl. PageKite blamed human error and committed to consolidating certificates and adding expiry and availability monitoring.

title: EU West transformer and generator failure takes down an AZ
trigger: A utility 110kV transformer failed, and a PLC that should have brought backup generators online did not finish, likely due to a detected ground fault, so UPS batteries drained.
impact: Nearly all EC2 instances and 58% of EBS volumes in one EU West Availability Zone lost power from 10:41 AM PDT on 7 August, launch APIs degraded region-wide, and EBS recovery snapshots ran until 10 August.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem for the power event; a separate snapshot deletion bug was noticed when a customer snapshot returned an error.
fix: Power and networking were restored manually and EBS volumes recovered via re-mirroring and recovery snapshots, with follow-ups for PLC redundancy, per-AZ control plane isolation, in-place EBS recovery and safer snapshot cleanup.
summary: In the AWS EU West (Dublin) Region, a utility transformer failure cut power to most of one Availability Zone, and a PLC failed to start the backup generators. EC2 instances and many EBS volumes went dark, network gear lost power, and EC2 management servers kept queuing RunInstances calls for the dead zone until launches across the region slowed. EBS re-mirroring exhausted spare capacity, forcing slow snapshot-based recovery. An unrelated EBS cleanup bug had also deleted blocks still referenced by customer snapshots.

title: Botched network change triggers EBS re-mirroring storm in US East
trigger: During a capacity upgrade in one US East Availability Zone, primary traffic was wrongly shifted onto the low-capacity backup EBS network, cutting many storage nodes off from both networks.
impact: Roughly 13% of EBS volumes in the zone became stuck at peak, up to 45% of single-AZ RDS instances lost I/O, other zones saw API errors and launch failures for about 11 hours, and full recovery took until April 24 with 0.07% of volumes unrecoverable in a consistent state.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem beyond noting that alarms were too coarse to separate a specific control plane API failure from the general EBS errors.
fix: AWS fenced off the degraded cluster from the control plane, tuned timeouts and throttled node chatter, added fresh capacity and restored leftover volumes from snapshots, then committed to automating network changes, larger capacity buffers, better backoff and a fix for an EBS node race condition.
summary: An incorrect traffic shift during a network upgrade isolated a large set of EBS storage nodes in one US East Availability Zone. When connectivity returned, the nodes all hunted for free space to re-mirror their data at once, exhausting cluster capacity and leaving volumes stuck. Long-running create-volume calls exhausted threads in the regional EBS control plane, so API errors spread to other zones, and a race condition crashed more nodes. EC2 and RDS customers saw hung disks and failed launches for days.

title: Overloaded MongoDB check-in shard takes Foursquare down for 11 hours
trigger: One check-in database shard received a disproportionate share of writes, and adding a new shard to relieve it caused the whole site to go down.
impact: Foursquare was down for about 11 hours, though no data was lost.
detection: Around 11:00am EST the team noticed one shard performing poorly under uneven write load.
fix: Engineers re-indexed the shard to fix fragmentation and memory use, bringing the site back at 11:30 after testing, then added shards, worked with the MongoDB makers, and planned graceful degradation and better status communication.
summary: Foursquare stores user check-in history across MongoDB shards partitioned by user ID. One shard became overloaded, and attempts to rebalance failed; introducing a new shard unexpectedly took the entire site offline, while moving data freed less space than expected due to fragmentation. After hours of failed migration and restart attempts, a re-index of the shard resolved the memory and fragmentation problems. Foursquare added shards, began work with MongoDB on the issue, and launched a status blog plus a clearer error page.

title: Config auto-repair feedback loop overwhelms Facebook database cluster
trigger: An update to a configuration value's persistent copy was read as invalid, so every client tried to repair it by querying a database cluster.
impact: For about 2.5 hours many users found Facebook down or could not reach it, its worst outage in over four years at the time.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Facebook stopped all traffic to the database cluster by taking the site offline, let the databases recover and fixed the root cause, then turned off the automatic config verification system pending a redesign.
summary: On 23 September 2010 Facebook was unavailable for about 2.5 hours. An automated system that replaced invalid cached configuration values with the persistent copy misfired when the persistent value itself was considered invalid. Every client queried the same database cluster, sending hundreds of thousands of queries per second, and each failed query was treated as another invalid value, deleting cache keys and generating more load. The loop persisted after the bad value was fixed, so Facebook shut off site traffic to let the databases recover.

title: Bad DNS config in new EU datacenter cuts off Blogger in Europe
trigger: A DNS configuration problem tied to a newly added European datacenter pointed blogger.com and *.blogspot.com at an invalid IP address.
impact: Users across Europe could not reach Blogger or any blogspot.com blog for roughly 10 hours starting around 2:30am PDT.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The DNS setting was corrected; Blogger added safeguards in its DNS management system to block that kind of change, earlier paging on DNS failures, and proactive DNS verification during big system changes.
summary: On a Saturday in late 2009, European visitors to Blogger and blogspot.com hosted blogs were unable to connect for about 10 hours. A misconfiguration in DNS associated with a new datacenter in Europe caused lookups for blogger.com and *.blogspot.com to return an unusable IP address. Google's Blogger team responded by adding validation checks to its DNS management tooling, tightening automated monitoring so on-call engineers get paged sooner for DNS faults, and having systems engineers verify DNS during major changes.

title: Every search result flagged as harmful after bad blocklist entry
trigger: A routine update to the list of malware-hosting sites included a lone slash as a URL entry, which matched every URL on the web.
impact: For roughly 40 minutes per user, between about 6:27 and 7:25 a.m. PST, every Google Search result carried a malware warning, and site owners saw their pages wrongly labelled.
detection: The on-call site reliability team spotted the problem quickly; the post gives no further detail on how.
fix: SREs reverted the list file, and Google committed to adding stronger validation checks on such files before release.
summary: Google Search maintains a blocklist of sites known to install malware, built with StopBadware criteria, and shows a This site may harm your computer warning on matching results. A periodic list update was checked in with the path / as an entry, and because / matches every URL, the warning appeared on every single search result. The update rolled out in a staggered way, so each user saw it for about 40 minutes until SREs reverted the file. Google promised more robust file checks.

title: Single-bit corruption in S3 gossip messages halts requests
trigger: A handful of internal state messages carried a one-bit corruption that left them readable but wrong, and with no checksum on that state the bad data propagated through the S3 gossip protocol.
impact: Amazon S3 in every datacenter, US and EU, returned mostly errors from 8:40am PDT; the EU recovered by 3:10pm and US request and error rates were normal again by 4:58pm, roughly eight hours later.
detection: Alarms fired as error rates climbed across all S3 datacenters at 8:40am PDT.
fix: Engineers stopped all server-to-server traffic, shut down request processing, wiped system state and restarted; follow-ups added checksums on state messages, reduced gossip about failed servers, faster full-state restore and alarms on gossip rates.
summary: On a Sunday morning Amazon S3 began failing nearly all requests worldwide. Servers were spending almost all their time exchanging gossip about cluster state, and many crashed while doing so. The root cause was a single flipped bit in a few internal messages: unlike customer objects, which are MD5-protected, this state data had no checksum, so the corruption spread silently. Reducing load did not help; AWS had to halt inter-server communication, clear state and restart, restoring the EU first and the US by late afternoon.

title: Foreign key migration queues behind long read and stalls API
trigger: A planned schema migration renamed unused invoicing tables and recreated their foreign keys, which needed an AccessExclusive lock on a heavily used parent table.
impact: The GoCardless API stopped serving requests for about 15 seconds and clients timed out; no request or merchant counts are given.
detection: Alerts on API request timeouts fired as soon as the migration started.
fix: The migration finished on its own after about 15 seconds; recommended follow-ups include removing long-running queries, enabling log_lock_waits and log_min_duration_statement, and setting lock_timeout in migrations so they abort instead of blocking traffic.
summary: A schema change that should have been instant caused a short GoCardless API outage. Re-adding a foreign key in Postgres takes an exclusive lock on the referenced table as well, even with NOT VALID. The ALTER TABLE waited behind a long-running read on that busy table, and every subsequent query lined up behind the pending lock, so API calls hung. Replaying the migration on a backup ran in milliseconds, showing lock contention rather than work was the problem. The post gives late January but no year.
